title: Start solving: a practical introduction
summary: Find the right pages, reproduce known results, and turn an idea into a test someone else can repeat.
text:
Liber Primus combines visible artwork, rune text, numbers, and hidden file content. Learn how these layers differ before treating them as one cipher. A title image can have no runic paragraph and still carry a signed OutGuess message.

1. Know the collection
The first release contains 17 images, including two title pages. The second release contains 58. In the archived source snapshot, LP1 has known readings and LP2 has readings for 56 and 57; LP2 pages 00–55 remain unsolved. This is dated documented knowledge, not live proof that nobody has solved anything else.
Use IDs such as LP2-31. “Page 31” without a release or archive name is ambiguous. The numbering cross-reference maps release IDs to archive filenames.

The illustrated cover with compasses comes from an earlier puzzle stage and has its own entry. It is different from LP1-00, the plain title page, and does not change the release numbering.

[Image: The warning page used for the first reading exercise]
LP1-01: start here. Its known Atbash reading makes a short, checkable first exercise.
[Image: LP2-31, an unsolved page used in the statistics guide]
LP2-31: a later investigation. Its recorded measurements describe the text; they do not supply a decryption.

2. Reproduce one short reading
Open the warning in the reader. Compare the original image with its runes, then follow the complete warning reading and its Atbash explanation. Use the 29-symbol alphabet, not English A–Z. Count a multi-letter rune as one symbol.

Start in the browser

No installation is needed for this first check. Atbash reverses the 29-rune alphabet, so an input index c becomes 28 − c. The warning starts with these three runes:

	Input rune	Index	28 − index	Label
	ᚱ	4	24	A
	ᛝ	21	7	W
	ᚱ	4	24	A

Compare the shapes with the original warning image and the alphabet chart. The labels begin A WA…: the opening article and the start of WARNNG. Spaces and punctuation are not rune indices, so they are not transformed by the subtraction.

Continue with the worked Atbash table, or download the complete warning trace (CSV) to inspect every rune. The trace explanation describes its columns and source record. Checking three symbols confirms those three calculations; it does not yet verify the entire page.

Then verify the complete reading with Python

python scripts/verify_bundle.py REFERENCE-DATA-CONTENTS.json
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py --check-all
Download and extract the reference-data ZIP, then run these commands from the extracted folder with Python 3. Keep the folders together: the script reads the included text and parameter files. After the file check, the warning command prints its literal reading; --check-all checks all 17 known runic-page outputs. All three commands run locally with the Python standard library and make no AI requests. A full repository checkout also works.

The first command checks the extracted files against the bundle’s own manifest and should report 0 problems. It does not authenticate the manifest. If it reports missing or changed files, follow the setup check before interpreting a decoding result.

What success looks like

The warning output begins A-WARNNG.BELIEUE-NOTHNG-FROM-. Those spellings are expected literal rune labels, not evidence that the script failed. The complete control check prints:

PASS: 17 literal page readings match the published controls exactly.

This confirms that the supplied recipes reproduce the stored known outputs. It does not independently authenticate the source files or validate a proposed solution to an unsolved page. Use the download catalogue for file hashes and the transliteration guide for the difference between literal labels and contextual English.


Optional second check: one row of the number grid
Open LP1-05 and find the five-by-five grid below the text. Its first row mixes four printed numbers with one rune word. In the known reading that word is labeled SHADOWS.
Leave the printed entries 272, 138, 131 and 151 unchanged.
Use the worked rune-cell table to check the word’s seven rune values. Their sum is 341.
Add the row: 272 + 138 + 341 + 131 + 151 = 1033.
This verifies one row, not the whole square. The full explanation shows all five rows, five columns and two main diagonals. If you have Python, python scripts/check_number_examples.py reproduces those checks from the included page and alphabet records.
The important distinction is the input: the printed decimal numbers stay as numbers, while rune words are replaced by additive prime values. Do not apply a prime-index lookup to every entry or replace the words with ordinary English spelling. Those would be different procedures.
New to the terminal? Running the reproduction scripts walks through setup, expected results, trace columns, and common errors.
3. Learn the other layers
Rune indices and prime values: cipher arithmetic versus prime sums.
Vigenère: keys, direction, and continuity across pages.
The cover payload chain: OutGuess, hexadecimal, XOR, signatures, and transposition.
Spelling and prime sums: a reproducible numerical property versus an explanation of a spelling’s purpose.

For the ideas behind the decoded passages, follow the philosophy reading route, then compare the William Blake parallel. These guides distinguish the manuscript words, interpretation, and possible outside sources.

Before choosing a large test, read search space and bounds: count the choices, decide what would count as success, and distinguish a completed search from an interrupted one.

4. Make an idea testable
Choose a page, a region, a transformation, and a success criterion. “Try primes” is too broad. “Subtract consecutive prime-minus-one values modulo 29 from LP2-31, starting at the first rune, advancing the prime sequence only for runes, continuing across punctuation without resetting, and skipping no runes” specifies a candidate transformation. You still need an exact acceptance rule before calling it a hypothesis test. It does not establish that this is the correct method.
Check Have we tried it? for the technique and scope. Browse the published experiment families or describe a technique to find related records. Open the individual record and compare its inputs, boundary rules, parameters and exclusions with your proposal. An empty result means no published match here, not that an idea is new. Follow the reproducibility guide.

Follow one completed experiment

The first-experiment walkthrough takes you through the published trigram-repeat test: read its chart, compare its scope with a proposed idea, inspect the downloaded counts, and reproduce the calculation. It also explains an important distinction: a script can pass its reproduction check even when the experiment does not support the tested hypothesis.

Find the family behind your idea

If you do not know a cipher's name, start with what your idea does. The solving-method map groups approaches and links their narrower experiments. Its guides also cover methods with no linked test; having a guide does not mean that a method has been tried on your page.

	Your idea changes…	Start here	First choice to make explicit
	The order of existing runes	Reading routes or page order	Which objects move, and whether every symbol is used once.
	The value of each rune	Substitution or numerical keystreams	Whether the rule is fixed or changes with position.
	Which symbols survive	Positional extraction or null removal	The selection rule and treatment of skipped positions.
	How marks become symbols	Alternative notation	Measurements, grouping and orientation before assigning letters.
	How numbers are interpreted	Number representations or arithmetic expressions	The base, allowed operations and maximum search size.
	The proposed plaintext	Cribs or language comparisons	The cipher assumptions under which the comparison is meaningful.

Combining two rows does not remove their choices. For example, “read a spiral, then subtract primes” needs both a complete route and a complete numerical schedule. Keep the operation order fixed and record every added offset, reversal, reset or spelling option.

Compare the tested question, not just its title

Read the scope. Compare source files, page regions, symbol representation and boundaries. Two tests on the same page can use different inputs.
Compare the choices. Check the actual keys, offsets, routes and exceptions. A family label does not mean every variant was searched.
Read the acceptance rule. An exact opening-crib test answers whether those openings match under its parameters. It is not a search for every possible readable continuation.
Identify the next distinct question. If your idea is outside those bounds, state exactly what changes. If it is inside them, reproduce the record before duplicating its search.

Use the experiment-organization guide to decide whether that next question belongs as a variant of an existing test. A controlled extension is useful; a new title for the same calculation does not add coverage.

Choose one first investigation

You do not need to learn every technique at once. Choose a route that produces a small result someone else can inspect.

	If you want to…	Start with	Keep as your result

	Read and interpret	Compare the warning and later instructions	Exact passages, their locations, and your interpretation stated separately

	Inspect artwork	Compare the insect drawings	Page IDs, visible similarities and differences, and any named comparison source

	Check arithmetic	Reproduce LP1-05’s mixed-grid conversion	The original cells, rune-value substitutions, and all twelve line sums

	Measure a text	Reproduce LP2-31’s IoC	The input hash, rune counts, exact fraction, and a statement of what it cannot establish

	Study a decoding	Trace the Welcome’s repeating key	A few input/output steps, the key position, and the treatment of recorded exceptions


Before expanding a numerical search, check what your operation preserves. For example, whole-stream IoC cannot choose between rearrangements of the same symbols. For literary or visual work, a well-supported comparison is useful even when it supplies no cipher key.

A first observation using only your phone

Open LP2-49 in the reader. Beneath the three runic rows, find the third row of the letter-and-number grid. Count grid rows from one and columns from left to right. This row reads:

21 3M 0F 0X 1g 2H 0x 1R

[Image: Third grid row of LP2-49, including uppercase 0X in column four and lowercase 0x in column seven.]
Detail from the original JPEG, region [600, 1560, 1200, 160]. Download the complete original.

Compare column 4, 0X, with column 7, 0x. The initial character is zero in the archived transcription; the second character differs in case.
Write the observation with its location: “LP2-49, grid row 3: column 4 is transcribed as 0X; column 7 as 0x.”
Keep a proposed explanation separate. This difference does not yet tell you whether the entries encode letters, coordinates, or numbers.

You have now made a small claim another reader can check. The grid transcription guide explains ambiguous characters and leading zeroes; its coordinate exports let you check the same positions in structured data. If you disagree with a glyph, preserve the original transcription and document the proposed correction with the image location.

Find the page behind a quotation

Suppose you remember the phrase “circumference practices” and want to cite it. A complete reading can cover several sheets, so finding the section is only the first step.


Search for "circumference practices", including the quotation marks. LP1-10 is the literal-reading match. Other sheets can appear because their records include the same complete section text.

Open LP1-10’s known reading. The word crosses its first two literal lines: CIRCU/ then MFERENCE. Compare the page’s original image when checking the underlying runes.

Keep the location with your note: “LP1-10, literal reading, lines 1–2; word joined across the line break.” A statement about what the circumference means is your interpretation and needs its own explanation.


With Python, repeat the lookup using python scripts/reading_concordance.py "circumference practices" --literal. Add --json to retain the exact excerpt, character offsets, and page-record checksum. The concordance guide explains those fields and why character positions are not rune indices. This exercise works with a known reading; it does not search for English words inside unsolved ciphertext.

Ready to contribute
You should be able to identify an exact image, distinguish raw from corrected transcription, reproduce a known reading, and explain what would count against your hypothesis. You do not need to understand every cipher before inspecting a well-defined detail.
For a worked descriptive analysis, use the index-of-coincidence baseline: exact rune counts, downloadable results, reproduction commands and the limits of frequency evidence.
Sources and verification
Pinned historical walkthrough. Recipes reproduce published controls; they are not new solutions. Local computational verification: 19 October 2026.

title: Cicada 3301: the puzzles before and beyond Liber Primus
summary: Follow the 2012, 2013 and 2014 routes, with archival sources, reproduced steps and the gaps between them.
text:
Liber Primus belongs to the 2014 Cicada puzzle. The earlier puzzles explain where several familiar tools and references entered the story. Follow the evidence from one artifact to the next: a hidden payload, a decoded address, a book lookup or a verified message. An account of a historical solution and a fresh reproduction are different kinds of evidence.

Start with the first image: an illustrated, reproducible walkthrough.

Follow a solution yourself

Each link below opens a worked step with preserved inputs and a downloadable replay. These checks reproduce particular transformations; they do not certify the entire historical chain.

	Stage	What you can reproduce	Detail that matters

	2012 opening JPEG	Appended message, ASCII shift and extracted payload	The original JPEG and duck decoy have different roles.

	2012 Reddit / Mabinogion	Title decoding and all 76 book-code lookups	Duplicate posts affect the ordering. Compare both selection rules.

	2012 countdown and coordinates	Two distinct JPEG payloads and 12 coordinate pairs	Similar artwork does not identify the carrier file.

	2012 Britannica	Every character lookup against the preserved source	The heading is line zero; spaces count.

	2012 Blake second chance	All 22 lookups with numbered working lines	Count spaces and punctuation, and preserve the plate’s line breaks.

	2013 Liber AL	44 lookups and two literal digits	Use numbered verses; remove spaces but retain punctuation.

	2013 Twitter to Gematria	988 offset records, audio XOR and OutGuess payload	Sort the hex offsets before reassembly; the XOR uses only the audio prefix.

	2014 Emerson	The historical book-cipher control	Use the declared paragraph, sentence, word and letter rules.



2012: from one JPEG to a distributed puzzle

The first image invited readers to find a hidden message. The contemporary solver account records appended text leading through an ASCII shift to a duck image. The duck’s wording suggested OutGuess; extraction from the original JPEG supplied a subreddit and book-code coordinates. The subreddit text then had to be decoded and ordered before the coordinates could be applied.

The telephone-stage instruction directed solvers back to three primes associated with the original image: 3301 and its dimensions, 509 × 503. Their product is 845145127, used as the historical domain name. The subsequent countdown led to geographic coordinates and physical posters. The community timeline records the poster stage; the artifact archive preserves the later Britannica and Agrippa book-code branches.

For the details most likely to prevent a successful replay, start with post ordering and Mabinogion counting. The Britannica branch already has a complete local lookup trace. The Blake second-chance route uses another text layout and should not be merged into the original opening sequence.

2013: a book code, a disk image and data reconstruction

The next opening image carried a book riddle and coordinates pointing to Liber AL vel Legis. The chapter-and-verse counting guide explains the published rules and their current replay status. The reported output led to a disk image.

The disk-image inventory records audio, data files and a boot filesystem. Our Twitter-to-Gematria replay sorts 988 offset-tagged hex records into a 64,167-byte stream, XORs it with the same number of bytes from 761.mp3, and checks the resulting JPEG and hidden payload against the pinned archive. The archival account provides the source trail; our replay does not reconstruct the live 2013 feed.

The archived Instar Emergence audio connects to material discussed in the later manuscript. Our prime-sum guide documents the parable metadata connection. That cross-year link is distinct from claiming the audio decrypts an unsolved page.

2014: the route into Liber Primus

The archived opening uses an image payload and a book code for Emerson’s Self-Reliance. Our Emerson guide and reproduction record expose the exact source and all lookups. A stage-organized contemporary repository preserves later work on RSA, matrices, Vigenère, transposition and another book-code step. Its historical “unsolved” labels describe that archive’s state, not an automatic current verdict.

For the manuscript itself, use the release and numbering guide, known readings, and original-page reader. The later-message guide continues beyond the 2014 releases.

How this history will be documented

This is a route into the historical material, not yet a complete replay of every stage. Each detailed walkthrough needs the original artifact, the clue that motivated the next operation, its exact transformation and output, and a statement of what was freshly checked. Preserve branches and failed or unavailable historical services instead of drawing a falsely seamless chain.

The first JPEG’s byte-level trail and the subreddit’s ordered post inventory have downloadable replays. The Liber AL coordinates have a complete archived-text replay. Blake’s second-chance code has a complete text-file replay and an illustrated line-layout comparison; fine punctuation in the historical image remains uncertified. The 2013 Twitter-to-Gematria byte chain has also been replayed, while other later multi-file stages remain. Historical phone numbers and onion addresses belong in records as outputs; reproducing an old lookup does not require contacting whoever might control them today.

title: Solving methods: a map of families and variants
summary: Browse overlapping method and diagnostic families, then narrow an idea to a reproducible test.
text:
Start with the kind of operation an idea proposes, then narrow it to a specific rule and test. This map includes decoding methods, ways to search for keys, and diagnostic checks. They overlap: a proposal can combine a route, a numerical key and a reset rule. Combining families adds choices that must be counted.

A family page is not a completed experiment. Open its guide to understand the method, or expand its linked records to compare the exact questions tested. The records cover only their stated inputs, variants and bounds. No linked record means a gap in this map, not an untouched or promising approach.

What the record types mean: distinguish bounded solving tests from measurements, controls, audits and reproductions.

Symbol substitutions

Fixed alphabet substitutions
Replace each rune consistently with one other symbol.

Related records (1)
Compare these questions and exclusions with your proposal. A linked result does not cover every variant of this family.

LP2-00–55: fixed alphabet transforms against the warning opening
Record type: Bounded solving test. Applies a fixed decoding, extraction or payload-retrieval rule to declared unsolved material, or excludes a specific direct-generation rule. Its result covers only those bounds.
Question tested: Do shifts, alphabet reversal, or whole-stream reversal recover the first 12 decoded warning runes at the start of an archived LP2-00–55 page?
Outside this test: Other openings or positions, heading removal, regional or line-wise reversal, arbitrary substitution alphabets, other affine multipliers, Vigenère, corrections and language scoring.



Homophonic and many-to-one substitutions
Allow several ciphertext symbols to represent the same plaintext symbol.

No experiment linked yet. The guide documents the approach; it is not a result.


Repeating-key and polyalphabetic ciphers
Change the substitution according to position in a repeated key.

Related records (1)
Compare these questions and exclusions with your proposal. A linked result does not cover every variant of this family.

LP2-00–55: two known Vigenère keys and nine openings
Record type: Bounded solving test. Applies a fixed decoding, extraction or payload-retrieval rule to declared unsolved material, or excludes a specific direct-generation rule. Its result covers only those bounds.
Question tested: Do either of the two known Vigenere keys recover a 12-rune known-reading opening at the start of an LP2-00–55 page under uninterrupted repeating-key decoding?
Outside this test: Other keys, interruption placement, noninitial positions, heading removal, cross-page carry, alternative alphabets, transposition and language scoring.



Fractionation and coordinate alphabets
Split symbols into coordinates, rearrange the components, then regroup.

No experiment linked yet. The guide documents the approach; it is not a result.


Block and matrix transformations
Transform groups of runes together instead of treating each position independently.

No experiment linked yet. The guide documents the approach; it is not a result.


Codebooks and mixed letter-word systems
Map defined groups to words, syllables or phrases under a consistent dictionary.

No experiment linked yet. The guide documents the approach; it is not a result.



Keys, sequences and state

Arithmetic keystreams
Generate shifts from a declared numerical sequence.

Question tested: Does uninterrupted prime-minus-one arithmetic recover any of nine fixed 12-rune openings at the start of an LP2-00–55 page?
Outside this test: Other beginnings, offsets above 28, interruptions, heading removal, reversed input, word or row resets, cross-page carry, other numerical schedules and language scoring.

Outside this test: Unknown plaintext or keystream mixing, degree above eight, extra output maps, skipped clock positions, internal resets, alternative transcriptions and LP2-56–57.



Autokey and ciphertext feedback
Use earlier plaintext or ciphertext to update later decoding state.

Related records (5)
Compare these questions and exclusions with your proposal. A linked result does not cover every variant of this family.

Ciphertext symbols and differences around LP2 doublets
Record type: Manuscript measurement. Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule.
Question tested: Do doublet symbols or their neighboring ciphertext differences show extra local ordering beyond the observed zero mask and each page difference inventory?
Outside this test: Plaintext recovery, key inference, probability of the 86-event zero mask, independent full image transcription, English context scoring and post-selection significance.

Nonzero difference uniformity and order under EA-stalling keys
Record type: Manuscript measurement. Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule.
Question tested: Conditional on the 86 zero differences, do the remaining LP2-00--55 differences match the uniform and lag-one independence predictions of one independently uniform nonzero-key running-sum model?
Outside this test: Plaintext or key recovery, structured and nonuniform keys, cross-page transitions, other lags, alternate rune mappings, image transcription and selection-adjusted inference.

Solved GP EA frequency versus unsolved LP2 doublets
Record type: Control. Checks a search, decoder or scorer using synthetic inputs or reference text; it does not identify the cipher of an unsolved page.
Question tested: Is the observed LP2 doublet rate compatible with the EA frequency in known decoded GP text under one proposed nonzero-key running-sum equation?
Outside this test: Plaintext recovery, key inference, independent full image transcription, external English-corpus transfer, other equations and corrected post-selection significance.

LP2-54–55: reset ciphertext state at selected F runes
Record type: Manuscript measurement. Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule.
Question tested: Does the reset interruption rule produce an unusually high maximum periodic IoC across the declared 64 masks and periods 2–30?
Outside this test: Plaintext autokey; Other interruption symbols; Arbitrary primers or keys; Heading removal; Page-local state resets; Other period ranges; Language-score or plaintext claims; Significance of original exploratory search.

Record type: Source or input audit. Checks image provenance, extraction or input coverage against a declared reference; it does not establish a decryption.
Question tested: Do the seven published LP2 reviewed-text corrections change the joined-page rune-token sequence, word-length distribution, or whole-stream IoC under the site's published counting rule?
Outside this test: Unrecorded disputed marks; new photographic review; alternative word delimiters; punctuation-driven cipher resets; page-local tokenization; LP2-56–57; any claim that the entire transcription is correct.




What the record types mean
Bounded solving test
Applies a fixed decoding, extraction or payload-retrieval rule to declared unsolved material, or excludes a specific direct-generation rule. Its result covers only those bounds.
Manuscript measurement
Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule.
Control
Checks a search, decoder or scorer using synthetic inputs or reference text; it does not identify the cipher of an unsolved page.
Alphabet-wide analysis
Studies a declared mathematical mapping over the alphabet, rather than decoding an unsolved page.
Source or input audit
Checks image provenance, extraction or input coverage against a declared reference; it does not establish a decryption.
Historical reproduction
Replays a documented historical step with specified source material and conventions.
Method replay
Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading.
These describe the role of a record, not its outcome or confidence. A control linked to a method is not a test of that method on every unsolved page.

From a family to a test
For example, “try spirals” names a route family. A test must also fix the pages, grid dimensions, padding, starting cell, directions, any added substitution and the criterion for success. Changing one of these choices creates a variant; changing several may create a new experiment family.
Use Have we tried it? to inspect published scope. Related methods can be useful even when the exact variant is not covered. Download the family map.

title: 2012: telephone primes, countdown and coordinates
summary: Follow the prime product and compare two cicada JPEGs with independently extracted payloads.
text:
The Reddit book code supplied a telephone number. The next clue sent solvers back to the original JPEG, then onward to a website whose image changed between stages. This walkthrough separates the reported telephone instruction from the image extractions we can reproduce now.

From the telephone clue to a domain

The archived telephone account and recording describe an instruction to multiply three primes associated with final.jpg, naming 3301 as one. The original image is 509 pixels wide and 503 pixels high. Both dimensions are prime, so 509 × 503 × 3301 = 845145127. That number supplied the historical domain label 845145127.com.

The opening-image audit reads those dimensions from the preserved JPEG and checks primality and multiplication. A resized copy could destroy this clue. The telephone instruction is historical source evidence; this replay did not call the number or verify the recording independently.

Two files with the same-looking artwork

[Image: Countdown-stage JPEG: black cicada with spread wings on a white background.]
Countdown carrier: 20,858 bytes. Download preserved JPEG.

[Image: Locations-stage JPEG: a visually similar black cicada with spread wings.]
Locations carrier: 20,892 bytes. Download preserved JPEG.

These previews look alike, but the files have different hashes and different hidden messages. A fresh OutGuess extraction from each file exactly matched its corresponding archived payload. This does not claim that their decoded pixels are identical, or that the byte-length difference alone identifies the hidden content.

	Carrier	Extracted bytes	Message content
	Countdown	1,001	A return time: 17:00 UTC on 9 January 2012
	Locations	1,221	Twelve latitude/longitude pairs

The stage archive associates these with the countdown and subsequent location publication. It distinguishes the payload’s coordinate list from additional locations reported on the webpage. The count of twelve here applies only to these extracted bytes, not every reported poster location.

Preserve the coordinate notation

The payload is a PGP cleartext-signed message. Its final coordinate line starts - -33.90281, 151.18421. The first dash and following space are cleartext escaping; removing that prefix leaves a negative latitude. Removing both dashes would move the point into the northern hemisphere. This format handling does not itself verify the signature.

Another line separates the two numbers with whitespace rather than a comma. The coordinate ledger retains each original line alongside its parsed latitude and longitude, so the parsing decisions remain visible. It does not assign street addresses or claim that posters were independently confirmed at those points.

Repeat the extraction

Extract the reference-data ZIP. With Python 3, check the two carriers, stored payloads and coordinate parsing:

python scripts/replay_2012_countdown.py --check

To run OutGuess yourself, supply an installed executable. The script uses temporary output files and compares the newly extracted bytes with the preserved payloads:

python scripts/replay_2012_countdown.py --check --outguess /path/to/outguess

Script · Source hashes and extraction receipts · Countdown payload · Locations payload. Running without OutGuess checks stored evidence only. Signature verification and the subsequent QR-poster route remain separate work. Continue with the 2012 history and the later Britannica book-code branch.

title: The first Cicada image: JPEG bytes, the duck and OutGuess
summary: Reproduce the opening ASCII shift and hidden payload, inspect the original images, and follow the clue into the subreddit.
text:
The opening Cicada image contains two different leads. One is readable text appended to the JPEG file; the other is an OutGuess payload embedded in the image data. Following the first lead explains how solvers found the tool needed for the second.

[Image: Opening 3301 image: white text on black inviting readers to find a hidden message]
Archived opening JPEG, 509 × 503 pixels. Download original bytes. A screenshot preserves its appearance but need not preserve either hidden lead.

1. Inspect the file, not only the picture

JPEG images use an end marker, hexadecimal FF D9. In this archived file, text follows that marker. It invokes a Roman emperor and contains the encoded string lxxt>33m2mqkyv2gsq3q=w]O2ntk. Our byte-level report preserves the exact trailer and its offset. Finding appended text is different from extracting the OutGuess payload.

2. Shift character codes, including punctuation

Subtract four from every character’s ASCII value. The beginning lxxt>33 becomes http://: l → h, x → t, > → :, and 3 → /. A letters-only Caesar substitution would leave the punctuation wrong. The full output is the historical address http://i.imgur.com/m9sYK.jpg.

cipher = "lxxt>33m2mqkyv2gsq3q=w]O2ntk"
decoded = "".join(chr(ord(c) - 4) for c in cipher)
print(decoded)
assert "".join(chr(ord(c) + 4) for c in decoded) == cipher

The inverse check verifies the character transformation. It does not by itself show that a destination still exists or belongs to the original puzzle.

3. Read the duck as a clue to a tool

[Image: Archived duck decoy image whose wording hints at getting the message out]
The destination image redirects attention to OutGuess. Download archived duck image.

The contemporary solver account explains the wordplay linking the duck’s wording to OutGuess. The next operation is applied to the original opening JPEG. The duck is the instruction clue, not the carrier used for the reproduced extraction below.

4. Extract the second message from the original JPEG

outguess -r final.jpg extracted.txt

Our fresh run of the existing clean guarded OutGuess build returned successfully and extracted 535 bytes, byte-for-byte equal to the separately archived payload. Its diagnostic reported seed 228 and length 535. The receipt records the executable hash and output hash; the guarded-build record documents that build’s provenance and limitations.

The message points to the subreddit a2e7j6ic78h0j and supplies 76 line-and-character coordinates. Download the fresh extracted bytes or the archived text. Matching these bytes confirms this extraction; it does not solve the later book code.

5. The next stage needs an ordered text

The coordinates are pointers into a text, not a self-contained cipher. The Mabinogion counting guide explains the subsequent decoding, post-order and spacing issues. A complete replay must preserve the ordered post list and each character lookup. Substituting an arbitrary modern edition or a current Reddit display order can change the result.

The dimensions become relevant later, after the telephone-stage instruction asks for three associated primes. All three values are prime, and 509 × 503 × 3301 = 845145127. The audit checks that arithmetic, but it should not be presented as the rule that decoded the appended string. Continue with the telephone, countdown and coordinate walkthrough for that later step.

Reproduce these checks

Extract the reference-data ZIP with its folders intact. The standard-library command checks the preserved JPEG, trailer, dimensions, shift, prime arithmetic and stored payload comparison:

python scripts/replay_2012_opening.py --output opening-check.json

To perform a fresh extraction as well, supply your OutGuess executable. This is a separate dependency; it is not bundled with the reference data:

python scripts/replay_2012_opening.py --outguess /path/to/outguess --output opening-extraction.json

Each command requires a new output filename. Without --outguess, the report explicitly says no extraction ran. Audit script · Source manifest.

Source and verification boundaries

The images and comparison payload come from a pinned artifact archive. The contemporary account supplies the solving context. Their opening-post dates differ, so this page does not infer an exact first-post timestamp from the archive’s filename or heading. The checked facts concern the preserved bytes. No historical phone number or domain was contacted, and no signature verification or complete subreddit replay is claimed.

title: 2013: from Twitter offsets to Gematria Primus
summary: Reassemble 988 offset-tagged records, XOR the audio bytes, and extract the signed whitespace message.
text:
The 2013 puzzle reached Gematria Primus through a byte reconstruction, not through a rune cipher. An archived account of the Twitter stage preserves offset-tagged hex strings, the assembled byte stream, its JPEG result and the extracted hidden message. We rebuilt each transformation from those preserved files. This verifies the archived byte path; it does not reconstruct the entire live Twitter feed.

[Image: Six-stage reconstruction from 988 offset-tagged records through the XOR with 761.mp3, the Gematria JPEG, OutGuess and a whitespace-encoded message.]
The checked route. Each arrow is a transformation reproduced locally against a separately preserved output. Download diagram.


1. Put the offset records in byte order

The archived full.txt has 988 records of the form offset: hexadecimal bytes. The offset is hexadecimal too. The dump runs in descending order, so its first line is not the beginning of the file. Sort numerically by offset, decode each hex string and place its bytes at that offset. The rows cover offsets 0 through 64,166 with no gaps or overlaps. Their 64,167-byte concatenation matches the archived twitter.bin byte for byte.

This matters because joining lines in their printed order, treating offsets as decimal, or padding an apparent gap would change every later result. The replay report records the row count, offset coverage and source hashes; the source manifest pins the upstream Git revision and exact files.


2. XOR the stream with the start of the audio file

The archived disk-image inventory includes 761.mp3. For byte position i from 0 through 64,166, compute twitter.bin[i] XOR 761.mp3[i]. Only the first 64,167 bytes of the 4,010,732-byte MP3 are used. The output exactly matches the archive’s 64,167-byte gematria.jpg; its SHA-256 is d4736b09cfac03097efcb5c2f48ffc71f46700835fc09f7549283956580eb35d. A JPEG header check gives 598 × 842 pixels.

Download 761.mp3 · Download the exact reconstructed JPEG. These files are preserved as bytes, not recompressed for display.

[Image: The archived black-and-white Gematria Primus sheet, showing 29 runes with their letters and prime values and a cicada illustration below.]
The JPEG produced by the XOR. Its visible table gives the Gematria Primus alphabet: rune forms, letters and prime values. The next message is embedded in the JPEG data; it is not readable from this visible table.


3. Extract the concealed signed text

A fresh outguess -r gematria.jpg extracted.asc run recovered 1,443 bytes. They match the archive’s gematria.jpg.asc exactly. The run reported seed 17; the retest receipt records the executable, input and output hashes. OutGuess is a separate layer from the audio XOR. Our byte check does not verify the PGP signature attached to the extracted text.

Four nonempty rows of the payload contain only spaces and tabs. Reading a space as 0 and a tab as 1, then grouping every eight bits as an ASCII byte, yields:

Come to emiwp4muu2ktwknf.onion
We shall await you there.
Good luck.
3301

The four rows contain 240, 200, 80 and 32 bits respectively. The address is a historical output of this reconstruction, not a link to a service we contacted.


Reproduce and inspect the limits

Download the reference-data bundle, extract it, and run python scripts/replay_2013_twitter.py --check. It verifies the five source files against both SHA-256 and their pinned Git blob hashes, checks row coverage, reassembles the byte stream, repeats the XOR and decodes the whitespace message. Run python scripts/test_replay_2013_twitter.py for an independent byte-by-byte assembly and reverse-XOR check. If you have OutGuess, add --outguess path/to/outguess to the first command to re-extract and compare the hidden payload.

Replay script · Independent checker · Machine-readable result. The archive, rather than a captured live 2013 feed, is the input to these checks. The result shows how this copy of the Gematria table was produced and how its hidden message was read; it does not establish how the feed was populated in real time, authenticate the signed message, or imply a key for the unsolved Liber Primus pages.

title: Historical book codes: exact texts and counting rules
summary: Compare Mabinogion post order, Blake plate lines, Liber AL verses, Britannica and Emerson, with explicit replay status.
aliases: Marriage of Heaven and Hell code
text:
Finding the right title is only the beginning of reproducing a book code. The actual key is a particular representation of the text: its ordering, line breaks, punctuation and numbering. This guide compares the historical Cicada examples and identifies what has been replayed here versus what remains an archival instruction.

The coordinates do not all mean the same thing

	Puzzle	Lookup unit	Critical detail	Liberpedia status

	2012 Mabinogion	Decoded post line : character	Post order, repeated titles and spacing	76 lookups replayed on the pinned archive; historical provenance limits below

	2012 Britannica	Physical text line : character	CICADA heading is line zero; spaces count	All lookups replayed

	2012 Blake second chance	Plate-layout line : character	The Voice of the Devil layout	All 22 lookups replayed; fine image punctuation not certified

	2013 Liber AL	Chapter : numbered verse : character	Remove spaces/newlines; preserve punctuation	44 lookups and two literals replayed on the pinned working copy

	2014 Emerson	Paragraph : sentence : word : letter	Referenced PDF and disclosed extraction rules	Complete historical control


2012: the Mabinogion was also a Reddit ordering problem

The puzzle’s working text was decoded from post titles. Substituting a convenient edition of The Lady of the Fountain can change the lines before any character is selected. The contemporary ClevCode account describes using posting order, resetting the shift key on each line, and advancing it only on letters. It also records a spacing adjustment after periods to repair displaced book-code lookups. Preserve that adjustment as a separate transformation rather than quietly editing the source.

The archived reconstruction script sorts records by creation time, handles image posts separately and suppresses repeated titles. Its anomaly log records repeated and later posts. That is evidence that copying the current visible listing is not a sufficient reconstruction procedure. It does not establish which “fourth post” a reader encountered or justify an arbitrary reorder.

Reproduced: why the third and fourth lines change places

Our fresh replay ledger starts from 192 archived post records. It compares two declared selection rules: keep the earliest occurrence of each title across all authors, or first retain only posts whose author field is CageThrottleUs. Both sort by creation timestamp, with post ID as a tie-breaker, exclude JPEG/PNG image URLs, strip only outer title whitespace and suppress duplicate working titles. They retain 186 and 185 text lines respectively; the opening payload uses the first 76.

	Rule	Line 3	Line 4	Opening extraction

	Earliest copy, any author	o4e2a · anonymous copy	o4efi · named account	CAMT US…

	Named account only	o4efi · named account	o4eu9 · later named copy	CALL US…


The anonymous o4e2a and later named o4eu9 posts contain the same working title. Keeping the former inserts that text before o4efi. No manual line swap is needed for the named-account rule. Coordinates 3:5 and 4:20 select M and T in the first ordering, and L and L in the second. This explains this archive’s discrepancy without guessing which post a current reader called “number four.”

Decode and inspect every lookup

The title string a2e7j6ic78h0j7eiejd0120 gives the numeric key by interpreting digits normally and a–j as 10–19. Subtract successive key values modulo 26 from ASCII letters, repeat the key as needed, and restart it at each title. Punctuation does not advance the key. This replay uppercases letters but retains internal spacing and punctuation exactly as archived. Row and character coordinates both start at one.

Under the named-account rule, all 76 coordinates extract CALL US AT US TELE PHONE NUMBER TWO ONE FOUR THREE NINE OH NINE SIX OH EIGHT. The ledger retains every input title, timestamp, selection decision, decoded line and lookup. The comparison was exploratory, prompted by the ordering complaint; the author filter is not cryptographic authentication. It reproduces the archived text, not a freshly retrieved 2012 Reddit page.

No extra space was inserted after a period in this replay. The contemporary account’s spacing repair remains a separate historical observation: archive agreement does not prove its bytes are identical to that solver’s original copy. Preserve both facts rather than declaring either source universally correct.

Extract the reference-data ZIP, then run python scripts/replay_2012_subreddit.py --output subreddit-replay.json with Python 3. The script checks source hashes, inverse letter shifts and coordinate selection, and preserves both outcomes. Replay script · Archived post records · Source manifest. The opening coordinates come from the freshly extracted JPEG payload.

2012: Blake’s plate layout is part of the key

The second-chance clue points to The Marriage of Heaven and Hell. The community wiki account identifies the work and reports the resulting onion address. The artifact archive makes the practical dependency clearer: format The Voice of the Devil as lines on the referenced full plate. It supplies a formatted text file and lookup script.

A modern paragraph transcription can preserve every word yet fail the coordinates. The useful comparison is plate image → explicitly numbered lines → selected characters. The archive reports cginiziglyaobyph.onion; that is a historical output, not a link or a newly verified service. The independent trace below checks every lookup. The plate’s broad line layout has been compared visually, but its faint punctuation still limits a character-by-character image audit.

Reproduce the second-chance lookup

[Image: Historical reproduction of Blake’s Voice of the Devil plate, with text above intertwined figures.]
William Blake, The Voice of the Devil. The archived image referenced by the reconstruction, preserved without enhancement. Its 18 body-text lines supply the layout; the title is excluded. Download image.

Start line 1 at All Bibles, beneath the heading. Count lines and characters from one. Spaces, punctuation and the numbered-list labels all occupy positions. Preserve the split princi- / ples across lines 3 and 4. Do not reflow the text into paragraphs or remove the line-ending hyphen.

For coordinate 1:22, All Bibles or sacred  occupies the first 21 positions; the next character, c, begins the output. Coordinate 4:26 selects the period ending line 4. That period becomes the dot before the onion suffix. The downloadable trace shows the text before and after every selected character.

Show the 18 numbered working lines
	Line	Exact working text

	1	All Bibles or sacred codes, have been

	2	the causes of the following Errors.

	3	1. That Man has two real existing princi-

	4	ples Viz: a Body & a Soul.

	5	2. That Energy, call'd Evil, is alone from the

	6	Body, & that Reason, call'd Good, is alone from

	7	the Soul.

	8	3. That God will torment Man in Eternity

	9	for following his Energies.

	10	But the following Contraries to these are True.

	11	1. Man has no Body distinct from his Soul;

	12	for that call'd Body is a portion of Soul discern'd

	13	by the five Senses, the chief inlets of Soul in this

	14	age.

	15	2. Energy is the only life and is from the Body

	16	and Reason is the bound or outward circumference

	17	of Energy.

	18	3. Energy is Eternal Delight.


All 22 coordinates produce cginiziglyaobyph.onion. This is the historical output, not a currently verified destination. Download the full lookup trace, working text, source manifest and script. Extract the reference-data bundle, then run python scripts/replay_2012_blake.py --check.

The image comparison supports the line arrangement, including the split word; this small reproduction cannot certify every punctuation mark. The successful text-file replay is narrower evidence than proving a perfect transcription of the original plate. The script uses the previously extracted second-chance image payload; it does not repeat extraction or signature verification.


2013: numbered verses, not screen lines

The community walkthrough identifies Crowley’s Liber AL vel Legis and explains that spaces are omitted while punctuation matters. The archived reconstruction specifies chapter and numbered-verse parsing, removing the verse labels, spaces and newlines before character selection. Browser wrapping is not the verse boundary.

Retain two outputs: the raw extraction, containing dashes in URL separator positions, and the interpreted URL with those dashes replaced by slashes. They are different stages. A missing first character should trigger comparison of the verse label, leading text and indexing origin; it is not a reason to move every coordinate until a plausible URL appears. The independent replay below now checks every coordinate against a pinned archived working copy.

Reproduce all 46 output characters

The preserved chapter files contain 66, 79 and 75 numbered verses. Our script checks that verse numbers are consecutive, removes the numbering, then removes ASCII spaces and LF newlines. It preserves punctuation, capitalization and all other characters. Both verse and character positions begin at one. It also compares two parsing methods to ensure that a number inside a verse has not silently split the text.

For example, verse I:1 is Had! The manifestation of Nuit.. Its working text begins Had!The: positions 1 through 7 are H, a, d, !, T, h, e. Therefore I:1:6 selects h. Removing the exclamation mark would change that lookup. Keeping the verse label would also change the positions. This is why a similar-looking copy can lose the first letter of the address.

	Output position	Instruction	Selected character

	1	I:1:6	h

	2	I:2:15	t

	3	I:3:26	t

	4	I:5:4	p

	5	I:6:15	s

	6	I:10:26	:

	7	I:14:136	-

	8	I:15:68	-


The complete extraction is https:--www.dropbox.com-s-r7sgeb5dtmzj14s-3301. There are 44 chapter/verse/character lookups and two literal digits. Replacing the extracted dashes with slashes is a separate interpretation, recorded alongside the raw result. No historical service was contacted.

Download the full character-by-character trace, source manifest or replay script. The trace includes the original and processed verse for each lookup. Extract the reference-data bundle and run python scripts/replay_2013_liber_al.py --check; omit --check to print the report. Python 3 is sufficient.

This confirms the counting rule for these archived bytes. It does not identify the original solver’s exact edition, freshly extract the opening JPEG, or verify the archived message’s PGP signature. Those are separate provenance checks, not consequences of obtaining a readable address.


What every downloadable replay should contain

The exact source file, its hash and provenance, plus the source image or edition where applicable.
The unmodified coordinate list, with literal digits distinguished from lookups.
All preprocessing rules in order, including removed characters, retained punctuation and reset boundaries.
A row for every lookup: coordinate, selected source unit, character position and raw output.
The raw concatenated result and any later interpretation, each labeled separately.
A check that does not depend on silently repairing the answer.

These examples show why there is no single universal “Cicada counting rule.” Reproduce each mechanism before using it as a precedent for an unsolved page. Continue with book-cipher basics, reproduction records, or the Cicada puzzle history.

title: Running the reproduction scripts
summary: Set up the repository, verify a known reading, understand a rune-by-rune trace, and diagnose common errors.
text:
Reproducing a reading means starting with the manuscript's rune text, applying the documented cipher, and checking that you get the same result. It is a useful first step into solving: you can see how a method works before changing it or trying it on an unsolved page.

This walkthrough uses LP1-01, the warning. Its Atbash cipher reverses the rune alphabet, so you can follow the calculation by hand as well as run it in Python. By the end, you will have decoded the page, checked your result, and inspected the first two runes step by step.

For a published experiment, use the smaller ZIP linked in that experiment's Reproduce & download section. Its own START-HERE file names the verification command and prerequisites. Original image inputs, when needed, are downloaded separately. The first-experiment walkthrough demonstrates this route.

1. Download and open the files

Download the reference-data ZIP and extract it into an empty folder. Open that folder: you should see directories named scripts, text and data. Keep them together. The script supplies the instructions; the other folders supply the manuscript text, cipher settings and known readings it needs.

Open START-HERE.txt in the extracted folder for a task-by-task command list: decode a known reading, find a phrase, measure rune distributions, locate repeats, or replay an earlier puzzle chain. You can also read those instructions before downloading.

Open a terminal in this folder. A terminal is the window where you type the commands below. On Windows, you can use File Explorer's Open in Terminal command. If you navigate there with cd, put quotation marks around a folder path that contains spaces.

The reference-data ZIP is enough for this walkthrough. If you want to edit the site or work with draft experiments, get the complete repository instead using Code → Download ZIP. Readers who already use Git can clone it:

git clone https://github.com/jelliottdev/jelliottdev.github.io.git
cd jelliottdev.github.io

2. Check Python

You need Python 3. On Windows, try py --version; on macOS or Linux, try python3 --version. If neither command is available, install Python from the official Python downloads or your operating system’s package manager, then reopen your terminal. A command that prints a Python 2 version is not suitable.

	Terminal	Run the warning example
	Windows PowerShell	py scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning
	macOS / Linux	python3 scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning
	If python already selects Python 3	python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning

The wiki’s other recipes use python as shorthand. Substitute the command that worked on your machine; the script path and arguments stay the same. The calculation runs on your computer; it does not use the site's AI assistant.

3. Decode the warning and check the result

Check the extracted files first

Before decoding, check that the extracted files match the bundle’s recorded sizes and hashes. Run this from the folder containing scripts, text and data, using the Python command that worked above:

python scripts/verify_bundle.py REFERENCE-DATA-CONTENTS.json

A successful check reports a file count followed by 0 problems. The count can change as the wiki grows. Missing or changed files are listed with FAIL:, and the command exits unsuccessfully. The checker reads files without modifying them; files you add yourself are outside its manifest and are not checked.

This is a check against the included manifest, not independent proof of who created it. You can also compare the ZIP itself with the download catalogue. See bundle verification for the distinction between checking the archive and checking its contents.

If two copies disagree, use the transcription comparison workflow to locate exact-text and rune-sequence differences before deciding which input to use. A matching hash confirms a copy, not a manual reading of the image.

Run the known control

Run the warning command from the table above. In the examples that follow, python means whichever Python 3 command worked on your machine.

python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning

The script reads LP1-01, applies Atbash, and compares its output with the stored reading. It then prints === LP1-01 === followed by the decoded text. Open the complete warning reading beside it to compare the output with the explanation.

The spelling may look unusual. The output uses literal rune labels, which preserve distinctions that ordinary English can hide. Keep those spellings when checking the result; the guide also provides contextual English to help you read the message.

Once this example works, check the other known readings:

python scripts/reproduce_reading.py --list
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py --check-all

--list shows the nine named sections available to the script. --check-all decodes them and should finish with:

PASS: 17 literal page readings match the published controls exactly.

A control is an example whose expected result is already known. Matching it helps check that the implementation and inputs work together. There are nine sections but 17 pages because some sections span several images. This command checks those known readings; it does not attempt the unsolved pages or extract hidden image content.

4. Read a rune-by-rune trace

python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning --trace

A trace shows the intermediate steps rather than only the finished text. Here, each row follows one rune from its input alphabet position to its output. The format is CSV (comma-separated values), so you can also open it in a spreadsheet. The first two steps are explained below; expand the CSV sample to inspect the exact exported columns and rows.

Atbash maps index x to 28 − x. The first rune has index 4, so its output index is 24, labeled A. The second has index 21, so its output is 7, labeled W. These are zero-based alphabet indices, not prime values. A two-letter Latin label such as NG still represents one rune.

You only need the input index, output index and Latin label to follow this Atbash example. The remaining fields help when a method crosses page boundaries or skips particular runes:

	Field	Meaning

	page_rune_ordinal	Zero-based rune position within the page; resets at each new page.

	section_rune_ordinal	Position under the control’s section/boundary rule. It can continue across pages.

	input_index, output_index	Positions in the 29-rune alphabet before and after the transformation.

	subtracted_value	The applied Vigenère or prime-minus-one amount. Blank for Atbash, direct reading, or a copied interruption; blank is not a recorded zero.

	key_position_before, key_position_after	The consumed-keystream counter before and after the rune, including the control's starting offset. Equal at a copied interruption. Blank for methods without a keystream.

	key_slot_before	For Vigenère, the counter before the rune modulo key length. A copied rune leaves this slot unused. Blank for other methods, including the nonrepeating prime stream.

	latin	The output rune’s Latin label, before contextual English editing.

	copied	Whether this position is listed as an interruption in the control. False does not mean the index changed: direct readings also have false entries.


Exact CSV header and first two rows
page,page_rune_ordinal,section_rune_ordinal,input_rune,input_index,subtracted_value,output_index,latin,copied,key_position_before,key_position_after,key_slot_before
lp1-01,0,0,ᚱ,4,,24,A,False,,,
lp1-01,1,1,ᛝ,21,,7,W,False,,,

Non-rune characters are preserved in the literal output but do not get trace rows. For a key-dependent example, run python scripts/reproduce_reading.py welcome --trace and follow keystream positions and interruptions. The specific LP1-10 correction is applied before transformation and trace output; see transcription layers.

Save a reading or trace

Use --output to keep the result as a file. The script checks the reading against its stored control before writing anything, saves UTF-8 text, and refuses to replace an existing file.

python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning --output warning.txt
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning --trace --output warning-trace.csv

The filenames above are created in your terminal’s current folder. You can choose another existing folder; quote the path if it contains spaces. The script does not create missing folders. The text file contains the same page headings and literal reading as the terminal output. The CSV contains only the header and trace rows; the “Saved” confirmation is printed to the terminal, not inserted into the file.

When importing the CSV into a spreadsheet, select UTF-8 and a comma delimiter if asked. Each rune has its own row. A multi-page section such as Welcome keeps the page ID in every row, so the trace can be filtered without losing its page attribution. Keep this original export alongside any spreadsheet you edit.

This option saves a named section, with or without --trace; it does not combine with --list or --check-all. A saved trace documents the known control’s computation, not a new experiment on an unsolved page.

When you are ready to try another method

The warning example needs only Python and the reference-data bundle. Other tasks work on different layers of the manuscript. Reconstructing already-extracted text is different from extracting it from a JPEG yourself, which is why their software requirements differ.

For image-based work, extract the original-images ZIP into the same folder as the reference data. See the bundle instructions for the complete command list.

Check those image files with python scripts/verify_bundle.py ORIGINAL-IMAGES-CONTENTS.json. Each download has a separately named manifest. Prefer these names to the generic CONTENTS.json, which another bundle may replace when extracted into the same folder. Passing the reference-data check does not check images from the image bundle.

	Task	Requirements	Instructions

	Known rune readings	Python 3, standard library only	Warning control

	Locate words in known readings	Python 3, standard library only; searches contextual English	Known-reading concordance

	Reproduce rune prime sums	Python 3, standard library only; uses decoded rune sequences	Prime-sum checks

	Check prime positions and numerical examples	Python 3, standard library only	Prime values and positions

	Recompute whole-page IoC	Python 3, standard library only; uses archived rune streams	IoC baseline

	Measure single-rune entropy	Python 3, standard library only; uses the archived frequency counts	Entropy examples and limits

	Locate repeated rune sequences	Python 3, standard library only; reports overlapping windows and source positions	Bigram and trigram reports

	Redraw the frequency chart	Python 3 and Matplotlib; reads the saved IoC counts	Frequency chart and command

	Reconstruct the exported cover chain	Python 3, standard library only; uses stored extractions	Cover chain

	Reproduce the illustrated-cover RSA message	Python 3, standard library only; uses the recorded factors and stored payload	RSA reproduction

	Reproduce the Emerson book cipher	Python 3, standard library only for the stored paragraph source	Book-cipher reproduction

	Check visual-record structure	Python 3, standard library only	Opening-page inventory

	Recount image pixels with --pixels	Python 3 and Pillow	Image regions and measurement rules

	Extract hidden JPEG payloads again	Python wrapper plus an OutGuess executable	OutGuess extraction

	Verify signed messages	GnuPG and the documented public key	PGP signatures


Install an optional package only when you need it

You can complete the warning walkthrough, prime-sum checks, concordance, and IoC calculation without installing any Python packages. To redraw the chart, install Matplotlib into the same Python environment that will run the plotting script. To recount image pixels, install Pillow. The package names and Python import names differ for Pillow: its code is imported as PIL.

python -m pip install matplotlib
python scripts/plot_rune_frequencies.py --output my-rune-frequencies.svg

The installation command may download packages; the plotting command reads local files. If you use py or python3 for the scripts, use that same command before -m pip. This avoids installing a package for one Python interpreter and running the script with another.

For a separate project environment, create a local .venv folder and invoke its Python directly. Activation is optional:

Windows PowerShell

py -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install matplotlib
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts/plot_rune_frequencies.py --output my-rune-frequencies.svg

macOS / Linux

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install matplotlib
.venv/bin/python scripts/plot_rune_frequencies.py --output my-rune-frequencies.svg

Keep the environment separate from the preserved evidence files. Record package versions when sharing a generated figure: python -m pip show matplotlib reports the installed version. Visual output can vary across package or font versions even when the underlying numerical counts agree.

When a command fails

“Command not found” or “not recognized”: check the Python command first. If it names outguess or gpg, that is a separate executable, not a missing rune dataset.

“Can’t open file” for the script: check the terminal’s current folder. Open the extracted folder that contains scripts, rather than its parent folder or the ZIP itself.

A missing text/ or data/ file: extract a fresh reference-data bundle and keep its directories together. Moving just the script breaks the relative paths it uses to find its inputs.

No module named matplotlib or No module named PIL: install the optional package for the Python interpreter running that particular task. Neither error means the basic reading checks need those packages.

“Output already exists”: choose a new output filename or inspect the existing result. Scripts that refuse overwrites do so to preserve earlier output, not because the calculation failed.

Boxes instead of runes: the terminal font may lack runic characters. Check the numeric indices and Latin labels, and compare with the browser reader. Missing glyphs alone do not establish bad input bytes.

“Output differs” or a hash mismatch: preserve the full error and identify the affected file. Compare with an unchanged copy and the checksums. Do not change the expected output merely to make the check pass.

Keep the result reproducible

Once you can reproduce a known reading, try the guided first experiment. It shows how to replay a published shuffle comparison, inspect its files, and explain why a passing reproduction check is different from a positive experimental finding.

Record the repository commit, Python version, command, and output. In a Git checkout, git rev-parse HEAD prints the commit ID. For a ZIP download, retain the archive and its checksum; do not claim a commit ID you have not verified. When you move from a control to a new hypothesis, follow documenting a reproducible attempt. A passing control is a starting point, not evidence that the same method solves another page.

Reproducing rune prime sums provides a read-only command and explicit spelling comparisons.
Implementation and verification

The commands and trace fields above are documented from the reproduction script and its control parameters. The first trace rows and all 17 literal page outputs were checked locally on 19 October 2026. Operating-system launch commands are alternatives; this verification used Python 3.12 on Windows.

title: Reproduce your first experiment
summary: Read a completed test, inspect its chart and files, and distinguish a passing rerun from a positive finding.
text:
Start with repeated trigrams against page shuffles. A trigram is a window of three consecutive runes. The experiment asks whether the archived LP2 pages have more matching pairs of these windows than shuffled versions with the same rune counts. It measures a property of the text; it does not attempt to decode it.

[Image: The trigram experiment’s histogram: 55 observed matching pairs, with 798 of 999 shuffled totals at least as large.]
The orange line marks the observed total. The bars count simulated datasets in intervals of five pair counts. Open the full experiment and its files.

Read the record before running it


Read the question and scope. This test uses LP2-00–55, includes headings, removes separators, and permits overlapping windows. It compares windows within each page, never between pages. Those choices define what was tested.

Read the finding beside its limit. The observation is 55 matching pairs. In 999 simulated datasets, 798 totals are at least that large. The corrected upper-tail p-value is 0.799, so the test does not show an excess under this model. That is not proof that the pages are random.

Open the full account. Its small examples explain why three occurrences of one pattern give three matching pairs. Its shuffle description states exactly what the comparison preserves and destroys.

Inspect a file. Download the per-page CSV. LP2-31 has 269 runes, 267 windows and zero matching trigram pairs. LP2-50 remains present with zero runes. These are descriptive page counts, not separate significance tests.


Reproduce the result

If you have Python, download this experiment's reproduction files and extract them into an empty folder, preserving the directories. Open a terminal in that folder. Verify the included files, then run the experiment and its independent checker:

python scripts/verify_bundle.py EXPERIMENT-lp2-trigram-repeats-CONTENTS.json
python experiments/records/lp2-trigram-repeats/run.py --check
python experiments/records/lp2-trigram-repeats/check.py

The verification command should report 0 problems. The recorded simulation used Python 3.12.10. The runner should report that all observed repeats and 999 complete-dataset shuffles reproduce, followed by "observed_total": 55, "exceedances": 798, "monte_carlo_p": 0.799 and "below_threshold": false. The final command checks the observations with a different counting approach and audits the saved comparison. See setup instructions if your terminal uses py or python3 instead. This experiment needs no original JPEGs or external Python packages.

Report what passed

A passing rerun means the published calculation was reproduced. It does not mean the hypothesis was supported: in this case, the result is a lack of evidence for the specified excess. Keep that distinction when reporting your own work. Changing the window length, removing headings or comparing across pages creates a different test and needs a declared plan.

What kind of result are you reading?

The registry groups related methods into families, but its records do not all answer the same kind of question. Before interpreting an outcome label, read the question it belongs to:

	Kind of check	Example	What the result establishes

	Arithmetic audit	Mixed-square candidate words	Sixteen supplied totals are achievable under the declared rune-label rules. This does not establish that a word is a key or that a number has only one word equivalent.

	Descriptive extraction	N-rune distances	Records the labels produced by four fixed distance/boundary configurations. Keeping unmatched gaps visible prevents a selected fragment from appearing to be a complete reading.

	Statistical comparison	Repeated trigrams	Compares one specified count with a declared shuffle model. A result that is ordinary under that model does not prove the text random.

	Exact mathematical exclusion	Direct polynomial streams	A finite-difference obstruction excludes every modulus greater than one for the defined direct-output rule through degree eight. It does not cover polynomial keys mixed with unknown plaintext.

	Necessary model constraint	Word-local repetition	Distinct ciphertext units require distinct corresponding plaintext units under one shared deterministic word function and context. This does not establish that the unknown plaintext repeats, so it does not by itself reject the model.

	Bounded cipher search	Fibonacci shifts	No tested configuration matched any of nine fixed 12-rune openings. This excludes those exact matches within the stated bounds, not every Fibonacci-based cipher.

	Tool and payload check	Default-key OutGuess sweep	Distinguishes reproduced payloads, unverified output bytes, rejected retrievals and abnormal exits. An abnormal exit is not evidence that an image has no payload.

	Historical control	Emerson book cipher	Reproduces the documented historical string with fixed source and counting conventions. It does not establish that the same book or method decrypts another page.


Would your search recognize an answer?

Before interpreting “nothing found,” give the search a problem whose answer you know. A planted control starts with known plaintext, encrypts it under a specified rule, and asks the proposed search to recover it. Keep the plaintext aside for checking; do not let the search use it unless known plaintext is explicitly part of the model. This separates several failures that otherwise look identical.


Is the answer inside the search? Record whether the true key, generator, offset and alignment are included. An omitted-key control should remain visibly separate from one that includes the true key. The bounded search controls compare both situations rather than treating every missed answer as a scoring failure.

Can the decoder represent it? Even the correct key can fail when the encoder skips key slots and the decoder assumes uninterrupted addition. The alignment controls retain exact rune recovery separately from score acceptance. The worked alignment guide explains why a wider beam cannot recover a path prohibited by the skip bound.

Would the scoring rule accept it? Test intact known text before involving a cipher. In the eight-language scorer control, the fixed English model accepts every tested English and French excerpt, but no Finnish or Welsh excerpt. The same failure label can therefore mean “wrong candidate” or “meaningful text this score rejects.” These results apply to the recorded excerpts and preprocessing, not every text in those languages.

What does choosing the best candidate change? Give each null control the whole search, including its key budget and selection rule. A single wrong-key output is not a control for the winner of thousands of attempts. The search-maximum experiment retains complete searches at five nested dictionary sizes, with all settings fixed.

Does the candidate predict anything unused? Reserve part of the plaintext for checking after candidate selection. In the known-crib seed controls, two-rune openings admit false matches, including under a wrong generator or incorrect crib. Matching that opening and predicting the withheld remainder are different achievements.


Read the two outcomes separately

	Exact planted plaintext recovered?	Score accepts it?	What to investigate

	Yes	Yes	The pipeline succeeds on this fixture. Test other declared conditions before claiming wider recovery power.

	Yes	No	The scoring gate rejects the answer. Inspect language, text representation, length and threshold.

	No	Yes	The score accepts an incorrect output. Inspect the complete sequence; a plausible-looking score is not exact recovery.

	No	No	Check coverage and decoder behavior before blaming the scorer. The answer may be absent or unreachable.


This table is available for planted controls because their plaintext is known. For an unsolved manuscript page, the exact-recovery column is unknown. A high score cannot fill it in. Preserve the distinction when reading the experiment figures: acceptance counts and exact-recovery counts measure different things.

Use controls resembling the proposed search in length, symbol conversion, key mechanism, interruption rules and budget. A successful plain-addition control does not validate an unrelated skip-aware decoder. Reusing one fixture to tune settings also makes it development data; reserve other fixtures before tuning if you want a separate check. None of the linked tests establishes a universal false-positive rate or rules out every cipher in its family.

What has actually been ruled out?

The following published results show why “we tried it” needs more than an outcome label. They all use exact calculations, but their conclusions have different logical strength.

A proof can cover parameters that were never enumerated

The polynomial experiment does not loop through a large list of coefficients, origins or moduli. Its argument says that every allowed modulus must divide a particular greatest common divisor. When that gcd is 1, no integer modulus greater than one can work. The program supplies the manuscript-specific integer differences needed by the argument. All 55 nonempty rune pages in LP2-00–55 have this obstruction in both tested representations for every degree bound 1–8.

That is stronger than finding no candidate in a finite coefficient range, but only for the stated rule: the polynomial directly generates the observed rune indices or prime values at a fixed stride. A polynomial generating a key that is then added to unknown plaintext is a different construction. The word “polynomial” alone is not enough to transfer the result.

Compare the fixed alphabet transform search: all 6,496 declared cases completed without matching the specified warning opening. That search has complete coverage of its listed cases, but its success criterion is one particular opening. A different plaintext opening is not contradicted by the result.

A necessary constraint may leave a model possible

The word-reset experiment finds no exact repeats among the selected interior ciphertext tokens. Under one shared deterministic word function with identical key and reset context, equal plaintext units would give equal ciphertext units. Consequently, the corresponding plaintext units must all differ. To turn that constraint into a rejection, you would need an additional justified premise that some of those plaintext units repeat. The experiment does not supply that premise.

[Image: A shared deterministic reset preserves exact repetitions; a shared symbol map plus independent within-word shuffling preserves symbol counts instead.]
Changing word order inside a token and changing the symbol map are different operations. The full account lists all four observed anagram pairs and explains the assumptions for each model.

A counterexample shows where a conclusion stops

The position-divisor experiment rules out assigning a fixed divisor greater than one to each rune when numbered positions advance by one. Repeated-rune gaps remove the unknown starting position, so trying more starting integers cannot repair the contradiction.

Allow positions to advance by two instead, assign divisor 2 to every rune, and start at 2: every numbered position is even. That satisfies the bare divisibility requirement. It does not tell you which rune to emit and is not a solution. It is a counterexample to the broader claim that the same argument excludes every stride. Extra requirements, such as distinct divisor labels or a deterministic factor-selection rule, must be checked separately.

What the checks have verified

These three newer records include an elementary argument, a calculation on hashed archived inputs, and a second implementation that uses a different computational approach. Their downloadable bundles reproduce those checks without network or AI calls. The two text formats share an archival source, so agreement is not an independent visual review of every manuscript rune.
