For the broader approach and its other variants, see the arithmetic-keystream family guide.

title: Euler’s totient and prime-minus-one
summary: Count coprime integers, calculate composite totients, and distinguish the LP2-56 shifts from the historical RSA replay.
text:
Euler’s totient function, written φ(n), counts the integers from 1 through n that are relatively prime to n. Two integers are relatively prime when their greatest common divisor is 1. “Relatively prime” does not mean that both integers are themselves prime.

Small examples
Coprime means “relatively prime”: the two integers have no positive common divisor other than 1. For example, 8 and 9 are coprime even though neither is prime. Their prime factors are 2 and 3 respectively, so they share none. This is also the condition that permits a modular inverse.
For n = 8, the qualifying integers are 1, 3, 5, and 7, so φ(8) = 4. For a prime p, every integer from 1 through p − 1 is relatively prime to p. Therefore φ(p) = p − 1. In particular, φ(2), φ(3), φ(5), φ(7) are 1, 2, 4, 6.

	n	Integers counted	φ(n)	n − 1

	8	1, 3, 5, 7	4	7

	9	1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8	6	8

	11	1 through 10	10	10


The 9 row demonstrates the meaning of “relatively prime”: 4 and 8 are composite, but both are counted because neither shares a divisor greater than one with 9. The numbers 3, 6, and 9 are excluded because they share the factor 3. The function counts a relationship to n, not how many primes occur below n.

For prime p, the only positive divisors are 1 and p. An integer k between 1 and p − 1 cannot share the divisor p, so its greatest common divisor with p must be 1. There are exactly p − 1 such integers. This proves the identity used by the LP2-56 method without needing a table of precomputed totients.

Composite inputs: count the numbers that survive

For 15 = 3 × 5, discard numbers divisible by either factor. The survivors are 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13, and 14: eight numbers, so φ(15) = 8.

Counting from 1 through 15
	Step	Count
	Start with all integers	15
	Remove multiples of 3	−5
	Remove multiples of 5	−3
	Add back 15, removed twice	+1
	Remaining coprime integers	8

This gives φ(pq) = pq − q − p + 1 = (p − 1)(q − 1) for two distinct primes p and q. Distinct matters: φ(9) = 6, not (3 − 1)² = 4.

The factorization formula

For a positive integer n, use φ(n) = n × ∏(1 − 1/p), with one factor for each distinct prime divisor p. The product symbol ∏ means multiply those factors. For example, φ(12) = 12 × (1 − 1/2) × (1 − 1/3) = 4. Although 12 = 2² × 3, the factor for 2 appears only once. NIST DLMF, equation 27.3.3.

The totient is multiplicative for coprime inputs: φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b) when gcd(a, b) = 1. It is not valid for arbitrary a and b; a = b = 3 is the counterexample above. Also φ(1) = 1. NIST DLMF, multiplicative functions.

Why the cover’s RSA replay uses the totient

The historical cover-message replay uses the product formula for two published prime factors. It then finds a private exponent d for which e × d ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)). This is a modular inverse, not ordinary division by e.

A small arithmetic example makes the inverse visible: choose n = 15 and e = 3. Since φ(15) = 8, d = 3 works because 3 × 3 = 9 = 1 + 8. For message integer 2, the public operation gives 2³ mod 15 = 8; the private operation recovers 8³ mod 15 = 2.

from math import gcd
n, e = 15, 3
phi_n = sum(gcd(k, n) == 1 for k in range(1, n + 1))
d = pow(e, -1, phi_n)
c = pow(2, e, n)
assert (phi_n, d, c, pow(c, d, n)) == (8, 3, 8, 2)

This toy example illustrates the arithmetic only. The actual historical message has a much larger modulus, multiple blocks, and a specific padding format; follow the RSA reproduction guide for those details. On LP2-56, totients instead supply shifts in a rune sequence. Sharing the same function does not make that page an RSA ciphertext.

Why the LP2-56 method has two names
The archived walkthrough describes LP2-56 using “phi(prime).” The prime-minus-one guide uses the equivalent expression p − 1. These are the same shifts when the input sequence consists of primes. Substituting φ(n) for consecutive integers n would produce a different sequence.

	Sequence used as input	Inputs	Totients

	Consecutive primes	2, 3, 5, 7, 11	1, 2, 4, 6, 10

	Consecutive integers starting at 2	2, 3, 4, 5, 6	1, 2, 2, 4, 2


The first two shifts agree, but the third already differs. “Use totients” therefore leaves an essential question unanswered: totients of which input sequence? It also differs from the prime-counting function, which counts how many primes are at most a given number.

A recorded consecutive-integer test
The consecutive-integer totient experiment starts at φ(1) and tests offsets 0–28, both addition and subtraction, on LP2-00–55 without interruptions. Its 3190 distinct page outputs do not match any of nine declared 12-rune openings. This is a narrow opening test, not a general rejection of totient-based decoding. The record provides a counting diagram, complete candidate outputs and a checker that calculates every totient directly from greatest common divisors.

How to reproduce the identity
from math import gcd
def phi(n):
    return sum(gcd(k, n) == 1 for k in range(1, n + 1))
assert phi(8) == 4
assert [phi(p) for p in [2, 3, 5, 7]] == [1, 2, 4, 6]
This deliberately simple implementation is useful for small examples. Reproduce the actual page with python scripts/reproduce_reading.py lp2-56, including its recorded interruption and modulo-29 arithmetic.

What the identity does not determine
It does not specify the starting prime, direction, reset behavior, or copied rune positions. Those parameters remain part of the keystream convention.

Another function associated with a name found in the manuscript is the Möbius function μ(n). It returns a sign or zero from a prime factorization; it does not count coprime integers and cannot be substituted for the totient.
The 27 × 27 map experiment

The LP2-00–02 totient-map replay checks the selected three-rune-node readings, all 16 primary transition fits, and the choices still needed to traverse the map. It includes a coverage map, a comparison of three nodes producing the same SOON key, downloadable inputs and scripts, and a frequency-preserving mirror control. Reproducing the supplied words does not establish a unique or intended decryption.

Sources
Pinned LP2-56 walkthrough · Exact reproduction parameters.

title: The Möbius function: squarefree numbers and signs
summary: Distinguish the arithmetic function from a Möbius strip, calculate examples, and specify what a proposed manuscript application would require.
text:
The Möbius function, written μ(n), assigns −1, 0 or 1 to a positive integer according to its prime factorization. It is a different mathematical object from a Möbius strip or the manuscript’s crossed-loop drawing. The word MOBIUS occurs in Some Wisdom; identifying that word does not select which meaning, if any, should become a cipher operation.

The three cases

The definition in NIST’s Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, equation 27.2.12, can be applied as follows:

For n = 1, μ(n) = 1.
If a prime square divides n, μ(n) = 0. For example, 12 contains 2² as a factor.
Otherwise, count the distinct prime factors. With k such factors, μ(n) = (−1)^(k): −1 for odd k, and 1 for even k.

A positive integer with no prime-square divisor is called squarefree. Six is squarefree because 6 = 2 × 3. Twelve is not, because 12 = 2² × 3. Squarefree does not mean prime.

Work through small examples

	n	Factorization	Rule	μ(n)

	1	No prime factors	Defined starting value	1

	7	7	One distinct prime	−1

	6	2 × 3	Two distinct primes	1

	30	2 × 3 × 5	Three distinct primes	−1

	12	2² × 3	A repeated prime factor	0


Compare Euler’s totient φ(n), which counts integers coprime to n. For a prime p, μ(p) is always −1, while φ(p) = p − 1. These functions do different jobs even though both are defined using integer arithmetic.

Reproduce the examples

This trial-division implementation uses Python 3 without extra packages. It is intended for small examples; factoring very large integers is a separate computational problem.

def mobius(n):
    if isinstance(n, bool) or not isinstance(n, int) or n < 1:
        raise ValueError("Use a positive integer")
    sign = 1
    factor = 2
    while factor * factor <= n:
        if n % factor == 0:
            n //= factor
            if n % factor == 0:
                return 0
            sign = -sign
        factor += 1
    return -sign if n > 1 else sign

assert [mobius(n) for n in (1, 7, 6, 30, 12)] == [1, -1, 1, -1, 0]
assert [mobius(n) for n in range(1, 13)] == [
    1, -1, -1, 0, -1, 1, -1, 0, 0, 1, -1, 0
]
print("Examples match")

The code removes a prime factor once, then checks whether it is still present. A second occurrence makes the result zero. Each distinct factor changes the sign; a remaining value greater than one contributes the final prime factor. When the input is 1, no factor is processed and the sign stays 1.

What would applying it to the manuscript mean?

First identify the inputs. Every Gematria Primus rune value is prime, so applying μ separately to those values produces −1 for every rune. That operation loses all distinctions between rune identities. It is not equivalent to applying μ to word sums, printed decimal numbers, or a sequence of positive ordinal positions.

Zero-based rune indices introduce another issue: the F index is 0, outside the positive-integer domain of this definition. Adding one, replacing zero, or choosing prime values instead would each be an additional rule. State it explicitly rather than letting a software convention choose the input.

The function name alone supplies no direction, grouping, starting position, output alphabet or success criterion. A proposed use therefore belongs in a bounded reproducible experiment. This guide explains the mathematics and verifies the examples; it does not claim that μ is an established Liber Primus cipher or that applying it has been exhaustively tested.

LP2-40: the proposed “FOR EVERY” crib

A crib is a guessed plaintext passage, not a recovered reading. One proposal begins by assuming that the first eight runes of LP2-40 mean FOR EVERY, then works backward to a possible running key. The following audit reconstructs its numerical intermediate steps; it does not establish that the guess is correct.

The proposed rune labels are F O R E U E R Y, using U for the English V. Their zero-based indices are [0, 3, 4, 18, 1, 18, 4, 26], and their Gematria Primus sum is 271, a prime. The manuscript’s first eight stored indices are [0, 9, 19, 26, 6, 23, 25, 8]. A prime sum is a property of the proposed spelling; it does not independently identify the plaintext.

Reconstruct the arithmetic

Leave the initial F unchanged. For each remaining proposed plaintext index P, apply (28 − (P + 18)) mod 29: shift by +18, then Atbash. Add the consecutive prime-minus-one schedule starting at 2−1 after the exempt F. These choices reproduce the stated intermediate:

Shift, then Atbash:
0  7  6 21  9 21  6 13

Add prime minus one:
0  1  2  4  6 10 12 16

Intermediate, modulo 29:
0  8  8 25 15  2 18  0

Stored ciphertext:
0  9 19 26  6 23 25  8

Required added key, modulo 29:
0  1 11  1 20 21  7  8

The final row is obtained by subtracting the intermediate from the ciphertext modulo 29. A signed representation may use −8 instead of 21; these are the same residue. This audit exempts only the initial F. It does not infer a rule for later F runes, other interruptions or other pages.

From the repository or reference-data bundle, run python scripts/audit_lp2_40_crib.py. The audit script reads the archived ciphertext and alphabet, prints every stage with input hashes, verifies the prime-minus-one values by coprime counting, and reverses the reconstructed arithmetic back to the proposed crib. It makes no network request and performs no Möbius-driven decryption.

A fitted key is not yet a prediction

For any proposed intermediate X and observed ciphertext C, defining K = C − X (mod 29) guarantees X + K = C. Reconstructing the eight symbols with that fitted key is therefore not an independent test of the guessed words. The evidence would come from a separately specified key-generation rule predicting symbols that were not used to choose it.

The proposed next step assigns different combinations of plaintext, ciphertext and signs to states derived from nearby Möbius values. That needs a complete specification. Each μ value has three possible outputs, so a three-position tuple has up to 27 formal labels before any restrictions from the sequence. Eight binary states do not follow automatically: the conversion to bits, including treatment of zero and sign, must be stated.

A runnable experiment needs the input sequence and starting index, seeds, exact references to previous or current symbols, state-update order, a fixed table mapping every reachable state to an operation, and an interruption rule. It must also state whether it can encrypt and decrypt without consulting the desired answer. Once those choices are frozen, test held-out text or another declared target instead of revising the table whenever a letter misses.

The arithmetic above is reproducible; the supplied description does not yet define that full selector. Its later matrix and Slidefair suggestions are separate proposals, not additional evidence for this unfinished Möbius rule. Compare search space and bounds, autokey and doublets, and the consecutive-integer totient experiment. That last experiment uses a different schedule and does not test this layered, crib-driven construction.

QuagMirrors: distinguish the implementations

QuagMirrors combines keyed alphabet substitutions with changing arithmetic and feedback from preceding symbols. It is a useful example of why an experiment needs a versioned algorithm: the published source contains four implementations with different rules. Their shared name does not make a result from one a test of the others.

This is a source audit, not a decryption result. The files were inspected at revision 88ef1e60b0738b8b28db96bc9dc44dc4da8dd307. Each contains a 729-value ciphertext array and nine hardcoded 29-entry substitution tables. A static check confirms that every table is a permutation of indices 0–28. That establishes that the tables individually map symbols one-to-one; it does not establish that the complete feedback algorithm is invertible or that its output is plaintext.

	Source file	What a reproduction must preserve

	OG_quag_mirror.py	Branches on current and previous Möbius states; a conditional mirror bypass at index 30; stops after 153 loop iterations.

	Mobius_AT_QuagMirror.py	Overrides the first intermediate value and first two mirror selections; stops after six iterations.

	quag_mirror_WIP.py	Uses its own feedback branches and sign convention; contains a cutoff at 500 iterations.

	quag_mirror_v4.py	Explicitly skips index 17 without updating the index or feedback state, then continues with the next ciphertext symbol; stops when its processing index reaches 48.


These are limits and branches visible in the source, not assertions that every program reaches its cutoff successfully. In particular, a skipped ciphertext symbol and an incremented key position are different operations. In v4 the skip is removed from the list before continuing, so the following symbol uses the same processing index. A rewrite that advances the key at that point would test a different algorithm.

How to turn this into a bounded experiment

Choose one file at the pinned revision. Record its exact bytes and dependency versions, and compare its ciphertext array with the archived manuscript transcription before running it.
Record all seeds, substitution tables, exceptional positions, feedback equations and stopping conditions. State which symbols advance each counter.
First reproduce the original output without repairing or extending its rules. If a correction is necessary, save that as a separate variant with an explanation.
Choose the scoring window and success criterion before evaluating new text. Keep the opening used to develop the rules separate from held-out evaluation.
If searching variants, declare the complete set of allowed choices. Repeat that same search on control inputs; comparing the best tuned output with one untuned random output gives an unfair comparison.

For example, allowing three arithmetic operations and twelve substitution choices independently at each of 17 positions creates up to 36^17 operation paths before accounting for duplicate outputs and state constraints. This is an illustrative search bound, not a measured coverage result for these nine-table scripts. The number of distinct outputs may be much smaller, and feedback can make choices dependent. A meaningful experiment must enumerate its actual rules rather than borrowing a probability from a different variant.

Group future results under one QuagMirrors family, with separate records for each frozen implementation and changed variable. No completed QuagMirrors experiment is claimed here. Compare search space and bounds, feedback equations and doublets, and the difference between fitting a crib and predicting new text.

Primary source: the four pinned QuagMirrors implementations. Inspection does not establish the derivation of the hardcoded mirror tables, a full-page reading, or an exhaustive negative result.

The 27 × 27 map experiment

The LP2-00–02 totient-map replay checks the selected three-rune-node readings, all 16 primary transition fits, and the choices still needed to traverse the map. It includes a coverage map, a comparison of three nodes producing the same SOON key, downloadable inputs and scripts, and a frequency-preserving mirror control. Reproducing the supplied words does not establish a unique or intended decryption.

Sources and related references

NIST DLMF definition, checked 20 October 2026. Manuscript context: LP1-05 and the Möbius visual-feature guide. For other frequently confused arithmetic operations, compare prime indices and totients.

title: Direct reading
summary: When rune labels already form a readable sequence.
text:
Direct reading means that the recorded rune sequence produces readable text without shifting or rearranging its alphabet indices. The runes still need to be identified and labeled correctly. Turning those labels into ordinary English is a separate editorial step.

Identity transformation
Direct reading uses p = c: label each rune without changing its index. Here c is the input rune index and p is the output index in the same 29-symbol alphabet. There is no key to subtract and no permutation to undo. Distinguish the literal labels from contextual English.

Read PARABLE one rune at a time

The first seven runes in the archived LP2-57 sequence produce the heading PARABLE. The reproduction trace gives:

	Rune	Input index	Output index	Latin label

	ᛈ	13	13	P

	ᚪ	24	24	A

	ᚱ	4	4	R

	ᚪ	24	24	A

	ᛒ	17	17	B

	ᛚ	20	20	L

	ᛖ	18	18	E


Notice what the table does not use: the runes’ prime values. These numbers are zero-based alphabet indices. Prime values are relevant to a separate calculation such as a rune sum, not needed to read this heading.

[Image: LP2-57 with the red PARABLE heading above the body text and insect-like image]
Complete parable reading. Open the reader to compare the heading with the full original image.

Why the literal output can still look unfamiliar

Later on LP2-57, the literal labels give LICE, TUNNELNG, and DIUINITY. Contextual English renders these as LIKE, TUNNELING, and DIVINITY. C/K and U/V are label conventions, while the NG rune can stand for the ending represented as ING in ordinary spelling. These readings do not require a new shift of the rune indices.

Keep both forms available. Contextual English makes the passage easier to understand; the rune sequence is the appropriate input for rune counts and prime-sum calculations. Inserting an extra I rune into TUNNELNG would change the numerical input, whereas displaying the same NG rune with a different Latin label would not.

How to replicate
Extract the reference-data ZIP and run these commands with Python 3 from its folder. No extra packages or AI service are needed.
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py some-wisdom
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py loss-of-divinity
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py instruction
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py lp2-57
These cover LP1-05, LP1-10–13, LP1-16 and LP2-57. The loss-of-divinity control includes the documented correction before the identity transformation. That source correction and the cipher operation are separate steps.

To reproduce the heading table and inspect every rune:

python scripts/reproduce_reading.py lp2-57 --trace

The trace’s subtracted_value column is blank because no subtraction is applied. Its copied flag is False: that flag identifies specifically recorded interruption positions, not every rune whose index happens to stay the same. See how to read a trace for all fields.

Readable does not mean exhausted
Several direct-reading pages also have OutGuess payloads. Visual details and numerical patterns need their own evidence. Being able to read the visible words does not establish that every layer of a file has been explained.

Conversely, obtaining familiar letters from a short runic fragment does not establish a direct reading for a whole unsolved page. Compare the complete sequence, word boundaries, and recorded controls before extending a local observation into a broader claim. The identity operation itself is easy to apply to any page; interpreting its output is a different question.

Sources and verification
Known-reading compilation · Reproduction script · Pinned historical walkthrough. The LP2-57 trace above was checked on 20 October 2026. Recipes reproduce published controls; they are not new solutions.

title: Transposition ciphers
summary: Reorder symbols without substituting their values.
text:
A transposition rearranges the positions of symbols while keeping the symbols themselves. It is the difference between moving letter tiles and replacing the letters printed on them. Liber Primus research includes a documented column rearrangement in the LP1 title-page payload chain; this guide explains that operation and how to check it.

Preserve symbols, change positions
A permutation uses every position once, preserving length and symbol counts. Atbash and Vigenère change values; a pure transposition does not. Reversal is one simple permutation. Swapping columns of a fixed-width grid is another.

A four-column example

Start with two rows, ABCD and EFGH. Number the columns from zero and read each row in the order [2, 0, 3, 1]. The order means “take the old column 2 first, then 0, then 3, then 1.”

[Image: Columns 2, 0, 3, 1 turn rows ABCD and EFGH into CADB and GEHF. Reading across these rows gives CADBGEHF; reading down columns gives CGAEDHBF.]
The numbers above the cells identify their original columns. Moving columns and choosing a reading direction are separate decisions. This is an invented teaching example. Download the diagram (SVG).

	Output position	Read input column	First row	Second row

	0	2	C	G

	1	0	A	E

	2	3	D	H

	3	1	B	F


The reordered rows are CADB and GEHF. Reading them from top to bottom gives CADBGEHF. Reading down columns instead would produce CGAEDHBF, a different result. The permutation alone therefore does not specify the complete readout: you must also state the row and column traversal.

Reverse the operation

To undo the rearrangement, put each output character back into the input column from which it came. The inverse order for this example is [1, 3, 0, 2]. It differs from the original order, so applying the original permutation a second time does not generally restore the text.

rows = ["ABCD", "EFGH"]
order = [2, 0, 3, 1]
assert sorted(order) == list(range(4))
encoded = ["".join(row[c] for c in order) for row in rows]
inverse = [order.index(c) for c in range(4)]
decoded = ["".join(row[c] for c in inverse) for row in encoded]
print(encoded, inverse, decoded)
assert encoded == ["CADB", "GEHF"]
assert decoded == rows

This self-contained Python example prints the rearranged rows, inverse order, and recovered rows. Checking the round trip catches mistakes about which way the permutation maps positions. It does not establish that a chosen permutation solves a manuscript page.

The historical column operation
The cover-chain guide explains how the stored OutGuess payloads combine into a signed message. Its 70-character grid supplies the following five rows. This example needs only Python 3:
rows = [
    "IDGTKUMLOOARWO",
    "ERTHISUTETLHUT",
    "IATSLLOUIMNITE",
    "LNJ7TFYVOIUAUS",
    "NOCO5JI4MEODZZ",
]
order = [2, 8, 9, 1, 12, 13, 11, 4, 5, 7, 3, 0, 6, 10]
assert sorted(order) == list(range(14))
assert len(rows) == 5 and all(len(row) == 14 for row in rows)
result = "".join(rows[r][c] for r in range(5) for c in order)
assert len(result) == 70
print(result)

The first input row becomes GOODWORKULTIMA. The complete output is:

GOODWORKULTIMATETRUTHISTHEULTIMATEILLUSIONJOINUSATFV7LYUCMEOZZD5J4ONIO

Keep the final ONIO as produced. The historical interpretation supplies another N to form an onion-address ending, but adding a character is not a transposition. The cover-chain explanation preserves this distinction and the historical address.

What cannot change under a pure transposition?

See what cipher operations preserve for a side-by-side comparison with substitution and position-dependent shifts, including a runnable five-rune example.

The total length and each symbol’s count must remain the same. Consequently, a sum of fixed rune values and whole-stream IoC remain unchanged too. These are useful checks: if a purported rearrangement changes one of them, it also changed, added, or removed symbols.

What can change is adjacency and location. Word-like sequences, repeated neighboring pairs, column statistics, and which symbols fall on a particular row can all change. An improvement in one of those measurements must be evaluated against the choices tried; preserving the global counts does not guarantee meaningful output.

These statements assume a fixed symbol sequence. Adding padding to fill a grid, dropping a final partial row, or splitting a multi-letter rune label into separate Latin characters changes the input. For rune work, choose the actual rune as the unit; see transcription layers. The historical example above instead rearranges the Latin characters of an extracted message.

When the last row is incomplete

This is an invented example, not a proposed manuscript decoding. Put ABCDEFGHI into rows of width four:

A B C D
E F G H
I

The final row has one occupied position. Using the earlier order [2, 0, 3, 1], one explicit rule is to visit those columns in each row and skip positions that do not exist. The rows then become CADB, GEHF, and I. The combined output is CADBGEHFI: all nine original characters occur once.

	Last-row decision	Result under this row readout	Effect on the input

	Keep occupied positions; skip absent cells	CADBGEHFI	Preserves all nine characters.

	Pad the row as I···	CADBGEHF·I··	Adds three placeholder characters. Here · is an invented pad symbol.

	Discard the incomplete row	CADBGEHF	Removes the original I.


Neither padding nor deletion is a pure permutation of the original nine-character sequence. A padding rule also needs a removal rule when decoding; deleting every occurrence of the pad character can erase real data if that character was already present.

Reproduce the occupied-position rule

from collections import Counter

source = "ABCDEFGHI"
width = 4
order = [2, 0, 3, 1]
rows = [source[i:i + width] for i in range(0, len(source), width)]
result = "".join(row[c] for row in rows for c in order if c < len(row))
assert result == "CADBGEHFI"
assert len(result) == len(source)
assert Counter(result) == Counter(source)
print(result)

The condition checks whether a position exists; it does not discard any character based on its value. Column-first traversal of this same ragged grid would give CGAEIDHBF, so the fill direction and read direction still matter. The fourteen-column historical example above has five complete rows and does not require any of these short-row choices.

Define the search space
Record grid dimensions, fill and read directions, padding, and permutation. Fourteen columns admit 14! = 87,178,291,200 orders. A fragment selected after many choices needs stronger support than a prediction from an independently specified order. See controls and scope.
Sources and verification
Pinned historical walkthrough. Recipes reproduce published controls; they are not new solutions. Local computational verification: 19 October 2026.


A bounded reading-route experiment
The archived-layout route experiment tests sixteen row/column traversal configurations on LP2-00–55, retaining source-coordinate traces. None of its 880 cases matches the nine declared known openings. This limited criterion does not rule out other plaintext beginnings or transposition methods.

A separate within-word reversal experiment reverses runes inside transcription-defined segments while preserving segment order. It tests both splitting at line breaks and joining across them: 110 distinct page outputs, with no matches to the same nine beginnings. Its source-position diagram shows where those boundary conventions produce different routes. These segments are not independently established plaintext words.

The segment-order reversal experiment tests the other meaning of “read the words backwards”: read the last segment first but keep its runes in forward order. Its 110 distinct outputs also match none of the nine beginnings. For an invented input AB | C | DEF, within-segment reversal gives BA | C | FED, while segment-order reversal gives DEF | C | AB. Applying both gives whole-stream reversal, so those combined operations do not create an additional reading rule.

title: OutGuess extraction
summary: Choose the correct original image, extract its hidden payload, check the expected bytes, and follow the signed message to its next step.
text:
OutGuess retrieves a hidden payload from an image file. A visible title, artwork, or runic passage can coexist with a separate signed message inside the JPEG. Extracting that message is a different operation from decoding the visible runes.

Choose the image first

Two different images are often called “the cover.” The illustrated compasses collage is 1033.jpg; the plain Liber Primus title page is LP1-00. They have different hidden messages and different extraction sizes.


[Image: The dark 2014 opening image with white text]
Opening image
Script ID: opening-2014

[Image: The illustrated compasses collage]
Compasses cover
Script ID: 1033

[Image: The plain Liber Primus title]
LP1 title page
Script ID: lp1-00


Expected size of the full extraction, not the JPEG or separated message body
	Image / script ID	Extracted bytes	What to follow next

	opening-2014	1,150	Emerson book-cipher coordinates

	1033	1,498	RSA parameters and encrypted message

	lp1-00, lp1-01, lp1-02	2,899 each	Three hexadecimal bodies combined with XOR

	lp1-03	31,809	A hex-encoded JPEG inside the signed body

	lp1-10 through lp1-13	1,234 each	Historical instructions and magic-square material


Equal byte counts do not mean equal messages. Use the expected SHA-256 for the specific image’s extraction, as recorded in its manifest.

Prepare the files and tool

Use a repository checkout, or extract both the reference-data ZIP and original-images ZIP into the same directory. Keep their scripts/, data/, and images/ folders intact.
Install or build OutGuess for your operating system. The downloads contain reproduction scripts, not an OutGuess executable. The recorded extraction used the pinned upstream source.
Open a terminal in the directory containing those folders. Use Python 3 to run the wrapper below. If OutGuess is not on PATH, replace outguess after --outguess with its full executable path, quoted if it contains spaces.

Use the original JPEG, not a screenshot, thumbnail, or image saved through an editor. Resizing or recompressing the image can change the carrier bytes even when it looks the same.

Run one extraction

Choose one command for the file you want to inspect:

python scripts/extract_payload.py opening-2014 --outguess outguess --output opening-payload.bin
python scripts/extract_payload.py 1033 --outguess outguess --output compasses-payload.bin
python scripts/extract_payload.py lp1-00 --outguess outguess --output title-payload.bin

The wrapper first checks the original image’s hash. It then extracts into a temporary file using the literal key string Default key, compares the resulting payload hash with the recorded control, and saves your output only if they match. It refuses to overwrite an existing destination. The script makes no network or AI request.

For LP1-00, the underlying retrieval command is:

outguess -r -k "Default key" images/lp1-00.jpg title-payload.bin

Running OutGuess directly does not perform the wrapper’s input or output checksum checks. A successful retrieval message is therefore not equivalent to a match with the published control.

What success looks like

The wrapper prints Verified 2899 bytes. SHA-256: … for LP1-00, with the full checksum rather than the ellipsis. For 1033, expect 1,498 bytes; for opening-2014, expect 1,150. This establishes that the extracted bytes match the archived control. It does not verify a PGP signature or explain the message body.

Keep the output layers separate

	File layer	Purpose	Next operation

	Original JPEG	Preserves the visible image and hidden-data carrier	Check its hash, then extract

	.outguess.bin	Preserves the full extracted bytes	Compare the payload hash

	.signed.asc	Preserves the separated signed message	Verify the signature

	.body.txt	Contains the message body as a derivative	Interpret or decode the body’s specific format


The wiki supplies these layers separately in the payload inventory. Preserve the extraction unchanged. For LP1-00–02, the bodies are hexadecimal inputs to the three-image chain. For the compasses cover, the body supplies RSA parameters; for the opening image, it supplies book-cipher coordinates.

If the command fails

Python cannot find the script: check your working directory and extracted folder structure.
The OutGuess executable cannot be found: supply its full path. Having Python installed does not install OutGuess.
Input JPEG differs from the pinned original: obtain the original from Downloads and check that you selected the correct image.
Output already exists: choose a new output filename. The wrapper preserves existing results.
Extraction returns different bytes: retain the diagnostic, executable version, and input hash. The wrapper does not save unverified output under your requested destination.

Verified coverage
For the separate 77-image test, see the default-key OutGuess experiment. It records ten matching controls, 21 unverified outputs, five rejected retrievals and 41 abnormal exits. The per-image map distinguishes these outcomes; the failures do not prove that those files contain no hidden data.

The collection records ten default-key extractions: eight LP1 images checked on 19 October 2026 and the opening image and compasses collage checked on 20 October. This is a positive inventory of reproduced payloads, not an exhaustive search of every image, key, or steganographic method.

Eight-image LP1 manifest · Opening-image record · Compasses-cover record · Extraction wrapper. These records retain original-image and payload hashes. Signature evidence is separate from extraction evidence.


The default-key sweep now includes a saved-log audit: one reported seed/length pair occurs in successful exits with unverified bytes, rejected retrievals, and abnormal exits. Its Windows code corresponds to integer division by zero, but the saved logs do not locate the cause. The audit can be reproduced without running OutGuess; it does not replace the still-needed comparison with another documented build.

title: Embedded OutGuess payloads
summary: Eight LP1 images with reproduced extractions and verified signatures.
text:

	Image	Bytes	Files	Provenance
	LP1-00	2,899	Extraction · Signed block · Body	Source

	LP1-13	1,234	Extraction · Signed block · Body	Source
Default-key extraction and signature checks were repeated on 19 October 2026. The manifest records hashes and verification modes. This positive inventory does not rule out other hidden data.

LP1 title page, warning, and chapter title
LP1-00, LP1-01 and LP1-02 contain signed hex bodies. Decode and XOR them to recover another signed message. Follow the complete chain; examining one body alone misses that relationship.

Welcome: LP1-03
The body begins “Let the text guide you,” followed by a good-luck message and a hex-encoded JPEG. The embedded image is distinct from the visible manuscript image. Preserve the signed body separately from the decoded derivative. Full body.

[Image: Decoded LP1-03 embedded image: a narrow row of black runes and decimal digits on white]
JPEG decoded from the signed body; a derivative, not the carrier page.
Download the decoded JPEG (15,188 bytes). To reproduce it:
from pathlib import Path
body = Path("exports/steganography/lp1-03.body.txt").read_text()
image = bytes.fromhex(body[body.index("ffd8ffe"):])
with open("embedded.jpg", "xb") as f:
    f.write(image)
Read the embedded image’s transcription and reproduction guide.
LP1-10 through LP1-13
These historical instructions discuss a Tor hidden service, CGI uploads, three magic squares, and working alone. They are source documents, not current wiki setup instructions. Decorative borders use 3s on LP1-10 and LP1-11, 0s on LP1-12, and 1s on LP1-13. Similar prose does not make signed files byte-identical.

Magic squares: definitions, historical examples, and the payload number arrangement.
Reproduce, then interpret
Follow extraction, checksum verification, and signature verification as separate steps. This makes disagreements traceable to an operation and a file.
Sources and verification
Pinned historical walkthrough. Recipes reproduce published controls; they are not new solutions. Local computational verification: 19 October 2026.

title: Hexadecimal and byte streams
summary: An encoding of bytes, not by itself an encryption method.
text:
Two digits per byte
Hexadecimal uses 0–9 and a–f for values 0–15. Each digit encodes four bits; two encode one byte. Hex 41 is decimal 65, the ASCII byte for A. Leading zeros matter.

Read one pair by place value

For a two-digit hexadecimal byte, multiply the left digit’s value by 16 and add the right digit’s value. The letters a, b, c, d, e and f stand for 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15. Uppercase and lowercase denote the same values.

	Hex pair	Calculation	Decimal value	Eight bits

	04	0 × 16 + 4	4	0000 0100

	41	4 × 16 + 1	65	0100 0001

	5d	5 × 16 + 13	93	0101 1101

	77	7 × 16 + 7	119	0111 0111

	ff	15 × 16 + 15	255	1111 1111


The space in each bit string separates the two four-bit groups for readability. A byte has eight bits and can hold an unsigned value from 0 through 255. Interpreting that byte as a character is another step: 65 represents A in ASCII, but arbitrary payload bytes need not form readable text.

Leading zeros preserve byte boundaries

As integers, hexadecimal 4 and 04 have the same value. As a written byte stream, each byte still needs two digits. For example, 04 10 encodes two bytes with decimal values 4 and 16. Removing the first zero leaves 410, which has an unmatched digit; it does not encode the same two-byte stream under this convention.

The 0x prefix marks an integer literal in Python, as in 0x41 == 65. It is not part of the payload’s hexadecimal digit pairs. Python’s bytes.fromhex("41") decodes a byte, while bytes.fromhex("0x41") rejects the prefix. Likewise, do not convert an entire payload to an integer and back without preserving its byte length: leading zero bytes can otherwise disappear.

Written characters versus decoded bytes

A byte written 04 is one byte whose value is four. It is not the two text characters “0” and “4.” In the LP1-00 body, the first six hexadecimal characters are 775d04; decoding them gives three bytes, 77 5d 04. Encoding the literal characters as ASCII instead would give six bytes, 37 37 35 64 30 34.

hex_text = "775d04"
decoded = bytes.fromhex(hex_text)
characters = hex_text.encode("ascii")
print(decoded.hex(" "))    # 77 5d 04
print(characters.hex(" ")) # 37 37 35 64 30 34
assert len(decoded) == 3
assert len(characters) == 6

This is why the XOR trace operates after hex decoding. The characters used to write a byte and the byte they represent are different inputs.

Decode a cover body
from pathlib import Path
body = Path("exports/steganography/lp1-00.body.txt").read_text()
data = bytes.fromhex(body)
assert len(data) == 991
Whitespace may separate complete byte pairs. Each of the first three bodies has 1,982 hex digits and decodes to 991 bytes. Those bytes need not be readable. The next step is bytewise XOR.

Run from the extracted reference-data bundle or the repository root. Python’s bytes.fromhex accepts whitespace between complete byte pairs and either letter case. An unmatched final digit or a non-hex character raises ValueError. Do not repair such an error by silently dropping characters: check that you selected the message body, kept its bytes intact, and excluded prose or signature delimiters.

Do not decode prose as hex
LP1-03 contains prose followed by hex-encoded JPEG data. Isolate the hex portion before decoding and retain the complete signed body separately from the derivative image.
Sources and verification
Pinned historical walkthrough. Recipes reproduce published controls; they are not new solutions. Local computational verification: 19 October 2026.


For choosing and bounding other representations, see radix changes and byte encodings.

title: Exclusive OR (XOR)
summary: The bitwise operation used to combine the three cover-chain payloads.
text:
Exclusive OR, usually written XOR or ⊕, compares bits. Two equal bits give 0; two different bits give 1. Programming languages commonly use ^ for this operation on integers.

A byte example
00001111   (hex 0f)
00110011   (hex 33)
--------
00111100   (hex 3c)
XOR is not addition with carries and is not alphabet arithmetic modulo 29. It works independently at each bit position.

The three-image chain
The signed bodies from LP1-00, LP1-01, and LP1-02 are first decoded from hexadecimal. XOR their corresponding bytes to reconstruct a signed message. XORing their ASCII hex characters would be a different operation.

Follow the first five bytes

Three inputs: count the ones at each bit position

For two bits, XOR means “one or the other, but not both.” When repeated across three inputs, the rule is odd parity: the result is 1 if the number of input ones at that position is odd. It does not mean “exactly one of these three.”

	Number of ones	Example input bits	XOR result

	0	0, 0, 0	0

	1	1, 0, 0	1

	2	1, 1, 0	0

	3	1, 1, 1	1


For the last row, evaluate (1 ^ 1) ^ 1 = 0 ^ 1 = 1. The order of the three inputs does not matter. Apply the same rule independently to each of the eight positions in a byte.

Here is the cover chain’s first byte written in binary. Align the columns; do not add carries between them:

LP1-00   01110111   77
LP1-01   00010111   17
LP1-02   01001101   4d
         --------
XOR      00101101   2d

The rightmost column contains three ones, so its output is 1. The next column contains two ones, so its output is 0. Continue leftward to obtain 00101101. This is the byte value 45 in decimal, written 2d in hexadecimal and interpreted as a hyphen in ASCII. The input and output columns above are bytes, not rune indices or prime sums.

Compare the first five positions

Each row below combines the bytes at one offset in the three decoded streams. Offsets start at zero; all byte values in the table are hexadecimal.

	Offset	LP1-00	LP1-01	LP1-02	XOR output

	0	77	17	4d	2d

	1	5d	a1	d1	2d

	2	04	e1	c8	2d

	3	81	03	af	2d

	4	11	93	af	2d


For offset 0, 0x77 ^ 0x17 = 0x60, then 0x60 ^ 0x4d = 0x2d. The output byte 2d is the ASCII hyphen. The first five output bytes therefore form the five hyphens beginning the signed-message header. That recognizable prefix is a useful checkpoint, but it does not verify the remaining bytes or the signature.

How to replicate

Extract the reference-data bundle and run this Python 3 example from its top-level folder. It reads the three preserved message bodies, decodes them, and prints the reconstructed first line. It does not modify the inputs or write an output file.

from pathlib import Path

pages = ("lp1-00", "lp1-01", "lp1-02")
streams = [
    bytes.fromhex(Path(f"exports/steganography/{page}.body.txt").read_text(encoding="ascii"))
    for page in pages
]
a, b, c = streams
if not (len(a) == len(b) == len(c) == 991):
    raise ValueError("Expected three byte streams of length 991")
combined = bytes(x ^ y ^ z for x, y, z in zip(a, b, c))
print(combined.splitlines()[0].decode("ascii"))
assert combined.startswith(b"-----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE-----")
# -----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE-----

The length check prevents silent truncation by zip. Do not pad, cycle, or trim these documented inputs. This short example checks length and prefix only. For the full recorded input and output hash checks, run python scripts/reproduce_cover_chain.py. Follow the complete recipe for the separate signature verification and transposition.

Useful identities and their limits
A ⊕ A = 0 and A ⊕ 0 = A. Applying the same XOR mask twice recovers the input. The three inputs can be combined in any order because XOR is associative and commutative. Those identities explain the computation; they do not establish why a particular set of manuscript files should be combined.

Sources
Pinned 2014 walkthrough · Input and output hashes.

title: The cover payload chain
summary: The cover, warning, and chapter title combine into a signed message and a transposition.
text:
Looking for the cover with compasses? See the illustrated cover and its Blake artwork. It is separate from the title pages discussed here.


Three inputs
LP1-00, Liber Primus, LP1-01, the warning, and LP1-02, Chapter 1 — Intus carry OutGuess payloads. Extract and verify them. Their 1,982-digit bodies decode to three 991-byte streams.

Visible headings and the two title pages.
[Image: LP1-00: title]
LP1-00: title
[Image: LP1-01: warning]
LP1-01: warning
[Image: LP1-02: chapter title]
LP1-02: chapter title
What each stage produces
	Stage	Output to check
	Extract and verify the three messages	One signed hexadecimal body from each of LP1-00, LP1-01, and LP1-02
	Decode hexadecimal	Three separate streams of 991 bytes each
	XOR equal positions	A reconstructed 991-byte signed message
	Take its ciphertext and reorder columns	70 characters, retaining the literal ending ONIO
The visible Welcome text and its Vigenère key are not inputs to this chain. Likewise, the small image embedded in LP1-03 belongs to a different payload. Use exact page IDs when collecting the three source files.
XOR corresponding bytes
What XOR means, with a worked byte example.
XOR produces a 0 bit when input bits agree and 1 when they differ. Compute result[i] = A[i] XOR B[i] XOR C[i] on decoded bytes, not on hexadecimal text characters. For example, 0x0f XOR 0x33 = 0x3c.
python scripts/reproduce_cover_chain.py
python scripts/reproduce_cover_chain.py --output combined.asc
The script checks input and output hashes and refuses to overwrite files. Its 991-byte result is another signed message, requiring its own signature check.

Follow the first byte
The first decoded bytes are 77, 17, and 4d in hexadecimal. Pairing the same position in each stream gives:
0x77 XOR 0x17 = 0x60
0x60 XOR 0x4d = 0x2d
0x2d is the ASCII hyphen, the first character of the reconstructed PGP header. This checks one position only; the script checks the SHA-256 hash of the complete reconstruction. Decode the hex pairs first: XORing the character codes for the printed digits would use different inputs.
All three streams must have equal lengths. Do not pad a short stream, cycle it, or quietly discard unmatched bytes. If lengths disagree, check the extracted bodies and their hashes before proceeding.
Read the columns
Remove spaces from the first two ciphertext lines and arrange the 70 characters in five rows of fourteen:
IDGTKUMLOOARWO
ERTHISUTETLHUT
IATSLLOUIMNITE
LNJ7TFYVOIUAUS
NOCO5JI4MEODZZ
Within each row, take columns in zero-based order 2, 8, 9, 1, 12, 13, 11, 4, 5, 7, 3, 0, 6, 10. Concatenate the five reordered rows from top to bottom. This transposition gives:
GOODWORKULTIMATETRUTHISTHEULTIMATEILLUSIONJOINUSATFV7LYUCMEOZZD5J4ONIO

Follow the first four column selections
The first source row is IDGTKUMLOOARWO. Columns begin at zero, so column 0 contains I, column 1 contains D, and column 2 contains G. Apply the supplied order to that row:
	Output position	Source column	Character
	1	2	G
	2	8	O
	3	9	O
	4	1	D
The first four selected characters spell GOOD. Continue with the remaining ten column indices, then apply the same complete order to each of the next four rows. Here, output positions in the table count from one for readability, while source columns use the zero-based convention required by the script.
The instruction “read the columns” can otherwise be ambiguous: this recipe reorders characters within each row, then joins the rows. It does not read one entire vertical column from top to bottom before moving to the next.
Preserve the literal ending
The exact output ends in ONIO. The historical walkthrough restores a final N to render fv7lyucmeozzd5j4.onion. That character is an interpretation, not a permutation output. This is a historical address, not a claim of current reachability.
The supplied permutation reproduces the known result. It does not show that a unique ordering can be inferred without clues or applied to another page.
Sources and verification
Pinned historical walkthrough. Recipes reproduce published controls; they are not new solutions. Local computational verification: 19 October 2026.

title: PGP signatures and the Cicada key
summary: Verify archived messages and state what verification establishes.
text:
Signature validity and identity
A valid signature ties a signed message to a key. It does not decrypt its body, sign every byte of the enclosing JPEG, or by itself identify a real-world author. Historical association with Cicada is a separate provenance claim.
The full primary fingerprint of the exported key is 6D854CD7933322A601C3286D181F01E57A35090F. Check the key itself, not its filename or short ID.

Verify in a separate keyring
Install GnuPG, create an empty directory named verify-keyring, and run from the repository root:
gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --import exports/steganography/cicada-public-key.asc
gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --fingerprint
gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --verify exports/steganography/lp1-00.signed.asc
gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --verify exports/steganography/cover-chain.signed.asc
Compare the full fingerprint. A good signature and unknown trust can coexist: validity differs from identity-trust assignments. No private key is required.

Read the verification output
For an inspectable status stream, add --status-fd 1:
gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --status-fd 1 --verify exports/steganography/lp1-00.signed.asc
The fresh isolated check produced these status types: GOODSIG, VALIDSIG and TRUST_UNDEFINED. The VALIDSIG line identified the full fingerprint above. The trust warning did not mean the signature failed: this new keyring contained no identity-trust assignments. Do not assign trust merely to silence that warning. GnuPG documents these machine-readable records in its status-format specification.
The displayed user ID, Cicada 3301 (845145127), is a label associated with the key; matching that text is not the same as matching the fingerprint. Keep the verification result, key provenance, and real-world identity claim separate.
If verification fails
No public key: confirm that you imported the shipped key into the same directory supplied to --homedir.
No signed data: check that you selected the preserved .signed.asc block, not the extracted body or decoded binary stream.
Bad signature: compare the file checksum with the manifest and obtain an unchanged copy before drawing conclusions.
Rejected digest: inspect the exact diagnostic and the compatibility note below; a policy rejection differs from a verified signature.
Legacy digest compatibility
Some versions reject historical SHA-1 signatures by policy. If that is the reported cause, repeat this isolated check with --allow-weak-digest-algos on that command only. Record the flag; do not change global settings or treat SHA-1 as suitable for new signatures.

The earlier extraction manifest records the compatibility mode used in that run. A fresh isolated check with GnuPG 2.5.21 on Windows, --no-options, and no compatibility override verified all eight extracted signed blocks plus the reconstructed cover-chain message. The nine-file verification record stores input hashes, status lines, options and version. Do not assume a flag is necessary simply because another verification run used it.
--homedir selects the separate keyring directory; --no-options avoids reading the default options file. See GnuPG configuration options and digest compatibility options.
Why a valid signature is not a whole-file checksum

The preserved messages use a cleartext signed-message wrapper: readable text appears before an armored signature block. Its verification rules normalize the signed text. OpenPGP’s Cleartext Signature Framework specifies canonical CRLF line endings and excludes trailing spaces and tabs on each line from the signature calculation. The separator newline immediately before the signature block is also excluded.

As a result, two files can have different raw-byte SHA-256 checksums while representing the same text for cleartext-signature verification. This is not permission to edit the archive: preserve the original and use the catalogue checksum when the question is whether you have those exact bytes.

Why some lines begin with an extra dash and space

A body line beginning with a hyphen is prefixed with -  in the cleartext wrapper, so it cannot be confused with a wrapper delimiter. For example, the body text -example appears as - -example. Verification uses the unescaped text. This rule is called dash escaping; it is not an extra cipher layer.

Leave the preserved .signed.asc file intact and let GnuPG parse it. If you extract a body for another operation, retain that derivative separately and document the extraction rule.

	Question	Check to use

	Do I have the exact archived signed-block file?	Compare its size and SHA-256 with that file’s catalogue entry.

	Does the cleartext signature verify against this key?	Use GnuPG on the complete signed block and inspect the fingerprint and result.

	Did I decode the extracted hexadecimal body correctly?	Check the derivative’s declared bytes, length and hash under the chain recipe.


These checks complement each other. The cleartext rules above do not mean that arbitrary edits, different words or changed payload digits preserve a signature. They also do not describe every possible OpenPGP signature format.

Different files, different purposes
The manifest separately hashes full extractions, signed blocks, and bodies. Verifying an edited body is not equivalent to verifying the preserved signed block. See extraction and checksums.
Sources and verification
Pinned historical walkthrough. Recipes reproduce published controls; they are not new solutions. Local computational verification: 19 October 2026.

The later signed messages

The 2016 and 2017 messages connect navigation language with an instruction to verify signatures. Inspect the original 2016 carrier image, preserved message files and reproduced checks before interpreting their wording as a cipher hint.


For how this check fits the complete evidence trail, see source verification and transcription audits.

title: File hashes and checksums
summary: Identify exact bytes without confusing integrity, signatures, and decryption.
text:
What a checksum establishes
SHA-256 maps bytes to a 256-bit digest, displayed as 64 hex digits. A matching digest identifies expected bytes under the hash’s security assumptions, not their creator. Changed line endings can change a text file’s hash.

Choose the exact file you mean to check

The original JPEG, its thumbnail, a screenshot of the reader, and an image re-saved by an editor can all show the same page while having different bytes. For image analysis or OutGuess extraction, start with the original file linked by the page record. A screenshot is not a replacement for it.

	File you have	Compare against

	An original manuscript JPEG	That image’s entry in the catalogue

	A downloaded ZIP	The ZIP’s own checksum; after extraction, each member has its own checksum

	An extracted signed message	The signed-block entry, not the enclosing JPEG or message-body entry

	A text transcription	The same archived, corrected, or reading version—not a different text layer


Renaming a file does not change its content hash. Resaving it, changing text encoding, or converting LF line endings to CRLF can. File size is a useful preliminary check, but equal sizes alone do not establish equal contents.

Verify directly in the browser

Open Downloads and locate “Verify a downloaded file.”
Select the file you actually saved. The verifier computes SHA-256 locally in the browser and compares its hash and byte count against the catalogue.
Read the returned path, not just the word “Verified.” It identifies the catalogue entry whose bytes matched.

The file is not uploaded by this verifier. A “No exact match” result means no matching entry was found in this catalogue. It does not by itself say that the file is malicious or that an alternative archive is false. Check the intended version, whether the download finished, and whether an application modified the file.

Check a download
# PowerShell
Get-FileHash images/lp1-00.jpg -Algorithm SHA256
# Linux
sha256sum images/lp1-00.jpg
# macOS
shasum -a 256 images/lp1-00.jpg
Compare with the catalog or download entry. Hash the actual file, not its displayed preview.

Run from a folder containing images/lp1-00.jpg, or replace the path with your actual download location. The preserved LP1-00 original is 168,876 bytes and its expected SHA-256 is:

184e6f9de8695d99435c2bef4fd7e304a8a0f704dbe04439fa8bf13c4da395a7

Hexadecimal letter case does not change the digest value; PowerShell may display uppercase. Compare all 64 digits. A leading or trailing excerpt of the digest is not the full check.

Check the files inside an extracted bundle

The reference-data bundle includes a Python 3 checker. From the folder where you extracted it, run:

python scripts/verify_bundle.py REFERENCE-DATA-CONTENTS.json

It checks the recorded size and SHA-256 of each listed file, reports missing or changed members, and leaves your files untouched. A mismatch produces a nonzero exit status. Extra files, such as your own experiment outputs, are not part of this check.

If you extract the original-image bundle into the same folder, its separately named manifest remains available too:

python scripts/verify_bundle.py ORIGINAL-IMAGES-CONTENTS.json

Each bundle has its own named manifest; the transcription bundle uses TRANSCRIPTIONS-AND-READINGS-CONTENTS.json. The older name CONTENTS.json is also included for compatibility, but extracting another bundle into the folder can replace that generic copy. Use the separately named files when combining bundles.

The checker confirms agreement with the manifest you supplied. It does not authenticate that manifest, validate the transcription, or check files omitted from the list. Verify the downloaded ZIP against the published catalog separately when you need to establish which bundle you received.

Why invisible text changes matter

The byte sequence 41 0a is A followed by LF. 41 0d 0a is A followed by CRLF. An editor may display them as the same line, but their hashes differ. This small Python 3 example makes the distinction visible:

from hashlib import sha256

lf = b"A\n"
crlf = b"A\r\n"
print(lf.hex(" "), len(lf))
print(crlf.hex(" "), len(crlf))
assert lf != crlf
assert sha256(lf).digest() != sha256(crlf).digest()
# 41 0a 2
# 41 0d 0a 3

Keep the original byte file and any normalized text as separate artifacts. When documenting an experiment, name the version used and record its checksum before applying transformations. See reproducibility.

A hash check and a signature check answer different questions

A catalogue match checks whether your file agrees with the recorded bytes. Its value depends on which catalogue or source you chose to trust: replacing a file and its expected checksum together would still produce a match. A signature check instead verifies the signed content against a public key, whose provenance must also be established. Neither check proves that an interpretation or proposed cipher solution is correct.

Cleartext PGP verification normalizes certain formatting, including line endings. A valid signature can therefore coexist with a different whole-file hash. See the signed-text rules and dash escaping before comparing these two kinds of result.

LP2-56: exact target, algorithm assumptions, and input bytes.
The puzzle’s hash target
LP2-56 refers to a page identified by a hash. SHA-512 has 128 hexadecimal digits; it differs from this wiki’s SHA-256 distribution checksums. A hash is not normally reversible into its input. Candidate checks need the correct bytes and serialization.
See signatures for signed evidence and prime-minus-one for reproducing the text containing the target.
Sources and verification
Pinned historical walkthrough. Recipes reproduce published controls; they are not new solutions. Local computational verification: 19 October 2026.

title: Prime values and prime indices
summary: Distinguish a prime from its ordinal, and reproduce the 3299 and 9467 calculations.
text:
A prime’s value and its position in the ordered list of primes are different numbers. Specify which operation you mean before combining a prime with a page number or rune value.

Value versus ordinal
Write p_(n) for the nth prime, using one-based indexing: p_(1) = 2, p_(2) = 3, p_(3) = 5. Looking up p_(3299) gives 30,557. This means that 30,557 is the 3,299th prime; it does not mean that 3,299 has ordinal 30,557.
The rune alphabet instead uses zero-based positions 0–28. Rune index i has Gematria Primus value p_(i+1). Confusing these conventions introduces an off-by-one error.

Which way does the lookup go?

There are two different questions: “Which prime is in position 3299?” and “What position does the prime 3299 occupy?” Both use the number 3299, but they return different answers. In the first question, 3299 is an index; in the second, it is a value.

	Prime value	Its one-based position	Equivalent statement

	3299	463	p_(463) = 3299

	7649	971	p_(971) = 7649

	9467	1173	p_(1173) = 9467

	30557	3299	p_(3299) = 30557

	98597	9467	p_(9467) = 98597


For example, replacing the prime value 3299 with its position gives 463. Treating 3299 as a position and looking up the prime there gives 30557. “Take the prime ordinal” is ambiguous unless the direction is stated. The input to an nth-prime lookup need not itself be prime: p_(4) = 7 is perfectly well-defined, although 4 is composite.

The prime-counting function π(x) counts primes less than or equal to x. For a prime q, π(q) is its one-based position. For a composite x, π(x) still exists, but it is not the ordinal of x as a prime. Here π is a function name, not the circle constant.

The 3299 and 9467 examples
The decimal number 3299 appears in red on LP2-15. The arithmetic lookups p_(3299) = 30,557 and p_(9467) = 98,597 are exact. Their product is:
98597 × 30557 = 3012828529
 9857 × 30557 =  301200349
The second expression omits a 9 and gives a different answer. Preserve the operands as well as the final sequence when describing a hypothesis. These calculations establish arithmetic, not a relationship between manuscript pages.

LP2-15: the complete number panel, heading, and drawing.

Turning the product into a sequence is another decision

The product is an integer. Reading it as ten separate decimal digits, as five two-digit groups, or as a source of rune shifts gives different inputs. If you choose single digits and add consecutive primes, the first four sums are:

Product digits:     3  0  1  2
Consecutive primes: 2  3  5  7
Sums:               5  3  6  9

Using 0 instead of 7 at the fourth position changes that last sum from 9 to 2. Zero is a valid zero-based rune index for F, but it is not a prime. Such a replacement needs a separate, consistently applied rule: which F positions trigger it, whether they consume a prime, and whether the output is copied or transformed. The interruptions guide explains these alternatives.

Similarly, applying these sums modulo 29 is an additional operation, and applying them as shifts to ciphertext is different from interpreting them directly as rune indices. Write each step explicitly before judging whether the output looks meaningful. A change introduced to improve one fragment must be recorded and checked across the declared scope.

The complete ten-position calculation

Fix one rule: read the product’s decimal digits from left to right and add consecutive primes beginning at 2, without skipping, resetting or replacing any prime. This produces:

	Position	Digit	Prime	Sum

	1	3	2	5

	2	0	3	3

	3	1	5	6

	4	2	7	9

	5	8	11	19

	6	2	13	15

	7	8	17	25

	8	5	19	24

	9	2	23	25

	10	9	29	38


If a separate rule reduces those sums modulo 29, the sequence becomes 5, 3, 6, 9, 19, 15, 25, 24, 25, 9. Only the final sum changes: 38 mod 29 = 9. These residues could be interpreted as direct rune indices or as shifts applied to a specified ciphertext stream, but those are different operations. No ciphertext has been used in this table.

The reproduction script includes the digits, primes, sums and residues in product_digit_prime_addition. This provides a fixed arithmetic reference against which to describe another variant, including an F-triggered exception. The Unicode route discussed below is a separate proposed derivation; neither calculation demonstrates a connection between pages.

From the infinity code point to 7649

The proposed chain starts by identifying a drawn shape with the Unicode infinity character, U+221E, whose code-point value is decimal 8734. That identification and the use of Unicode are hypotheses about how to represent the drawing; the arithmetic that follows does not establish them.

Using the shortest binary spelling gives 14 bits. Flip each bit within that width:

8734: 10001000011110
flip: 01110111100001 = 7649

Equivalently, (2^14 − 1) − 8734 = 7649. This is a fixed-width bit complement, not decimal digit reversal and not reversal of the order of the binary digits. Width is part of the rule: flipping a 16-bit representation instead gives 65535 − 8734 = 56801. A programming-language operator with no declared width can behave differently again.

Next reverse the decimal digits of 7649 to get 9467. Both are primes and differ from one another, so they are emirps. Treating 9467 as a one-based prime index then gives 98597. The separate lookup for 3299 gives 30557, and their product is 3012828529 as shown above. These are individually checkable steps, each with its own representation choice.

What the Unicode names actually say

	Decimal value	Code point	Unicode name
	8734	U+221E	INFINITY
	7649	U+1DE1	COMBINING LATIN LETTER SMALL CAPITAL N
	9467	U+24FB	DOUBLE CIRCLED DIGIT SEVEN

7649 therefore has an N-related character name, but it is not ordinary capital N, whose code point is U+004E, decimal 78. Likewise, a character representing a double-circled seven is not automatically the number seven in a cipher. Turning these names into “N = 7”, then into an instruction to skip a symbol or substitute zero, introduces additional rules that the code-point lookup does not supply. The names can be checked in the official combining-mark chart and enclosed-alphanumeric chart.

How common is the emirp-to-emirp lookup?

Define a finite reference set: all integers from 1000 through 9999 that are prime and whose reversed decimal digits form a different prime. Count individual values, not reversal pairs; exclude palindromic primes. There are 204 such four-digit emirps.

For each value n in that set, calculate the nth prime p_(n), then test whether p_(n) is itself an emirp. Exactly 67 of 204 pass, approximately 32.84%. This independently reproduces the supplied count. The complete audit lists every input, its nth prime, and its pass/fail result.

This is a descriptive proportion for a declared population. It is not a p-value for the manuscript theory. The proposed numbers were not established as uniform random draws from that population, and the chain includes choices of symbol, code point, bit width, digit reversal, lookup direction and output interpretation. Squaring 67/204 would additionally assume two independent draws; that does not follow from selecting two numbers in a theory.

A claim about the prefix 301 would need to define what products were eligible, what counted as a match, and how many alternative transformations and prefixes were inspected. A short fragment that becomes readable only after replacing an inconvenient prime is a fitted result. Preserve that exception and test a fixed rule on new text rather than treating the fitted fragment as an independent confirmation.

Reproduce the chain and reference population

Run python scripts/audit_emirp_chain.py --check from the repository or extracted reference-data bundle. The standard-library script checks the binary widths, Unicode names, nth-prime lookups and all 204 reference cases. It uses exact trial division and makes no network requests. Use --output my-emirp-audit.json to save a new report without replacing an existing file.

This is an arithmetic audit, not a ciphertext experiment. The LP2-15 panel guide preserves the printed numbers; search space and bounds explains how to turn a chain of choices into a testable claim. The suggested subtraction and mirroring routes through pages 0–2 still need exact coordinates and traversal rules before their claimed 301 sequences can be reproduced.

How to replicate
python scripts/check_number_examples.py
Run with Python 3 from the repository or extracted reference-data ZIP. The script enumerates primes by exact trial division and checks both lookup directions and the products. Its JSON field prime_value_to_one_based_position reproduces the table above. It makes no network calls or model requests. See emirps and reversal for a distinct operation, and documenting scope before proposing a decoding chain.

Sources
Original page and provenance · Arithmetic source code. Prime notation is a mathematical definition; the page’s printed number does not itself specify this lookup operation.

title: Emirps and decimal reversal
summary: Check reversed primes without conflating reversal, mirroring, and prime lookup.
text:
An emirp is a prime whose decimal digits, reversed, form a different prime. Both primality and the difference condition matter. This is a property of a number’s decimal representation, not a cipher by itself.

Examples and non-examples
13 and 31 form an emirp pair. 11 is prime but palindromic, so it is not an emirp under this definition. 23 is prime, but its reverse 32 is composite. The pair 7649 and 9467 passes both prime checks.
Keep decimal reversal distinct from mirroring an image, reversing rune order, complementing digits, and taking a prime ordinal. Decimal reversal of 8734 is 4378. A transformation from 8734 to 7649 therefore needs a separately specified rule; “invert” alone does not define it.

Where this matters in the manuscript
The spelling and prime-sum article computes the three LP2-57 body sentence totals under a declared rune-only convention and checks their reversals. The boundaries and counting convention belong to the claim. Finding an emirp after changing a boundary is a different test.

The infinity character and 8734

The Unicode Mathematical Operators chart lists the infinity character as U+221E. The digits after U+ are hexadecimal: E represents fourteen. Converting the code point to decimal gives:

0x221E = 2 × 16³ + 2 × 16² + 1 × 16 + 14 = 8734

That conversion is exact for the Unicode character ∞. Choosing that character to represent the open crossed-loop drawing on LP2-15 is a separate hypothesis. A picture in a JPEG does not inherently have a Unicode code point, even when it resembles a familiar symbol.

	Specified operation	Result

	Convert hexadecimal 221E to decimal	8734

	Reverse the decimal digits of 8734	4378

	Replace each decimal digit d with 9 − d	1265

	Negate the integer 8734	−8734

	Complement the 14-bit representation of 8734	7649

	Complement the 16-bit representation of 8734	56801

	Reverse the decimal digits of 7649	9467


These are different operations, although several might informally be called “inverting.” The supplied proposal specifies a binary complement. It gives 7649 when the width is fixed at 14 bits: (2^(14) − 1) − 8734 = 7649. Fourteen is the shortest binary width that holds 8734; choosing 16 bits gives a different answer. The complete chain audit preserves this width choice, the subsequent decimal reversal and the prime-index lookups. Their arithmetic is reproducible; it does not establish that the drawing was intended as a Unicode instruction.

The same audit checks the supplied reference count: 67 of 204 four-digit emirps have an nth prime that is also an emirp. That proportion describes the defined set of numbers. It is not a probability that a proposed manuscript connection is intentional.

A code point is not a byte sequence

The same infinity character has code-point value 8734 and UTF-8 bytes E2 88 9E. The former is a number assigned to the character; the latter is one encoding of it. Reversing decimal digits, reversing hexadecimal characters, and reversing encoded bytes are distinct tests. Always record which representation is being used before applying a numerical operation.

This Python 3 check reproduces the character conversion, byte encoding, and two decimal transformations without any external package:

symbol = "\u221e"
value = ord(symbol)
reverse = int(str(value)[::-1])
complement = "".join(str(9 - int(d)) for d in str(value))
print(value)                          # 8734
print(symbol.encode("utf-8").hex(" ")) # e2 88 9e
print(reverse)                        # 4378
print(complement)                     # 1265
assert value == int("221E", 16) == 8734
assert reverse == 4378
assert complement == "1265"

For the later, independently checkable steps of the 301 calculation, see the two nth-prime lookups and their product. Keeping a correct multiplication separate from an unspecified earlier transformation makes the hypothesis easier to investigate.

How to replicate the predicate
from math import isqrt
def prime(n):
    return n >= 2 and all(n % d for d in range(2, isqrt(n) + 1))
def emirp(n):
    reverse = int(str(n)[::-1]) if n >= 0 else -1
    return n != reverse and prime(n) and prime(reverse)
assert emirp(7649)
assert not emirp(11)
Converting the reversed digits to an integer removes leading zeros. This convention must be stated if applying reversal to strings that are not already prime numbers. See prime indices and selection effects.

Reproducing rune prime sums provides a read-only command and explicit spelling comparisons.

Do archived rows have unusually many emirp sums?

The emirp row-sum experiment counts 41 qualifying rows among 594 archived rows on LP2-00–55. It repeats the prime-row baseline’s exact shuffle procedure: 539 of 999 simulated totals are at least 41, giving an upper-tail p-value of 0.540. This gives no evidence of a global excess under that model, not a conclusion about every individual row’s purpose.

The record has its own script, full row CSV, histogram and reproduction instructions. It sits beside the ordinary prime-row baseline in one family, with the changed numerical criterion explicitly compared. These are archived ciphertext sums; they do not retest the decoded sentence examples above.

Sources and evidence
Exact sentence sums and conventions · Checked numerical examples. No authorial purpose follows from the emirp property alone.

title: Magic squares in the 2014 puzzle
summary: Convert LP1-05 rune words into the 1033 square, check LP1-16’s 3301 square, and distinguish both from the embedded grids and LP2-15 panel.
text:
A magic square has equal sums in every row, every column, and both main diagonals. Its order is its width and height; its magic constant is that common sum. Equal row sums alone are not enough.

Which number grid are you looking for?
	Location	What is present	What is checked
	LP1-05	Five-by-five grid of numbers and rune words	After rune-value substitution, all twelve lines sum to 1033
	LP1-16	Five-by-five grid of printed numbers	All twelve lines sum to 3301 directly
	LP1-10–13 embedded messages	ASCII grids with differing borders	The displayed three-by-three interior alone is not magic
	LP2-15	Four-by-four decimal panel, with red 3299	Printed rows and columns have unequal sums
	LP2-49–51	Two-character letter-and-number entries between plant borders	256 entries in eight-column arrays; no numeral base assumed
These are different objects. Specify the page, whether the grid is visible or extracted, and any substitution before comparing totals.
Magic does not always mean normal
A normal order-n magic square uses each integer from 1 to n² exactly once. A general magic square need not use that range or distinct entries. Keep the definition separate from any additional rules in a historical challenge.

LP1-05: turning rune words into a 1033 square
The Some Wisdom page, LP1-05, prints a five-by-five grid containing both decimal numbers and rune words below CNOW THIS. The all-number version recorded in the historical walkthrough is a conversion of that mixed grid. Keep each printed number unchanged; replace each rune word with the sum of its Gematria Primus prime values.
[Image: LP1-05: red heading above a grid containing decimal numbers and rune words.]
Original-image detail, rectangle [500, 1900, 1400, 900]. Complete page · Original JPEG.
The resulting matrix is:
272 138 341 131 151
366 199 130 320  18
226 245  91 245 226
 18 320 130 199 366
151 131 341 138 272
All five rows, all five columns, and both diagonals sum to 1033. Entries repeat, so it is not a normal square. This is historical context, not a newly discovered Liber Primus solution.

Every rune cell, worked through
Row and column positions below start at 1. Latin labels identify the original runes; a multi-letter label can still represent one rune. Sum the listed prime values once each. Do not replace the unusual spellings with ordinary English or sum Unicode character numbers.
	Row, column	Rune labels	Prime values	Total
	1, 3	SHADOWS	53 + 23 + 97 + 89 + 7 + 19 + 53	341
	2, 1	AETHEREAL	101 + 5 + 67 + 11 + 109 + 73	366
	2, 2	BUFFERS	61 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 67 + 11 + 53	199
	2, 3	UOID	3 + 7 + 31 + 89	130
	2, 4	CARNAL	13 + 97 + 11 + 29 + 97 + 73	320
	3, 2	OBSCURA	7 + 61 + 53 + 13 + 3 + 11 + 97	245
	3, 3	FORM	2 + 7 + 11 + 71	91
	3, 5	MOBIUS	71 + 7 + 61 + 31 + 3 + 53	226
	4, 2	ANALOG	97 + 29 + 97 + 73 + 7 + 17	320
