Some Wisdom, LP1-05, makes three short assertions before the instruction “know this” and its arrangement of numbers and words. In contextual English, their sequence is:

The primes are sacred. A class of numbers receives a religious or evaluative description.
The totient function is sacred. The same description is applied to a mathematical function.
All things should be encrypted. The passage shifts from describing what is sacred to prescribing what should be done.

[Image: LP1-05, with the Some Wisdom text above a five-row arrangement of runes and printed numbers]
LP1-05: inspect the statements and the lower arrangement together. The magic-square guide explains the numerical reading of that arrangement separately.

This is an explicit connection between mathematical vocabulary and the book’s value language. It is stronger evidence for that connection than noticing a prime number elsewhere and assigning it a spiritual meaning. But “sacred” is not defined as a numerical test here. A prime is still defined by its divisors; the totient function counts positive integers up to a specified number that are coprime to it. Neither mathematical definition contains a claim about sacredness.

The encryption sentence is also an instruction, not a description of every page’s current encoding. Some Wisdom itself is a direct reading under the recorded rune-label conventions. The sentence therefore cannot serve, by itself, as proof that every readable passage must have another encrypted layer. A proposal for a second layer needs a defined input and operation, just as a proposal for an unsolved page does.

Read this beside primality and divinity: one passage calls primes sacred; another connects losing primality with losing divinity. The shared vocabulary makes an internal comparison worth pursuing. The texts do not state an equation between a person’s divinity and a word’s prime sum, or require applying the totient function to every rune. Those would be additional hypotheses.

To inspect the literal wording, run python scripts/reproduce_reading.py some-wisdom. It retains FUNCTIAN and THNGS, where the contextual English above uses FUNCTION and THINGS. See the rune-label conventions before treating those differences as alterations to the manuscript.

Circumference, primality and divinity

The three-passage reading map locates the recurring term and compares its contexts before the detailed interpretation.

The Loss of Divinity, LP1-10–13, assigns three behaviors to the circumference: consumption, preservation and adherence. It connects consumption and preservation with fear of insufficiency or inability to recover what is lost. Adherence includes following either dogma or reason for the sake of belonging and being right. The target described is therefore not simply religion; the same motive can attach to reason.

The second koan associates the inner voice with circumference. LP2-57's parable asks for the shedding of circumferences and the discovery of divinity within. Reading these occurrences together supports interpreting circumference as a surrounding or limiting aspect of identity. That is a textual interpretation, not a geometrical decoding rule.

The Loss of Divinity also uses “primality.” The primality and divinity guide compares all recorded occurrences and explains the distinction between arithmetic and metaphor. This connects naturally to prime-valued runes and the manuscript's numerical vocabulary, but the word does not establish which numbers to calculate. A numerical hypothesis must still name its input and boundaries; see reproducing prime sums.

Possession and attachment

The section that criticizes consumption and preservation also tells the reader to amass wealth, avoid attachment to possessions and be prepared to destroy them. Calling the passage a simple rejection of material possessions would miss that tension. A closer reading distinguishes possession from dependence on what is possessed. Whether the commands are literal, rhetorical or initiatory is not established by the decoded words alone.

The same section ends by commanding the reader to program mind and reality. The close reading of that instruction considers its position after the account of dependence and explains what the wording leaves unspecified.

For the opening passage’s sequence of losses and its closing instruction, follow pilgrimage, selfhood, and the Welcome.

The inward journey and emergence

The Welcome links going inward with emerging outward and invokes an instar. LP2-57 repeats the instar image, tunneling, the shedding of circumferences and emergence. This repeated vocabulary connects two distant sections more directly than an outside theory does. Compare LP1-04 with LP2-57.

The imagery permits a reading of transformation through inward examination. It does not by itself identify a biological species, a specific ritual, or a cipher key. The language of death and an end to self also belongs to this literary context; the known reading does not establish an operational instruction for a solver.

Outside works: start with a checkable parallel

The referenced works and possible influences index brings together documented book-cipher sources, cover artwork identifications, and literary comparisons, with the status of each connection.

William Blake and The Marriage of Heaven and Hell compares a close verbal parallel in LP1-04 with its external text. This is a more precise starting point than assigning the whole manuscript to a single movement. A possible allusion in one sentence does not automatically identify the source of its artwork, mathematics or other teachings.

The instruction following the first koan also has a possible literary association with Lewis Carroll's impossible-things dialogue. The wording, number and action differ; the comparison is weaker than a close verbal match.

For a closer reading of the three behaviors and the advice about wealth, see consumption, preservation, and adherence.

Sources and further reading

This is a close reading of the compiled known readings, supported by the linked page records and complete-section guides. For reproduction, use Running the reproduction scripts. The connections here are editorial interpretation, not additional decrypted text or authenticated statements of authorial intent.


Follow the recurring term in circumference, identity, and emergence, or use the known-reading concordance to locate a word or phrase yourself.

title: Self, identity and self-trust
summary: Why the Welcome both ends and commands the self; how the two koans compare with Emerson’s account of self-trust.
text:
How can a book promise an “end to self” and also tell the reader to command their own self? The tension is present within Liber Primus’s Welcome, before bringing any outside philosophy into the comparison. Its two koans then ask what an identity describes and what the speaking “I” refers to.

This guide compares those uses with Emerson’s Self-Reliance. The essay has a documented role in the earlier book cipher, but that does not establish it as the source of these manuscript passages. The comparison below is a reading of the texts, not a recovered cipher instruction.


Start with the passages


[Image: Original LP1-03, the first page of the Welcome whose known reading ends with an end to self]
LP1-03: the promised end to self. The next page continues the same section and ends with an instruction to command oneself.

[Image: Original LP1-14, the opening page of the second koan, which connects the I with the voice of the circumference]
LP1-14–15: the speaking I. Read both pages before interpreting the student’s denial.


	Passage	Question it raises	What the text supplies

	Welcome, LP1-03–04	What ends, and what can still be shaped or commanded?	The end of self, the shaping of ourselves, and self-command occur within one section.

	First koan, LP1-06–09	Does a description tell us who a person is?	The master rejects a name, occupation, species and account of consciousness.

	Second koan, LP1-14–15	What does the voice saying “I” refer to?	The master names the inner voice; the student’s denial becomes his example.


The table paraphrases the passages. Use the linked complete readings for literal rune labels, page boundaries, and decoding instructions.


Ending, shaping and commanding

At the end of LP1-03, the Welcome promises an end to self after listing struggle, suffering, innocence, illusions, certainty and reality. LP1-04 continues by saying that the pilgrimage shapes ourselves and our realities. It later calls the reader a being and a law unto themselves, then ends with self-command.

One possible reading distinguishes a fixed conception of oneself from the capacity to act and change. On that reading, ending an attachment to an identity need not mean ending all agency. This makes the sequence intelligible, but it remains an interpretation: the text does not formally define separate kinds of self.

A useful close reading keeps the difficulty visible instead of replacing every occurrence with “ego” and declaring the problem solved. That substitution introduces a term and a theory the passage has not supplied. Follow the pilgrimage and instar analogy for the surrounding language of inward travel and emergence.


An identity and a voice are different questions

The first koan repeatedly distinguishes who the student is from what a proposed answer describes. It ends with admission to study after an unfinished answer, not with a final definition of the person. The second koan gives the “I” a name—the voice of the circumference—and makes the student’s own thought the example.

The first story can therefore be read as questioning identification with a description; the second as questioning identification with the voice producing descriptions. This is a connection between their literary structures. Neither story supplies a scientific account of consciousness or demonstrates that all people think in an identical way. The self-reference explanation separates what the narrator reports from what the master claims it establishes.


Which self does Emerson ask the reader to trust?

Emerson’s instruction to “Trust thyself” appears in paragraph 3, beginning on printed page 2 of the preserved Dartmouth PDF. Reading that sentence alone can make the essay sound like an endorsement of whatever a person already believes.

Paragraph 21, beginning on printed page 9, makes the issue more demanding. Emerson explicitly asks what the “aboriginal Self” is and identifies the source he is seeking with “Spontaneity or Instinct,” then calls its primary wisdom “Intuition.” He connects it with a common source of life and distinguishes involuntary perception from voluntary acts of mind.

These are Emerson’s philosophical claims. The passage is not a psychological finding that an intuition must be correct. It also means that his self-trust cannot be adequately summarized as trusting every preference or defending a settled social identity. His question concerns the source of judgment, not merely its owner.

There is room for comparison with the koans’ refusal of ready-made identity descriptions. There is also a difference: Emerson develops an affirmative account of the source of self-trust, while the first koan leaves its student’s answer unfinished. That difference is more informative than treating both texts as interchangeable instructions to “be yourself.”

Paragraph numbers here refer to the preserved 50-paragraph derivative, counted from one; printed pages identify where those paragraphs begin. They are not universal locators across editions. The edition and extraction notes explain how the derivative was made.


What the comparison establishes


Documented: the cited manuscript passages have recorded readings, and Emerson’s essay is a reproducible source for the earlier opening book cipher.

Interpretive: these passages ask related questions about identity, inward authority and the source of judgment.

Not established: that Emerson supplied the koans, that every occurrence of “self” means the same thing, or that the comparison determines a cipher key.


To investigate an influence, identify a particular passage and compare wording, order and differences. To investigate a key, declare the input text and transformation separately. The historical Emerson control reproduces the earlier lookup; it does not test an Emerson-derived key on unsolved LP2 pages.


Sources and further reading

Manuscript sources: the linked complete readings and known-reading record, with status dated to the 5 October 2026 archive snapshot. Emerson source: paragraphs 3 and 21 of the preserved Dartmouth PDF and its linked paragraph derivative, inspected for this comparison. Continue with Self-Reliance, knowledge and authority, or the philosophical reading route.

title: Referenced works and possible influences
summary: Find documented book sources, cover artwork identifications, and literary parallels with their evidence and limits.
aliases: where did the drawings come from
text:
Outside works enter this research in several ways. A text used for a book cipher, an identifiable fragment of a painting, and a sentence resembling another author’s words are different kinds of connection. This index explains what has been documented and takes you to the passages, images, and reproduction details.

Which drawings have an identified source?

Use this directory when the question is “Where did that picture come from?” rather than “Which page contains it?” A named comparison, an identified composition and the exact digital file used to make a collage are different levels of evidence.

	Image	Evidence currently documented here	Inspect

	Compasses cover, 1033.jpg	Published identifications of fragments from three Blake compositions. The exact source reproductions are a further question.	Cover overview; Newton, Ancient of Days, Nebuchadnezzar.

	Reclining figure, LP1-14–16 and LP2-22	A published comparison with Jung’s Red Book, including reproduced comparison images. Source attribution remains unverified here.	Comparison images and page locators.

	Side-profile insect, LP2-14	The original manuscript drawing is located and described. No external source image is verified here.	Insect-image guide; original sheet.

	Detached wing, LP2-27	The original wing and its internal lines can be inspected. No external photograph or illustration is verified as its source here.	Wing-and-tree study; original sheet.

	Tree, LP2-32, LP2-55 and the 2016 message	R. Neil Marshman’s DeadTree.jpg on Wikimedia Commons; reflected and processed in the manuscript. The LP2-55 source alignment and LP2-32/2016 comparisons measure all three treatments under separate rules; the exact processing recipes remain unreproduced.	Photograph and attribution; shared-tree comparison.

	Branches, spiral borders and paired plants	Locations and visual comparisons are documented. A common source file, drawing tool or production process has not been established.	Branches and trees; spiral borders.


The cover’s Blake connections should not be carried over to the reclining figure merely because both are manuscript artwork. Likewise, evidence about the familiar Cicada logo would not by itself identify the source of a side-profile insect or detached wing. Each image needs its own comparison.

[Image: LP2-14: manuscript sheet containing the side-profile insect]
Side-profile insect · LP2-14
[Image: LP2-22: manuscript sheet containing the reclining figure]
Reclining figure · LP2-22
[Image: LP2-27: manuscript sheet containing the detached wing]
Detached wing · LP2-27

What makes a source-image comparison useful?

Begin with the candidate’s original publication or collection record, not just a reposted crop. Record the artist or photographer where known, title, date, edition or object identifier, and the exact reproduction being compared. A later upload date does not necessarily date the underlying artwork.

Show the manuscript crop and candidate side by side, retaining enough surrounding detail to check the match. Identify corresponding features: for a wing, branching veins and enclosed cells; for a figure, the pose, hand, feet and internal contours. Record any reflection, rotation, crop, scaling or thresholding used to align them. If several transformations were tried, retain that search history rather than presenting the best overlay as if it were the only comparison.

Stroke weight, soft edges or a resemblance to a filtered photograph can suggest a production method, but do not establish it. Keep three questions separate: whether a composition matches, which reproduction was used, and how it was transformed. An apparent match also does not by itself identify the manuscript’s authors or supply a cipher key.

For comparisons within the manuscript, the cuneiform study provides an example of fixed-window pixel comparison; the image-region guide explains coordinates and derivatives. Exact equality after decoding is a different claim from visual similarity. Neither should be reported without naming the compared files and regions.

Where each connection occurs

Start with the location before following a proposed influence. The earlier puzzle route, the illustrated cover, and the numbered manuscript releases are distinct objects.

	Work	Location in the puzzle	What connects them

	Emerson’s Self-Reliance	The 2014 opening message, before the compasses cover.	A reproducible book-cipher lookup yields the historical address of the cover site.

	Blake’s The Marriage of Heaven and Hell	LP1-04, in the Welcome.	A close verbal parallel concerning life and holiness.

	Carroll’s Through the Looking-Glass	LP1-09, the instruction following the first koan.	A possible comparison: four unreasonable actions versus six impossible beliefs.

	Three Blake compositions	The earlier 1033.jpg cover, not the plain LP1 title images.	Published identifications of visual fragments, discussed separately below.


The reader links open original manuscript images. The complete-reading and comparison guides explain the decoding and outside sources. For the corresponding passage in a particular edition, follow the source cited by that guide rather than assuming that page numbers or paragraph counts transfer between editions.

The Earls Barton tree comparison identifies a dated photograph and connects its reflected branch arrangement with the tree treatments on LP2-32, LP2-55 and the 2016 message. The LP2-55 source fit and cross-carrier checks measure related branch geometry. The exact image transformations remain unreproduced; the photograph does not establish a location for the puzzle authors.

Texts and literary parallels

Emerson: Self-Reliance

Connection: a documented book-cipher source in the earlier 2014 route.

Inspect: the source PDF, the paragraph, sentence, word, and letter counting convention, and the reproduced historical address.

Blake: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell

Connection: a close verbal parallel with the Welcome’s statement about life being holy. Other passages support thematic comparison.

Inspect: the actual wording and its context in both works, including the different uses of circumference.

Carroll: Through the Looking-Glass

Connection: a possible association with the instruction to do four unreasonable things.

Inspect: chapter V’s White Queen dialogue. Compare doing with believing, four with six, and a daily practice with the recollection about breakfast.


Emerson’s role in the earlier route does not prove that every later statement about selfhood comes from Emerson. Likewise, the Carroll comparison is not a quotation match. The linked articles preserve these limits alongside the evidence.

Artwork in the illustrated cover

[Image: The preserved 1033.jpg cover collage with central compasses fragments and narrow side panels]
The 1033.jpg cover belongs to the earlier puzzle route. It is separate from the plain LP1-00 title image.

The cover studies discussed in the linked guides identify fragments of three Blake compositions. Identifying a composition does not necessarily identify the particular impression, photograph, or digital reproduction used in the collage.


Newton
The upper central compasses panel. Compare the hand, instrument, and drawing, retaining the reported reflection.

The Ancient of Days
The lower central panel. Compare the fragment with the frontispiece to Europe: a Prophecy; the guide discusses rotation and the museum record’s qualified identification of the figure.

Nebuchadnezzar
The narrow side strips. Follow the divided figure and the artwork’s biblical subject without treating the title as cover plaintext.


These guides cite the published cover identification and museum descriptions separately. They also explain what to compare in the preserved image. For the visible motifs on the later manuscript pages, use the illustrated page index.

For the character associated with the lower panel, see Urizen: measurement and limits in Blake. That guide separates the figure’s literary background from the identification of a cover fragment.

Daniel and Newton's commentary

Connection: a proposed shared reference behind the cover's three Blake compositions. The cover reading map separates Nebuchadnezzar's story in Daniel 4, the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7, and Newton's writing about prophecy.

Inspect: the linked biblical passages and Newton's own commentary. The historical connections can be checked independently of the further hypothesis that one of these texts is a cipher source.

Jung: The Red Book

Connection: a published proposal comparing the reclining manuscript figures with an image in Jung's work. The comparison is not yet an independently verified source attribution here.

Inspect: the four manuscript locations and their orientations, the reported source-page locators, and the edition and ISBN information. The guide separates the observed drawings from the proposed source.

Young’s Night Thoughts
Connection: a proposed book lookup motivated by Blake’s illustrations and the 729-rune total of LP2-00–02. The count reproduces; a cipher result and the supplied scan’s edition remain unverified. The guide separates Young’s text, Edwards’s publishing role and Blake’s artwork, and defines what a repeatable lookup would require.

Terms and traditions are another kind of reference

The manuscript explicitly labels two dialogues as koans. That establishes the label in the known reading; it does not supply a traditional case number, teacher, lineage, or source collection. The koan guide explains the genre and follows the dialogues before considering outside attribution.

Similarly, instar is a biological term used in the Welcome and final parable. Its definition helps explain the analogy, but it does not identify a source book or prove that every insect drawing depicts the same species. Philosophical themes follows connections internal to the manuscript.

The self and identity comparison shows how to read two works together while retaining their differences: Emerson’s affirmative account of self-trust is compared with the first koan’s unfinished answer.

English Qaballa: order and value
Connection: a proposed comparison with an outside alphabet-assignment system. The guide identifies the Crowley passage, reproduces the step-eleven table, and explains why a 26-letter construction cannot simply be treated as a 29-rune cipher. No manuscript quotation match or decoding result is established.

How to add a useful comparison

Locate both objects. Give the manuscript ID and the outside work’s edition, chapter, plate, or collection record.
Show the correspondence. Preserve exact wording or specify the matching visual features. Record cropping, rotation, or reflection.
Record differences. A shared subject is less specific than the same arrangement of details or a close verbal match.
State the claim narrowly. Distinguish a useful comparison from an identified source and from a proposed cipher input.

If the comparison suggests a key, use the reproduction guide to define the operation and scope. A bibliography entry does not establish that a technique has been tried; that belongs in documented experiment records.

Hakuin: The Cicada’s Wing
A traceable English passage about emergence and harmful assistance, compared with LP2-57. The guide corrects a copied recipient name, supplies edition details, and separates the literary parallel from the detached wing’s unidentified source.

Sources and coverage

This is a directory of the sourced comparisons currently developed in Liberpedia, not an exhaustive list of influences or a claim about the puzzle authors’ beliefs. Each linked article supplies its primary text, collection record, historical walkthrough, or named attribution. New candidates should be added with that evidence rather than grouped together solely because their themes seem compatible.


The transcendentalism background page explains Emerson’s intellectual setting and separates that context from the documented use of Self-Reliance in the book cipher.


For the terminology behind these comparisons, see Blake prints: plates, impressions, and copies. Its illustrated explanation separates the printing method from the identity of a particular source image.


The Lady of Shalott: Tennyson and Waterhouse
The archived painting appears in the 2012 second-chance route. Its stored message points onward to a different image, identified in the walkthrough with Blake’s book. The guide separates that history from the poem and the unverified suggestion about the reclining manuscript figure.


Widsom in the Britannica scans documents three printed occurrences with image details and full-page downloads. The shared spelling is a source lead; borrowing by Liber Primus has not been established.

title: Testing knowledge, certainty, and authority
summary: Read the warning alongside inward discovery, adherence, and the instruction to impose nothing on others.
text:
The warning asks readers to test what the book says. Later passages direct them inward, criticize adherence, and tell them to impose nothing on others. These are related instructions, but they do not all answer the same question: how to check a claim, how to understand oneself, and how to treat another person are different problems.

Read the instructions together

[Image: Original LP1-01 warning page]
The warning places testing beside a demand to preserve the book.
[Image: Original LP1-16 instruction page with a number panel below the text]
The final LP1 instruction combines inward discovery with a limit on imposing it on others.

	Passage	Instruction or claim	Question it raises

	Warning · LP1-01	Do not accept the book without testing knowledge and finding truth.	What would justify accepting a claim?

	Welcome · LP1-03–04	The journey promises an end to certainty; the reader is told to command their own self.	Can self-direction coexist with uncertainty?

	Loss of Divinity · LP1-10–13	Adherence can attach to dogma or reason when motivated by belonging and being right.	Why is a person accepting or defending an idea?

	Instruction · LP1-16	Question, discover truth within, follow it, and impose nothing on others.	Where does directing oneself end and directing others begin?


The table paraphrases whole sections. It does not assign every phrase to every page in a range. Follow the complete readings for literal text, contextual English, and decoding instructions.

Belief, truth, justification, and knowledge

Epistemology studies questions about knowledge and justified belief. These distinctions help unpack the warning’s demand to test, without assuming that the manuscript endorses a particular philosophical theory.

	Term	Question to ask	Research example

	Belief	What claim does the person accept?	“I think this mark is a separator.” That identifies a position, not its evidence.

	Truth	Is the claim actually the case?	For an integer sum greater than 1, being prime or composite does not depend on how strongly someone favors either answer.

	Justification	What grounds support accepting the claim?	A declared counting rule, preserved input and independently checked calculation support a numerical claim.

	Knowledge	What makes the acceptance more than a lucky or unsupported correct answer?	Guessing a prime sum correctly and demonstrating the calculation are different achievements.


The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s analysis of knowledge explains the familiar “justified true belief” account and objections to its sufficiency. It should not be presented as a settled definition. For the broader field, see its epistemology overview. These references explain vocabulary; they do not establish a source for Liber Primus.

The distinction becomes especially useful when a calculation is correct but its interpretation is uncertain. Verifying that a selected string has a prime sum supports that arithmetic result. It does not by itself establish why those boundaries were chosen, whether a spelling was selected after inspection, or whether the authors intended the sum. Those are additional claims requiring additional evidence. See prime-sum reproduction and selection and chance comparisons.

A worked example: what does a prime sum establish?

Consider CWESTIAN in the final LP1 instruction. Under the recorded Gematria Primus values, its seven runes give 13 + 19 + 67 + 53 + 59 + 107 + 29 = 347. The spelling and its arithmetic are documented in the word-sum comparison. What can we conclude from that result?

[Image: Three separate questions: verify the arithmetic, evaluate a pattern against a stated comparison, and investigate whether the authors deliberately arranged it.]
A research distinction applied to the manuscript, not a diagram supplied by it. Open full size · Download diagram (SVG).

The arithmetic claim is directly checkable. Add the seven values and test the resulting integer. Since the square root of 347 is less than 19, it is enough to check the prime divisors 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, and 17. None divides it, so 347 is prime. That conclusion concerns this exact sequence and counting rule.

The pattern claim needs a comparison. “This sum is prime” and “this is surprisingly rare” are different statements. A comparison might examine other words with a specified length and encoding, or a declared set of alternative spellings. Those choices produce different questions. If many words, boundaries, reversals, or spellings were inspected before choosing this example, the comparison must account for that search. See null models and selection effects; this example does not supply a probability estimate.

The intention claim needs evidence about a deliberate choice. The book’s attention to primes makes the question reasonable, but a prime total alone does not show that this spelling was chosen to produce it. An explicit instruction or a consistent rule that successfully predicts additional cases would provide further evidence to evaluate. A small chance estimate would still not, by itself, identify an author’s purpose.

A useful research note therefore preserves the verified total while leaving the stronger questions open. It states which claim has been checked, which comparison has been performed, and which interpretation is being proposed. This follows the warning’s invitation to examine claims without turning that invitation into a ready-made statistical method.

Questioning a book while preserving it

The warning both invites scrutiny and forbids changing the book’s words or numbers. Those demands need not be contradictory. A reader can reject an interpretation while keeping the source intact. In research, the practical counterpart is to preserve the original image and transcription, then record corrections and proposed transformations separately.

This is an application of the passage, not proof of its intended meaning. It also explains why “the book tells us to do this” is not sufficient evidence for a solution: the warning itself withholds unconditional authority from the book. A proposed decoding still needs a defined input, a repeatable operation, and a way to distinguish its output from an attractive coincidence. See documenting a reproducible attempt.

Certainty is not the same as correctness

The Welcome includes certainty among the things the journey brings to an end. Read with the warning, this makes confidence an unreliable substitute for checking. That does not mean the text proves that knowledge is impossible. It can instead be read as challenging the reader’s attachment to already having the answer.

The first koan gives this tension a narrative form: the student offers increasingly abstract descriptions of himself, but admission follows his inability to finish an answer. The story supplies no final definition for a solver to insert. Its unresolved ending is part of the passage, not a blank that the wiki should silently fill.

Why “dogma or reason” matters

The Loss of Divinity criticizes following either dogma or reason for the sake of belonging and being right. Omitting “reason” would turn this into a simpler criticism of religious authority than the recorded text supports. The stated problem concerns the motive for adherence, not only the kind of argument followed.

In a research setting, agreement with a respected solver and a compelling calculation can both deserve examination. The calculation should remain independently checkable. Conversely, disagreeing with a group is not evidence that an alternative is correct. The manuscript’s language can motivate scrutiny without serving as a verdict on any particular hypothesis. For the surrounding account of dependence and identity, see circumference.

Inward truth and other people

LP1-16 places inward discovery and following one’s truth beside the instruction to impose nothing on others. One interpretation is that personal conviction does not automatically authorize control of another person. The Welcome’s instruction to command one’s own self supports that comparison.

“Truth inside yourself” does not settle how two incompatible factual claims should be evaluated. The passage offers no formal theory of truth. It would be too strong to label it a proof of relativism, or to conclude that a preferred cipher result needs no external check. Personal interpretation and a public claim about what a sequence decodes to have different evidential requirements.

Three instructions about directing oneself
The comparison becomes clearer when each instruction stays attached to its page. The excerpts below join words split by manuscript line breaks but retain the literal reading’s spelling. They are not substituted English spellings for prime-sum calculations.
LP1-04: COMMAND-YOUR-OWN-SELF. This short red line follows the passage about being a law unto oneself and the holiness of each intelligence. Its object is the reader’s own self. The text does not provide a practical program of habits or exercises here.
LP1-13: PROGRAM-YOUR-MIND.PROGRAM-REALITY. This follows the advice about wealth and attachment. The first command concerns the mind; the second extends the claim to reality. That extension needs interpretation: the phrase alone cannot establish a physical mechanism by which thought changes external events. See the close reading of this instruction.
LP1-16: FOLLOW-YOUR-TRUTH.IMPOSE-NOTHNG-ON-OTHERS. The final command supplies a boundary alongside personal conviction. Read together, the two sentences can support self-direction without treating another person’s agreement as something the reader is entitled to demand.
[Image: The small red instruction on LP1-04, read as AN INSTRUCTIAN. COMMAND YOUR OWN SELF.]
The first instruction is easy to miss below the main text. Inspect its location and original image.
What this comparison supports: the known readings repeatedly address how a reader directs their own thinking and conduct, and explicitly place a limit on imposition. What remains interpretive: whether those passages form one consistent ethical system, what “reality” means in LP1-13, and how the authors would resolve a conflict between inward conviction and public evidence. The book does not spell out those answers in these instructions.
For research, keep that distinction practical. A personal reading can explain why a passage matters to someone; a claim that a particular cipher produces that passage must still identify its input, operation and output. Neither individual certainty nor agreement from a group supplies the missing calculation.
Locate the wording yourself

The concordance searches the preserved contextual readings. Even that layer retains some unconventional spellings: the final instruction uses KWESTION. An exact search for question returns no hits in this snapshot; that is a spelling limitation, not evidence that the idea is absent.

python scripts/reading_concordance.py "believe"
python scripts/reading_concordance.py "kwestion"
python scripts/reading_concordance.py "impose"

Expected counts are 3, 1, and 1. KWESTION begins at contextual word 3 of the instruction; IMPOSE begins at word 13. These are one-based word positions, not rune offsets. For numerical work, return to the literal rune sequence and the spelling and prime-sum evidence.

For a closer reading of the three behaviors and the advice about wealth, see consumption, preservation, and adherence.

Sources and limits

This guide is an internal comparison of the nine recorded contextual sections, with literal readings and images linked above. The interpretations are editorial analysis, not additional plaintext. Emerson’s Self-Reliance provides a separately documented earlier-puzzle reference and a useful comparison; shared concerns about conformity do not establish that Emerson is the source of these instructions. Continue with the wider philosophical themes.

title: William Blake and The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
summary: The holy-life sentence on LP1-04, its literary parallel, and the limits of source and artwork attribution.
aliases: for all that liues is holy
text:
LP1-04 contains a close verbal parallel to the ending of William Blake's The Marriage of Heaven and Hell. It is a concrete comparison worth following; it does not establish that every philosophical or visual feature of Liber Primus comes from Blake.

The wording, side by side

	Source	Text	Location

	Liber Primus, contextual English	FOR ALL THAT LIVES IS HOLY	LP1-04, after the statement about each intelligence

	Blake	For everything that lives is holy.	Final sentence of the Chorus following A Song of Liberty


The wording is close but not identical: “all” replaces “everything.” The literal manuscript labels read FOR-ALL-THAT-LIUES-IS-HOLY after joining the archive's line wrap. LIVES is the contextual interpretation of LIUES, not an extra change to the rune stream. See the complete Welcome reading and literal-reading conventions.

Check the external sentence in Project Gutenberg's transcription of the 1906 edition, under Chorus near the end. This edition's printed page numbers are not identifiers for the original illuminated plates.

Find the sentence on the manuscript

[Image: The last two black-text lines in LP1-04's lower block. The encrypted runes corresponding to FOR cross the line break.]
A close-up of the original LP1-04 JPEG: the lower block's final two black-text lines, above the small red instruction. The image remains encrypted; the reading below comes from the Welcome decoding. Open the full page or download the unchanged original.

INTELLIGENCE-IS-HOLY.FO/
R-ALL-THAT-LIUES-IS-HOLY.

The slash marks the archived line break. Join FO/ R to recover FOR; the space shown here only separates the two pieces for explanation. The first sentence concerns each intelligence, while the next broadens the claim to all that lives. The small red line immediately below gives the instruction to command one's own self.

In the Welcome decoding trace (CSV), filter page to lp1-04 and inspect page_rune_ordinal 214 through 233 inclusive. These twenty runes produce FORALLTHATLIUESISHOLY. The label TH represents one rune, so counting Latin letters would give a different total. The CSV preserves each encrypted input rune, subtracted value and decoded index; see how to read the trace.

To locate the phrase in the stored literal reading without manually joining the wrap, run:

python scripts/reading_concordance.py "for all that liues is holy" --literal

The match is on literal text lines 12–13. These line numbers include the archive's intervening marker line and are not rune ordinals. The literal concordance guide explains the positions and retained source excerpts.

What the comparison supports

The shared wording supports describing this as a close verbal parallel and a plausible Blake allusion. The manuscript passage does not name Blake. A parallel cannot establish whether the authors consulted his work directly, encountered a quotation elsewhere, or intended the surrounding book to function as a key. Those are separate hypotheses.

For cipher work, a possible reference becomes a candidate source only after specifying a rule. Which edition, passage, characters, normalization and transformation? Choosing these after seeing promising fragments changes the scope of the test. Use the reproducibility guide and Have we tried it? to distinguish a source comparison from a documented technique test.

Read the surrounding argument

Blake's work also treats inward divinity and the limits of perception. In The Voice of the Devil, reason is described in relation to the outward circumference of energy. These provide additional comparison points with Liber Primus's Loss of Divinity and second koan. They are thematic or vocabulary comparisons, weaker than the closely matched final sentence. Similar words do not ensure identical meanings.

Within Liber Primus, the holy-life statement follows claims about the individual and intelligence, and precedes an instruction to command oneself. In Blake, the sentence closes a Chorus addressing religious authority and restrictions. Reading both settings prevents the shared line from becoming an isolated code token with no literary context. The philosophical themes guide traces the manuscript's internal connections.

Why the title joins Heaven and Hell

Before The Voice of the Devil, the 1906 edition, printed page 7, presents opposing forces as necessary to human existence. Its examples pair attraction with repulsion, reason with energy, and love with hate. It then associates religious labels of good and evil with passive obedience to reason and active energy. This prepares the reader for the reversal of familiar moral expectations in the next section.

Contraries here are opposing forces in the argument, not simply a logical error to be corrected. The text gives both sides a role in progression. Reading only the later circumference sentence can obscure that setting: reason appears within a relationship to energy, not as an isolated dictionary definition of a bad thing.

For Liber Primus, this suggests a question rather than an answer: does its criticism of adherence to reason concern the faculty itself, or the wish to belong and be right? Its wording specifies the latter motive. Do not substitute Blake’s opposition for the manuscript’s argument merely because both mention reason. Compare the complete passages before proposing a shared philosophical system.

The shared word “circumference”

In The Voice of the Devil, Blake describes reason as the “bound or outward circumference of Energy.” The sentence is on printed page 8 of the linked 1906 transcription. Its immediate subject is the relationship between body, soul, energy, and reason; “circumference” supplies a boundary metaphor.

Compare that with the manuscript’s three circumference passages. The Loss of Divinity assigns behaviors to the circumference. The second koan associates it with the voice of the I. The parable asks for circumferences to be shed. These are different grammatical and narrative uses, even though they share the unusual term and a possible idea of limitation.

	Comparison	What the wording supports	What remains unestablished

	Blake’s outward circumference and the manuscript’s circumference	A specific vocabulary parallel worth examining beside the known holy-life parallel.	That the manuscript uses “circumference” as an exact synonym for Blake’s reason.

	Reason in the two works	Both texts place reason in a critical discussion rather than treating it as an unquestioned authority.	That their criticism has the same target: the manuscript explicitly questions following reason for belonging and being right.


This distinction matters when interpreting the koan. The student’s inner voice is not automatically identical to reason, and a boundary metaphor is not automatically a geometric instruction. A useful reading needs to account for how the word behaves in each passage, not only its presence in both books.

Divinity within: another comparison to inspect

After the Proverbs of Hell, Blake’s prose account of poetic deities and priesthood ends with deities residing in the human breast. This passage is on printed pages 20–21 of the 1906 transcription. Its immediate concern is how poetic personifications become objects of religious authority.

Liber Primus’s final parable instead places inward divinity within a sequence of shedding and emergence. Both direct the reader inward, but the parable does not repeat Blake’s account of the origin of priesthood. This is a thematic comparison, rather than the close sentence-level match in the holy-life statement.

[Image: LP1-04, the Welcome page containing the holy-life statement]
Welcome, LP1-04: the close verbal parallel.
[Image: LP2-57, the final parable with an insect-like figure]
Parable, LP2-57: a broader comparison concerning divinity within.

The illustrated cover, the holy-life sentence, and these vocabulary comparisons are distinct pieces of evidence. Taken together they make Blake a concrete source to investigate. They still do not establish that every manuscript idea came from Blake, or that a particular edition was used as a cipher key.

The illustrated cover and other artwork comparisons
The compasses collage, archived as 1033.jpg, provides a separate visual connection to Blake. That entry displays the original and documents the published identifications of Newton, The Ancient of Days and Nebuchadnezzar.

The printmaking guide explains plates, impressions, and copies, with a diagram of relief printing.

Blake's work exists in distinct illuminated copies. The William Blake Archive's publication note for copy A records nine complete extant copies and separately identifies partial copies. An artwork comparison should identify the work, copy and plate or object, not merely link an image search for “Blake.”

For proposed connections elsewhere in the manuscript, pair the exact manuscript image with a catalogued source image, identify corresponding figures and composition, and record differences such as reversal, cropping or added objects. A general resemblance in flames, figures or ornament is a starting observation, not an attribution. Keep that comparison separate from a claim that the text supplies a decryption key.

How to check the textual comparison

Open LP1-04 in the reader and compare the original with the literal reading.
Follow the Welcome reproduction instructions to obtain the decoded sequence. Keep original spellings available.
Open the Gutenberg source above, find the Chorus after A Song of Liberty, and compare the sentence word by word.
For the other comparisons, find “outward circumference” in The Voice of the Devil and “human breast” in the prose after Proverbs of Hell. Read the surrounding paragraphs. Printed page numbers here belong to this edition, not to manuscript pages or illuminated plate identifiers.
Record the agreement and differences for each passage. Do not promote a likely allusion into a claim of authorship or a verified cipher result.

Sources and status

Manuscript evidence: LP1-04 source record and known readings, dated to the 5 October 2026 snapshot. External text: William Blake, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, Gutenberg edition 45315. Copy context: the William Blake Archive note linked above. Textual comparisons checked on 20 October 2026. This documents a literary parallel, not a newly completed cryptanalytic experiment.

title: Observations and measurements
summary: Start with a measured feature, then inspect its source, counting rule and relevant experiments.
aliases: could my scoring method miss the answer
text:
Start with the question you want a measurement to answer. A symbol count, a repeated sequence and an image-region count describe different features of the manuscript. This index points to the relevant guide, its inputs and its reproduction instructions.

Start with an observation

These are measured features or reproduced constructions, not proposed decryptions. Open the source and counting rule first; the linked experiment then shows which explanation or comparison was actually tested. A result on one representation or page range does not automatically apply to another.


Equal neighboring runes are scarce
There are 86 equal pairs among 12,901 within-page rune adjacencies on LP2-00–55 after removing non-runes. The lag comparison tests whether the deficit extends beyond immediate neighbors; the boundary audit locates pairs that cross stored separators. Neither identifies a cipher.

The stored separators define 2,896 rune tokens
The LP2-00–55 count includes headings and joins a page break when no delimiter intervenes. It assumes a stated parsing rule, not that each token is an English word. Compare equal-sized language samples and check disputed boundaries before drawing language conclusions.

Rune frequencies can be counted, but their meaning depends on the operation
Inspect per-page frequencies and index of coincidence with their exact rune-only denominators. A pure rearrangement preserves both; a changing substitution need not. Use cipher invariants before using a score to rank candidate readings.

Some rune sequences recur
The trigram record compares a fixed repeat count with page-wise shuffles. For a question about spacing rather than contiguous repeats, use lag matches. Neither measure yields a key length on its own.

Every entry of the LP2-15 number panel has a reproduced construction
Sixteen printed numbers match absolute distances from 3301 to Fibonacci-indexed primes arranged on the marked-origin spiral. The construction explains the panel; applying its sequence to ciphertext requires a separately specified key rule and search bound.

Five-dot groups share measured geometry
Groups on LP2-07, LP2-23 and LP2-56 align closely after stated reflections or rotations. Compare the original images, centroids and transform limits; the resemblance alone does not select rune positions or a cipher operation. The visual index distinguishes other marks and artwork.

Some image carriers contain extractable files
Follow each carrier to its extracted bytes, command and authentication status. The title and chapter pages separate visible text from hidden payloads; a successful extraction on one file does not imply the same payload on every page.


If you have a proposed mechanism, check Have we tried it? for a completed record with the same inputs and rules. The evidence-level guide distinguishes a source fact, a reproduced construction, a reported attempt and a completed test.

Choose a measurement


Does random-looking text imply a one-time pad?
Work through a finite example where each ciphertext symbol is uniform but the pair leaks a plaintext relationship. Distinguish independent keys, short seeds and the limits of a failed search.

How unusual are the word lengths in the historical corpus?
Inspect all 25,565 eligible file prefixes, exact ties and the effect of counting identical files once. The complete comparison includes every selected measure; its ranks describe this corpus and do not identify a language.

Could the plaintext be another language?
Compare the same passages in eight languages under explicit boundary and symbol-unit assumptions. Inspect full distributions, shorter aligned blocks, and controls using the established LP readings.

Does a spectrum label identify a hidden number?
A synthetic tone demonstrates why an FFT bin can read 1033.59375 Hz without the signal containing that exact frequency. Reproduce the calculation and compare zero-padding with a longer recording.

Why are there so few equal neighboring runes?
Locate all 86 doublets, inspect the three 4–2–1 groups, and separate count observations from proposed autokey explanations.

How long are the rune words?
Inspect token boundaries, compare rune-only and number-inclusive counts, and see what a comparison with an English corpus still needs.

Do runes match at a particular distance?
Count equal pairs at each lag, retaining the changing denominator and a stated shuffle expectation. A peak alone does not establish a key length.

How evenly are symbol frequencies distributed?
Calculate single-rune entropy in bits. The guide contrasts frequency balance with sequence order and randomness claims.

How unevenly are runes distributed?
Inspect per-rune frequencies and whole-page IoC. The guide supplies a baseline for the archived pages, a frequency chart and worked pair-count calculations.

Which rune sequences repeat, and where?
Count overlapping bigrams, trigrams or other window lengths. Reports include rune ordinals, source-file locations and the exact original slices.

Does a word or sentence have a prime or emirp sum?
Sum the declared rune values, reproduce known-reading examples, and compare explicit alternative encodings. Boundaries and text layers are part of the calculation.

How were dots, regions or colors counted?
Inspect original-image rectangles, pixel thresholds and connected-component rules. The opening-page inventory provides a scoped example with a reproduction script.

Do rows, columns and diagonals have equal totals?
Reproduce the documented square and compare it with other numerical arrangements. A symmetric grid need not be a magic square.

Which letter-and-number entries repeat?
Count exact, case-sensitive tokens on LP2-49–51. Download all 256 entries with grid coordinates and a frequency inventory; no numeral base is assumed.
Where does a word or phrase occur in the known readings?
Search contextual sections, or locate literal decoded wording on an exact page across line breaks. Reports distinguish word, character, and literal-line positions from rune offsets. Unsolved ciphertext is not searched as unknown English.


For completed records, the experiment reading guide distinguishes arithmetic audits, statistical comparisons, bounded cipher searches and tool checks, with examples of what each result establishes.

For cipher searches, begin with would your search recognize an answer? It connects the planted-key, decoder, language-score, search-budget and withheld-text controls, with a table separating exact recovery from score acceptance.

Understand your result

Keep the output beside the exact command that produced it. Then choose the question that matches what surprised you:


Two pages have the same IoC but different entropy. Is that an error?
Not necessarily. The worked six-symbol examples have equal matching-pair totals but different entropies. These scores summarize the same counts in different ways.

Why does a squared-frequency calculation disagree with IoC?
Check whether the calculation allows the same position to be selected twice. The pair-grid diagram shows which cells IoC excludes and how to convert between the two rates.

Entropy is below the uniform maximum. Does that show a pattern?
A finite random sample can have uneven counts. The two-symbol example distinguishes the source's entropy, the measured value, and the largest value the sample length permits.

I rearranged the runes, but the score did not change. Why?
Whole-stream IoC and single-rune entropy ignore order. A pure rearrangement preserves their inputs; it cannot improve either score. An order-sensitive measurement answers a different question.

There is a peak at one distance. Is that the key length?
The lag report counts matches and keeps each denominator. Interpreting the largest peak also requires a comparison model that accounts for all distances searched; see chance comparisons and selection.


None of these answers replaces checking the transcription. If the rune count itself differs, return to input layers and boundaries before comparing statistics.

Language comparison: choose the right control

A language ranking needs more than a list of scores. These four records answer different questions and share one experiment family:

Aligned language profiles: compare the same FLORES passages in eight languages. Word-length similarity and fixed-substitution repetition statistics have different assumptions.
Shorter aligned passages: check whether the ranking persists across eight disjoint sentence blocks, and whether known corpus languages match their corresponding reference profiles.
Known LP readings: check transfer to actual manuscript style and spelling. The pool ranks closest to English, but some individual known-English sections rank other language profiles first. The record also shows how an embedded hash can distort an unfiltered word count.
Exactly 2,896 tokens per sample: control the reference sample size. All complete reference samples are nearest to their own language profile, but the manuscript is farther from every profile than any of that language’s observed control samples. The reference ranges are descriptive, not confidence limits or rejection thresholds. Unlike the aligned-passage control, equal-token blocks do not cover identical translated passages.

Start with the baseline for the overall question, then use the controls to judge its limits. A nearest language is not a decryption or a probability that the plaintext uses that language. Each record provides its own scripts, exact inputs and download.


Why length and repetition can disagree

Consider the four-symbol example AAAA. Replacing every A with B gives BBBB. Applying successive shifts of 0, 1, 2 and 3 instead gives ABCD. Both transformations preserve the length, but only the fixed replacement preserves which positions match.

	Sequence	Length	Matching position pairs	Equal neighbors

	AAAA — input	4	6 of 6	3 of 3

	BBBB — fixed replacement	4	6 of 6	3 of 3

	ABCD — successive shifts	4	0 of 6	0 of 3


The matching-pair fraction is the index of coincidence. This toy example explains why a length comparison can remain relevant under a changing substitution even when the language's original IoC and doublet rate do not. Length still needs its own assumptions: preserved word boundaries and one counted plaintext unit per rune. Adding nulls or representing several letters with one symbol can change it too.

What would a first-place language mean?

It means that this profile has the smallest measured distance among the profiles supplied. There will be a first-place result even if every candidate is a poor match. Adding another language, changing the genre, or changing how letters become rune units can change the ordering. The eight-language comparison therefore does not rank every possible plaintext language.

A concrete example comes from the equal-token control. The manuscript’s letter-length distance to the English development profile is 0.0831, compared with a largest observed English control distance of 0.0508. English wins the relative comparison while still lying beyond that observed reference range. This does not reject English: genre, spelling and the correspondence between letters and runes remain uncontrolled. It shows why a ranking and an absolute fit assessment are different questions.

Use the full distributions to see where even the nearest profile disagrees, then check the known-English manuscript controls. Some short sections rank another profile first. A useful next test must state what it adds: a new fixed corpus, a different encoding assumption, or a previously untouched section. Choosing whichever spelling or grouping improves a score after seeing it creates a new hypothesis; it does not independently confirm the earlier one.

Download reusable data

These files let you inspect a published calculation or start a comparison without copying values from a table. Keep the source layer and counting unit attached to the data.

	Dataset and input	Files and method

	Whole-page rune statistics
Archived rune frequencies and IoC. Punctuation and decimal digits are excluded from the rune sequence.	CSV · JSON · Method

	LP2-31 lag coincidences
Equal rune pairs at distances 1–20. Each row retains its comparison count; no circular wraparound or inferred key period.	CSV · JSON · Chart and method

	Archived and decoded sums
Prime-value totals for 17 known-reading pages, before and after the recorded decoding.	CSV · JSON · Comparison

	Alphanumeric grid entries
Two-character tokens on LP2-49–51, preserving case and leading zeroes. Coordinates count grid rows, excluding surrounding runic text.	CSV · JSON · Import instructions

	LP2-15 number panel
All sixteen printed values, their differences from 3301 and prime checks, with grid coordinates and source hashes.	CSV · JSON · Method and exceptions

	LP2-56 dot measurements
Connected pixel components under a stated crop, brightness threshold, and area rule. Coordinates refer to the original JPEG.	JSON · Reproduce


For spreadsheets, import the grid’s token column as text so 04 remains two characters. The JSON preserves strings directly. For any downloaded file, the download catalogue supplies its exact byte count and SHA-256 hash.

A rune frequency and a grid-token frequency count different units. Likewise, an archived prime sum and a decoded prime sum come from different symbol sequences. Choose a common definition before putting results into one comparison.

Check the method before trusting its answer

A failed search can have several causes: the intended answer may be outside the tested keys, the decoder may not represent its alignment, or the scoring rule may reject meaningful text. These controls isolate different parts of that process. Choose the question that matches your method:


Could the transcription comparison miss an entire line?
Check whether text regions are found from the image or supplied by an existing row list. The eight-page control shows why equal row counts can conceal merged text and artwork detections. It does not claim that an archived line is actually missing.

Does a matching opening predict the rest of the text?
Keep every seed matching an assumed opening, then test its prediction on the remaining text. The synthetic controls separate a correct seed from an omitted seed, the wrong generator and an incorrect crib. What is a crib?

Would this score recognize meaningful text?
Give the scorer known text before asking it to recognize an unknown answer. The eight-language control measures fixed-threshold acceptance alongside letter shuffles. It tests the score, not a decoder or the manuscript’s language.

Can this decoder recover what its encoder produced?
Plant known rune sequences under explicit rules and retain the exact answer. The alignment controls distinguish prohibited paths, beam pruning, and a high-scoring but incorrect result. Start with the worked alignment diagram if those terms are unfamiliar.

Does the best result account for all the keys tried?
Repeat the complete search on controls and keep its maximum, just as you keep the observed winner. This record preserves nested dictionaries through 256 keys and separates a missing true key from one explicitly included.


A positive control supplies a known answer that the declared method should be able to recover or recognize. A negative control challenges the method with specified wrong keys or a chosen null input. Neither term means that a control represents every possible success or failure. Read the exact inputs and bounds before transferring a result to your own search.

For example, a no-skip decoder passing ordinary-addition controls does not establish that it handles key skipping. Likewise, a score rejecting these shuffled samples does not establish that it will reject the best output from a much larger search. Search space and bounds explains how to keep the claim aligned with the tested procedure.


Choose the input before comparing results

A manuscript page has several representations. Archived runes, corrected runes, decoded rune labels and contextual English are not interchangeable inputs. The image has additional information—placement, color and artwork—that a rune string does not preserve.

Name the source. Record the page ID, file and hash. State whether the input is archived, reviewed or decoded.
State the boundaries. Decide whether headings are included, whether separators are removed, and whether processing crosses words, lines or pages.
Keep the result with the rule. Include the script, command, parameters and output. A number without these details is difficult to compare or reproduce.

For example, the repeat script removes word separators, so a bigram can span two archived words. The prime-sum examples use known decoded runes, while the ordinary page-record sum uses archived runes. The guides explain these differences beside their outputs.

For repeating-period questions, use periodic IoC: it explains column assignment, unequal weights, and why a selected peak needs a matching comparison procedure.

Before using a measurement to rank candidate solutions

Evaluating candidate readings explains the difference between matching a known opening, ranking language-like output and reproducing a full reading. Its worked examples show why an opening test can reject readable text and accept a string whose remainder is meaningless.

Read what cipher operations preserve. A measurement that stays unchanged under every candidate transformation cannot distinguish those candidates. Whole-stream IoC, for example, cannot rank a set of pure transpositions of the same rune stream.

Also distinguish an observed value from evidence that it is unusual. A repeated pair is an observation; claiming it occurs more often than expected requires a stated comparison model. Selecting the best result from many lengths, keys or page subsets is itself part of the procedure and must be accounted for in that comparison. The reproducibility guide explains how to bound a proposed test and report its limitations.

Comparing patterns with chance walks through an exact six-arrangement example, including why the same input can give different probabilities under different selection rules.

Run a first check

Download the reference-data bundle, extract it with its folders intact, and follow the setup walkthrough. These two commands need only Python 3:

python scripts/rune_ioc.py --check
python scripts/rune_ngrams.py lp2-31 --length 2

The first compares the archived rune statistics with the shipped baseline. The second prints a descriptive repeat report for one page. Neither command tries to decrypt an unsolved page or calls the hosted assistant. Image-based checks additionally need the original-image bundle and, for pixel measurements, the documented optional dependencies.

Measurements and experiment records

For a complete example, follow repeated trigrams against page shuffles. It moves from a descriptive repeat count to a predeclared comparison, with a plotted null distribution, downloadable per-page counts and explicit limits on the conclusion.

These guides document methods and reproducible examples. To find whether a particular technique has been tested on specified inputs, use Have we tried it?. A related guide is background context; it is not proof that a proposed experiment has already been performed.

If your measurement suggests a hypothesis, preserve its scope and write a new reproducible record. A lack of a matching published record means the wiki does not document that test; it does not establish that nobody has tried it elsewhere.


Before treating an experiment as a rejection of a cipher, read what has actually been ruled out: exact proofs, bounded crib searches and necessary constraints justify different conclusions.

title: Index of coincidence: a reproducible rune baseline
summary: Matching-pair counts for every archived page, exact inputs, scaling, invariants and interpretation limits.
text:
The index of coincidence (IoC) measures how often two different positions in a text contain the same symbol. It summarizes the symbol distribution; it does not read the text or identify a cipher by itself. This guide provides a reproducible whole-page baseline for the archived Liber Primus runes.

Count matching pairs

Before using this number to compare candidate decodings, read what cipher operations preserve. A rearrangement or fixed reversible alphabet substitution cannot change whole-stream IoC.

Let N be the number of runes and nᵢ the count of rune i. The unscaled convention used here is:

IoC = sum(nᵢ × (nᵢ − 1)) / (N × (N − 1))

There are N × (N − 1) ordered choices of two distinct positions. A rune occurring nᵢ times contributes nᵢ × (nᵢ − 1) matching choices. Dividing gives the probability of a match when sampling positions without replacement. Counting unordered pairs instead divides both quantities by two and produces the same result.

For the three-symbol sequence F F U, only the two F positions match. The numerator is 2 and the denominator is 6, so IoC is 1/3. For F U it is 0; for F F it is 1. With zero or one symbol there is no pair to draw, so IoC is undefined. The JSON uses null in that case.

Why the two positions must be different

Label the positions in F F U as 0, 1 and 2. Without replacement, the six ordered pairs are (0,1), (0,2), (1,0), (1,2), (2,0), (2,1). Only (0,1) and (1,0) match, giving 2/6 = 1/3.

If the second position can equal the first, three more pairs appear: (0,0), (1,1), (2,2). All three necessarily match. The result becomes 5/9, not 1/3. The text has not changed; the sampling rule has.

	Pair rule for F F U	Matching pairs	All pairs	Match probability

	Distinct positions	2	6	1/3: this guide’s IoC

	Same position allowed	5	9	5/9: a different measurement


Let Q = sum((nᵢ/N)²) be the empirical match probability with replacement. There are N self-pairs, so removing them gives IoC = (N × Q − 1)/(N − 1) when N is at least 2. This relation explains the correction; it does not estimate a cipher’s key length.

Enumerate the pairs yourself

from fractions import Fraction

symbols = "FFU"
pairs = [(i, j) for i in range(len(symbols)) for j in range(len(symbols))]
distinct = [(i, j) for i, j in pairs if i != j]

def match_fraction(positions):
    matches = sum(symbols[i] == symbols[j] for i, j in positions)
    return Fraction(matches, len(positions))

assert match_fraction(distinct) == Fraction(1, 3)
assert match_fraction(pairs) == Fraction(5, 9)
print("Distinct positions:", match_fraction(distinct))
print("Same position allowed:", match_fraction(pairs))

This tiny enumeration is for checking the definition. The production script uses frequency counts instead of constructing every pair, which avoids a quadratic list as page length grows. Both methods should agree when they use the same pair rule.

Exactly what this baseline counts

Each page is measured separately using its archived text/lp…txt file.
Only the 29 symbols in the published rune alphabet count. A rune with a multi-letter Latin label is still one symbol.
All archived runes count, including rune headings. Punctuation, whitespace, line-wrap markers, Latin text and printed decimal numbers do not.
No transcription corrections, decryption, heading removal or page concatenation are applied. This is an archived-stream baseline, not a plaintext baseline.
A page with no archived rune transcription and a recorded count of zero has an undefined IoC. This does not imply that its image or embedded payload has no information.

Every record contains the input path and SHA-256, the rune count, a 29-entry frequency array, the numerator, denominator and IoC. The array follows the alphabet order stored in the same report. Its alphabet hash covers the UTF-8 concatenation of those 29 runes without separators. Unknown symbols in the Unicode Runic block cause an error rather than being silently discarded.

Reproduce the results

python scripts/rune_ioc.py lp2-31
python scripts/rune_ioc.py --check
python scripts/rune_ioc.py --output my-rune-ioc.json
python scripts/test_rune_ioc.py

Run from the repository or the extracted reference-data ZIP with Python 3; no extra packages, network access or AI are required. See script setup. The first command prints a single-page report. The second recomputes all 75 records and compares them with the published baseline. The third writes a complete report and refuses to overwrite an existing file. The fourth checks short controls, invariants and an independent enumeration of matching pairs.

Download the calculation script · Download all page results and input hashes. The reference-data ZIP includes the script and its inputs; downloading the script alone does not include the manuscript transcriptions.

Compare pages in a spreadsheet

Download the whole-page CSV for one row per manuscript page. It includes the input filename and SHA-256, alphabet hash, rune count, exact matching-pair numerator and denominator, ordinary and scaled IoC, and all 29 rune frequencies. The counting scope is repeated in each row so a filtered extract retains that context.

Columns count_0 through count_28 follow the rune alphabet’s zero-based indices. Blank IoC cells mean undefined, not zero: the title pages do not have enough archived runes for a pair calculation. Import the comma-delimited file with its header row, keep the hash columns as text, and sort entire rows rather than one column alone.

python scripts/rune_ioc.py --format csv --output my-ioc.csv

This recomputes the CSV from the archived transcriptions and refuses to overwrite an existing output. Add an exact page ID to export just that page. The downloadable CSV is a rendering of the published JSON baseline; the command above recalculates it from inputs. Sorting by IoC can help inspect the data, but a high or low rank is not a cipher classification or a probability that a page is unusual.

Examples from the archived streams

	Page	Runes	Unscaled IoC

	LP1-00	0	Undefined

	LP1-01	184	0.06402946

	LP2-31	269	0.03295789

	LP2-57	95	0.06270997


These are rounded display values. Use the integer numerator and denominator in the report for exact comparisons. The examples illustrate different input lengths and values; they are not a selection of statistically significant pages.

See the distributions behind the numbers

[Image: Two frequency bar charts on identical axes. LP2-31 has 5 to 13 occurrences per rune across 269 symbols. LP2-57 has zero to 15 across 95 symbols, with a larger concentration at rune index 18.]
Archived-stream frequencies for LP2-31 and LP2-57. Bars show the proportion of each rune, not raw counts. Open or save the full-size SVG; use the alphabet reference to look up an index.

LP2-31’s counts range from 5 to 13 per rune. LP2-57 has seven runes with no occurrences and one rune, index 18, with 15 occurrences. Concentration matters because a count contributes nᵢ(nᵢ − 1) matching pairs: a count of 15 supplies 210, while a count of 5 supplies only 20. Large counts therefore contribute disproportionately to IoC.

The dashed line is the equal-probability reference, 1/29 per rune. It is not a confidence bound or a minimum. A bar above it simply means that this rune occurs more often than the uniform proportion in this sample. The two pages have different lengths, and the chart does not estimate how surprising either distribution is.

To redraw the figure, extract the reference-data ZIP, install Matplotlib with python -m pip install matplotlib, then run:

python scripts/rune_ioc.py --check
python scripts/plot_rune_frequencies.py --output my-rune-frequencies.svg

The first command checks the saved counts against the archived inputs. The second reads those saved counts and renders the chart, refusing to overwrite an existing output. Matplotlib is needed only to redraw the figure; the numerical IoC checks use Python’s standard library. The plotting script fixes the axes and page selection so the two panels remain comparable.

What is the reference level?

For independent, uniformly distributed symbols from a 29-symbol alphabet, the expected match probability is 1/29 ≈ 0.03448276. This follows by adding the 29 possible matching outcomes, each with probability (1/29)². A finite sample need not equal this expectation. An observed value below it is possible; LP2-31 is one example.

The report also supplies scaled_ioc_29 = 29 × IoC, whose uniform independent expectation is 1. Always state whether a number is scaled. Do not compare this rune statistic directly with an English A–Z benchmark: the alphabet, multi-letter symbols, encoding and inclusion rules differ.

Why the uniform reference is not a minimum

Consider the two-symbol sequence F U. Each symbol occurs equally often, yet its IoC is zero: drawing two distinct positions must give different symbols. By contrast, two independent draws from a source that chooses F or U with equal probability match with probability 1/2. Equal counts in a fixed sample and equal probabilities in a generating process are different conditions.

For a fixed length N and an alphabet of K symbols, the lowest possible IoC comes from spreading the counts as evenly as the integer length permits. Write N = Kq + r, where q is the quotient and r the remainder. Then r symbols occur q + 1 times and the other K − r occur q times. Some counts may be zero when the text is shorter than the alphabet.

Minimum matching ordered pairs =
    r × q × (q + 1) + (K − r) × q × (q − 1)
Minimum IoC = minimum matching pairs / (N × (N − 1))

Why does balancing minimize the count? If one symbol occurs at least twice more often than another, moving one occurrence from the larger count to the smaller reduces the sum of matching pairs. Repeating that step ends when no two counts differ by more than one. This proves a bound over possible count distributions; it does not say that any particular cipher should produce the minimizing distribution.

Compare the three values for LP2-31

LP2-31 has 269 archived runes. Dividing by 29 gives a quotient of 9 and remainder of 8, so the most balanced distribution has eight counts of 10 and twenty-one counts of 9.

	Comparison	Unscaled IoC	Meaning

	Finite-sample minimum	2232 / 72092 ≈ 0.03096044	Lowest possible value for 269 positions and 29 available symbols.

	Observed LP2-31	2376 / 72092 ≈ 0.03295789	Calculated from the archived rune counts.

	Uniform independent expectation	1 / 29 ≈ 0.03448276	Average match probability under independent, equally probable symbols.


The observed value lies between the minimum and the independent expectation. That placement alone is not a significance test: it supplies neither a tail probability nor a measure of how often such a value occurs under a specified model. In particular, being below 1/29 is not evidence by itself of a deliberate balancing procedure.

Reproduce the comparison

import json
from fractions import Fraction
from pathlib import Path

report = json.loads(Path("data/evidence/rune-ioc.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
page = next(p for p in report["records"] if p["page"] == "lp2-31")
n, k = page["n"], len(page["counts"])
q, r = divmod(n, k)
minimum_pairs = r * q * (q + 1) + (k - r) * q * (q - 1)
