This is an editorial close reading of the compiled known readings, checked against the two literal page exports. For an external textual comparison in the Welcome’s closing passage, see Blake and the statement about life being holy. That verbal parallel does not establish the source of the entire journey narrative. Continue with the philosophical reading route and circumference and identity.


The later signed messages

The 2016 and 2017 messages connect navigation language with an instruction to verify signatures. Inspect the original 2016 carrier image, preserved message files and reproduced checks before interpreting their wording as a cipher hint.

title: Blake prints: plates, impressions, and copies
summary: Understand relief etching and distinguish a composition, an individual print, and the digital image used for a cover comparison.
text:
The cover studies refer to a design, a print, a copy, and a digital reproduction. These are different objects. Understanding the distinction helps explain why identifying a Blake composition does not automatically identify the image used in the compasses collage.

What is relief etching?

In Blake’s method, an acid-resistant drawing protected parts of a copper plate while exposed areas were etched lower. The remaining raised design could be inked and printed. Text and images could occupy the same plate; lettering was written backward so that the impression read in the intended direction. Prints could then receive further colouring and pen work. This summary follows Joseph Viscomi’s account of illuminated printing.

[Image: Schematic cross-section: ink sits on two raised areas of a plate; a print receives marks at the corresponding contact areas.]
A simplified relief-printing principle, not a reconstruction of a particular Blake plate. Heights and spacing are schematic. Open full size · Download SVG.

Blake called the process illuminated printing and its products illuminated books. Here “illuminated” names his way of making the work; it does not mean that the book is a medieval handwritten manuscript. Viscomi also distinguishes the history of the technique from later explanations of Blake’s motives for inventing it.

Which object are you comparing?

Design or composition
The arrangement of figures and other visual elements. Recognizing the hand and compasses concerns the design.
Printing plate or matrix
The physical surface from which an image is printed. It is not the paper image or a JPEG.
Impression
A particular print taken from that surface. Separate impressions can preserve the same design while differing in ink and finishing.
Copy of a book
A particular example of the book, identified by the catalogue. “Copy A” in the Europe record is not a claim about the puzzle image’s source.
Digital reproduction
A photograph or scan of an object. Its crop, resolution and colour appearance introduce another layer into a comparison.

Why the same design can look different

The Blake Archive describes variations caused by colour printing and subsequent finishing. Its 2012 publication announcement also explains that most of Blake’s large colour prints appear to have used a different kind of matrix from his relief-etched book plates. Do not assume that Newton, Nebuchadnezzar, and the Europe frontispiece were all made by one identical process.

For the cover, first compare the arrangement of details. Then ask whether a specific impression shares distinctive marks or colour placement. Finally compare the digital reproduction for matching crop and image defects. Record any rotation or reflection separately. A colour difference alone cannot decide whether the source was another impression or an altered reproduction.

Keep a useful comparison record

Save the collection identifier and source URL, the named copy or impression, and the exact region being compared. Separate observations from adjustments you made to align the images. The image-region guide explains pixel coordinates; the works index explains how to state the resulting claim. No printmaking term by itself supplies a cipher key.

title: Rune matches at a distance: lag coincidences
summary: Compare runes at fixed distances, reproduce exact pair counts, and distinguish descriptive peaks from evidence of a period.
text:
A lag is a distance between positions in a sequence. At lag 2, compare each rune with the rune two places later. Counting equal pairs gives an order-dependent description of the text: rearranging the same symbols can change the result, even when whole-page IoC stays unchanged.

A five-symbol example

For the teaching sequence ABABA, lag 2 makes three comparisons:

Position:   0  1  2  3  4
Sequence:   A  B  A  B  A

Compare 0 with 2: A = A
Compare 1 with 3: B = B
Compare 2 with 4: A = A

Matches: 3 out of 3

There is no comparison from the final A back to the beginning. This tool does not wrap around. Its complete result for the example is:

	Lag	Equal pairs	Pairs compared	Rate
	1	0	4	0
	2	3	3	1
	3	0	2	0
	4	1	1	1

The rate at lag 4 is also 1, but rests on just one pair. Always keep the denominator beside the rate. A large value supported by very few comparisons is not equivalent to a persistent pattern across many positions.

Reproduce the manuscript calculation

Extract the reference-data bundle with its folders intact. Python 3 and its standard library are sufficient:

python scripts/rune_lag_matches.py lp2-31 --max-lag 4
python scripts/rune_lag_matches.py lp2-31 --max-lag 20 --output lp2-31-lags.json
python scripts/test_rune_lag_matches.py

The first command reports 0/268, 9/267, 5/266, and 10/265 for lags 1–4. The JSON also gives reduced fractions and decimal rates. These are descriptive counts from the archived 269-rune stream, not a newly established key period or solution.

For the same measurement across all archived LP2-00–55 pages at lags one through five, see the short-lag profile. It keeps page boundaries and shows how the adjacency deficit compares with fixed-count page shuffles.

The default maximum lag is 20; explicitly choose a smaller value for a shorter stream. Valid lags run from 1 to one less than the rune count. The output option refuses to overwrite an existing file. The script uses rune_ngrams.py from the same bundle to identify runes; keep that helper beside it.

Inspect all twenty distances

[Image: Bar chart of equality rates at lags one through twenty on LP2-31, with a dashed count-preserving shuffle expectation. The reference line is not a significance threshold.]
All lags 1–20 under the same archived-rune rule. The number of compared pairs decreases from 268 to 249. Open full size · Download chart (SVG).

Download the CSV table for a spreadsheet, or the JSON report for the complete counting rule and shuffle model. Each CSV row retains its numerator, denominator, input path and source hash. The dashed line is an expected rate under the stated model, not a cutoff for an interesting result.

To reproduce the chart, use the extracted reference-data bundle and install matplotlib in your Python environment, then run:

python scripts/plot_rune_lags.py --output my-lag-chart.svg

The plotting script reads the included JSON; it does not recalculate or alter the rune stream. The counting script remains standard-library only. Keep the plotting-library version with shared figures; visual formatting can vary between versions. Existing output files are not overwritten.

What exactly is counted?

The script retains archived runes in order, including headings, and removes non-runes. Pairs may therefore cross word, line, and paragraph breaks, but never page boundaries. It performs no spelling conversion, correction, decoding, or interruption skipping. The report records the input file, its SHA-256, the alphabet, and its hash.

For a stream of length n and a lag d, the denominator is n − d. The numerator counts indices i = 0, …, n − d − 1 for which x[i] = x[i+d]. These are forward pairs counted once. They are different from the all-position ordered pairs in the ordinary IoC formula.

What would a shuffled stream give?

Under a uniform random rearrangement preserving the symbol counts, any two distinct positions have expected equality rate Σ c(c−1) / [n(n−1)]. Each fixed-lag pair uses two distinct positions, so averaging their equality indicators gives that same expectation. This derives an expected rate, not a distribution of possible peaks.

The report includes this fraction as shuffle_expected_rate_fraction. It is not a p-value, a confidence interval, or a threshold for a meaningful result. Pairs can overlap, and results at different lags share the same input. If you select the largest result after scanning many lags, a chance comparison must repeat that selection procedure. See null models and selection.

How all distances add up to IoC

Every pair of distinct positions has exactly one positive distance. If you calculate all lags from 1 through n − 1, you count every forward pair once. Consequently:

Matching forward pairs
Σ c(c−1) / 2
All forward pairs
n(n−1) / 2
Ratio of these totals
Whole-page IoC

Here c is each symbol’s frequency. Both totals are half the ordered-pair totals used in the IoC formula, so their ratio is unchanged. This is an identity for the observed stream, not just an average expected from shuffling.

In the ABABA example, combine the counts: (0 + 3 + 0 + 1) / (4 + 3 + 2 + 1) = 4/10. The same stream has three As and two Bs, giving IoC (3×2 + 2×1) / (5×4) = 8/20. Both equal 2/5.

Do not average the four rates equally. That would give (0 + 1 + 0 + 1) / 4 = 1/2, because it assigns a one-pair lag the same weight as a four-pair lag. Weight each rate by its number of comparisons, or simply divide the summed numerators by the summed denominators.

The LP2-31 chart above includes only lags 1–20, so its pooled rate need not equal whole-page IoC. For the identity, all 268 distances are required. Lag counts reveal how matching pairs are distributed over distances; their full total supplies no independent evidence beyond the same frequency counts.

What the result cannot decide

An elevated lag can motivate a more specific test; it does not identify a cipher or key length by itself. Changing the heading policy, page boundaries, or skipped positions changes the sequence being measured. Record those choices before comparing reports.

Renaming symbols consistently leaves equality unchanged. Reversing the whole stream also preserves the count at each lag, because it pairs the same positions in the opposite direction. This statistic therefore cannot choose between a stream and its reversal. For local repeated patterns and their source positions, use the n-gram tool; for the broader principle, read what operations preserve.

Files and checks

Calculation script · Checks. Tests also check the all-lag identity on every three-symbol sequence of lengths 2–6. They cover the hand example, valid lag bounds, symbol renaming, reversal, and the expected rate averaged over all six distinct arrangements of AABB. The archived-page check verifies the 269-rune scope and its comparison denominators. These validate the stated calculation, not the original photographic transcription.

title: Reclining figures and the proposed Jung comparison
summary: Compare the figures on four manuscript pages and follow the published Red Book attribution to its stated sources.
text:
A reclining human figure appears at the bottom of LP1-14–16 and LP2-22. These pages give researchers a specific image to compare across releases. A published comparison with C. G. Jung's Red Book is also discussed below; it remains separate from the observations visible in the manuscript originals.

Find the manuscript figures

On LP1-14–16 the head is on the left and the feet on the right. LP2-22 reverses that orientation. Opposite orientation alone does not establish that one image is an exact reflection of another.

[Image: Lower detail of LP1-14, showing the reclining figure in its original orientation.]
LP1-14, lower detail. Read the complete sheet · Original JPEG.

[Image: Lower detail of LP2-22, showing the reclining figure in its original orientation.]
LP2-22, lower detail. Read the complete sheet · Original JPEG.

LP1-14 and LP1-15 contain the second koan. LP1-16 contains the final instruction and its numerical material. On LP2-22, the figure lies below a separate three-crossbar drawing; the closing-page study locates both details.

The published Jung comparison

In his 11 February 2020 essay, under “Jung's Daniel,” Frank G. Bosman discusses a proposed resemblance between the reclining figure and an image in Jung's Red Book. He gives two locators: page 44 in the original sequence and page 281 in the 2009 edited text. These are locators reported by Bosman, not an independently verified source-image attribution by Liberpedia.

The distinction matters: a published comparison establishes that someone proposed the connection. Confirming the source of a drawing requires inspecting the cited image and documenting the matching details. Identifying a borrowed drawing would still not establish that Jung's surrounding prose supplies a cipher key.

Inspect the reproduced images

Bosman's post supplies a two-page reproduction labeled 43 and 44 and an enlargement of the illustrated scene. In the spread, the scene occupies the lower part of the right-hand page. These links show the images accompanying his proposal, rather than an independently catalogued scan.

In the enlargement, a reclining figure occupies the lower right, feet toward the left and head toward the right. A smaller standing figure appears to its left. The larger scene includes a dark border, a blue field with many pale dots, and two broad curved forms above. The manuscript's isolated line drawing does not reproduce that surrounding scene.

Compare the head-at-right orientation with LP2-22 above; the LP1 figures have their heads at the opposite end. Record body contours and internal lines as well as orientation before claiming a copied or mirrored drawing. On 20 October 2026, the two archive.org page links cited by Bosman failed to load during our check. The reproductions remain useful comparison material, but do not resolve the edition provenance or establish a particular source file.

Which book is meant?

The Red Book and Liber Novus name Jung's work. The Library of Congress exhibition explains that Liber Novus, meaning “New Book,” appears on its spine. Jung developed the work from earlier notebooks, revising the material and combining calligraphy with paintings, decorated initials, and borders.

Liber Primus is also a section title within Jung's work: the Oregon Friends of Jung library record lists Liber Primus, Liber Secundus, and Scrutinies among its contents. That internal title and Cicada's manuscript title refer to different works. A shared name is a reason to investigate a possible reference, not evidence that their page numbers or text can be interchanged.

Illustrated edition or Reader's Edition?

The Philemon Foundation's publication record distinguishes these editions. Record the ISBN as well as the title when citing a proposed image source:

2009 illustrated edition
W. W. Norton, edited and introduced by Sonu Shamdasani; translated by Mark Kyburz, John Peck, and Shamdasani. ISBN 9780393065671. The Foundation lists 404 pages and illustrations.
2012 Reader's Edition
A text edition containing the text, introduction, and scholarly apparatus. ISBN 9780393089080. Do not assume it reproduces every manuscript image or uses the illustrated edition's pagination.

For freely accessible examples of Jung's illustrated pages, the Library of Congress exhibition above supplies labeled enlargements. Its selection does not include the page 44 image cited by Bosman, so it establishes the book's visual context rather than verifying this particular comparison.

How to check the proposed source

Identify the edition. Record the title, editor or publisher, year, and whether the locator refers to a manuscript page, a printed page, or a scan's image number. Do not interchange Bosman's two page numbers.
Compare the whole composition. Examine the head, limbs, body contour, and surrounding marks. A generally reclining posture is less specific than a matching arrangement of these details.
Record transformations. Compare the unaltered images first. Label any reflection, rotation, crop, or change in proportions used for an overlay, and retain the originals.
Separate findings. State which features match, which differ, and whether the comparison identifies a composition or a particular digital reproduction. Keep any proposed textual or numerical operation in a separate test.

The cropped views above leave the original JPEG bytes unchanged. The download catalogue provides original files and checksums. For other candidate sources, use works and possible influences; for a reproducible test record, follow documenting an attempt.


For source attributions and open image-origin questions across the manuscript, use the artwork-source directory. It distinguishes published comparisons from verified source identifications.


The proposed Lady of Shalott comparison needs its own image evidence. Waterhouse’s painting is documented in an earlier 2012 route, but that does not identify this manuscript figure.

title: Evaluating candidate readings
summary: Distinguish a known-opening match, a language ranking and a complete reading, and interpret the limits of each test.
text:
A script can generate thousands of candidate readings without telling us whether any is a decryption. To interpret its result, first ask what the script was instructed to recognize. Matching a fixed beginning, receiving a high language score and reproducing a complete reading are different achievements.

For the other half of the question—exactly which possibilities produced these candidates—see search space and bounds.

What an opening test answers

Several experiments in this wiki compare the first twelve output rune indices with nine beginnings taken from known readings. The numerical-sequence family, for example, uses Warning, Welcome, Some Wisdom, the first koan, Loss of Divinity, the second koan, Instruction, LP2-56 and LP2-57. These are exact vectors stored in each plan, with hashes identifying their source traces.

This asks a useful, limited question: does this declared transformation produce one of those particular beginnings at the start of this input? It does not ask whether the output contains any possible English sentence. There is no established requirement that an unsolved page must repeat a known opening.

The comparison is in runes, not twelve Latin characters. A rune label such as TH can contain more than one letter. See rune counts and character counts before attempting to reproduce the comparison from a displayed transliteration.

A match can be too narrow for the conclusion

The following invented examples use ordinary characters so the distinction is visible. Suppose the test accepts any string beginning with THE , while the complete reference is THE DOOR IS OPEN. None of these strings is a manuscript result.

	Candidate	Opening test	What remains unknown

	THE DOOR IS OPEN	Passes	This also equals the supplied full reference, but that requires a separate comparison.

	THE XXXX XX XXXX	Passes	The opening test says nothing about the remainder.

	PLEASE OPEN THE DOOR	Fails	The readable sentence begins differently. This test was not designed to recognize it.


The second row is a correct positive result for the stated prefix test. The error would be reporting it as a complete decryption. Likewise, the third row is a correct negative for that prefix; the error would be treating it as proof that the text cannot be readable.

Read the actual result with its scope


Prime-minus-one shifts
3190 configurations on 55 nonempty LP2 pages produced no matches to the nine declared beginnings. The tested offsets, directions and uninterrupted advancement are part of that result.

Fibonacci shifts
3190 configurations produced 1540 distinct full page outputs. The repeated configurations do not add different candidates; neither count is a count of independent statistical observations.

Row and column reading routes
Sixteen declared routes per nonempty page produced no matches to the same nine beginnings. This does not cover arbitrary transpositions or a second cipher applied after rearrangement.


A precise report says “no declared opening matched under these rules.” It should not shorten this to “Fibonacci does not work” or “transposition was ruled out.” Conversely, keeping a method open is not evidence in its favor: it identifies what the recorded test has not settled.

What a broader language test would need

A language score could rank candidates that begin differently. To make that ranking reproducible, a new experiment would need to publish the scoring rule as carefully as the cipher operation. It should specify:


The representation. Decide whether the model scores rune indices, literal rune labels or interpreted English. Specify how spaces, punctuation and multi-letter labels are handled. Do not silently repair spelling before scoring.

The reference material. Identify the corpus, its version and hash, and the exact conversion into the scored alphabet. Separate material used to build or tune the score from material reserved to check its behavior.

The rule. Publish the formula or executable model, treatment of unseen sequences, length normalization and any acceptance threshold. “Looks like English” is not a reproducible numeric criterion.

The search. Record all keys, offsets, page subsets and score variants examined. A favorable score selected from many candidates needs a comparison that includes that selection process; see chance comparisons.

The controls. Show whether known readings score sensibly, and what happens to appropriate altered or shuffled inputs. A reading used to choose the score cannot also serve as untouched evidence that the chosen score generalizes.


The highest-scoring candidate always exists when a finite nonempty set has numeric scores. Its rank alone does not tell us that the candidate is meaningful. Publish the competing outputs and score differences, rather than showing only the winner.

The eight-language scorer controls now test a fixed English threshold on known text and letter shuffles. The planted decoder controls separately compare exact rune recovery with score acceptance: value rewriting often leaves a high-scoring but incorrect sequence. A separate search-maximum control now checks complete nested dictionaries through 256 keys; it does not calibrate larger or adaptive searches. The fixed-opening searches retain their original acceptance rule and results.

If a candidate looks promising

Cribs and text reserved for checking a prediction

A crib is an assumed piece of plaintext at a specified position. For example, assuming that the first three decoded rune indices spell a particular word supplies a constraint on the key. The spelling, rune encoding and location are part of that assumption. A word that merely sounds plausible is not independently known plaintext.

The withheld continuation is text that you did not use to choose the candidate. Freeze the key and decoding rules before inspecting it. Then ask whether the same rule predicts the continuation without new exceptions. If you use the continuation to change the key, choose a different path or repair the spelling, it has become part of development rather than an untouched check.

The known-crib seed controls make this distinction measurable. At two opening runes, the four searches containing their planted generator and seed retain 4, 6, 11 and 8 candidates. Only the true generating pair in each search predicts the complete remaining passage. Other controls obtain prefix matches even with a wrong generator or an incorrect crib. These are synthetic fixtures with known answers, not new readings of the unsolved pages.

For an unsolved passage, the continuation has no known answer to compare against. Record what would count as corroboration before inspecting it: exact additional text specified by an independent source, reproducible constraints, or a separately justified decoding result. Readability judged after trying many alternatives remains a selection process; a longer attractive phrase alone does not provide the same check as exact recovery of withheld known text.

Preserve the complete candidate

Save the complete output and the exact settings before making interpretive changes. Check the transcription against the image, then apply the same declared rule to the rest of the stated input. Mark every exception, skipped rune and inserted word. A short attractive phrase should not hide unexplained text elsewhere.

Distinguish a control from a prediction. Recovering a known reading can show that an implementation handles a documented method. If you designed a rule around that reading, recovering it does not independently establish the rule on an unsolved page. A useful follow-up specifies what additional text or feature the rule should explain before inspecting that result.

When changing a criterion or boundary rule after seeing an output, preserve the original record and describe the change in a related experiment. The reproducibility guide explains how to retain the inputs, commands and limits. Have we tried it? keeps those separate records together as a family without turning a narrow negative result into a universal verdict.


Before searching keys for a proposed word, check whether its rune repetitions fit the assumed cipher. The worked crib-pattern check gives an exact compatibility test for fixed one-to-one substitutions, including why separately plausible words can conflict under one shared mapping.


For a worked numerical example, see key alignment, skip limits and beam search. It shows how one rejected key slot changes the subsequent decoding and distinguishes a prohibited path from one discarded by scoring.

title: Word lengths and corpus comparisons
summary: Count rune tokens, reconcile the 2896 and 2902 conventions, and separate manuscript measurements from English-corpus claims.
text:
Word lengths can reveal structure that a one-rune-for-one-rune cipher preserves. Before comparing them with English, define the units and boundaries. A count of Latin letters, a count of runes, and a count that includes decimal labels can describe different datasets.

Count runes, not the letters in their labels

The rune labeled TH is one symbol. An illustrative encoding of THE as TH + E has length two; T + H + E has length three. Those are different spelling or conversion choices. An English reference corpus must use a documented conversion rule, not merely have its spaces and punctuation removed. See rune indices and labels and transcription layers.

Here, a token means a unit selected by a stated parsing rule. Calling it a token avoids assuming that every visible separator corresponds to an English word. A decimal label is visibly present, but it is not a rune.

A reproducible count for LP2-00–55

Our descriptive audit concatenates these archived pages in order, removes slash and newline wrapping, and preserves other delimiters. It includes headings and joins tokens across page boundaries where the transcription has no intervening delimiter. An internal apostrophe stays in its token and counts zero runes. Decimal numbers and the alphanumeric table do not contribute to the rune-only count.

Under those rules there are 2,896 rune tokens containing 12,956 runes. There are 448 tokens of length two (15.47%) and 720 of length three (24.86%). These are measured counts, not evidence by themselves of a particular cipher or a departure from English.

[Image: Histogram of 2896 rune-only tokens in LP2-00 through LP2-55; three-rune tokens are most frequent at 720, followed by four-rune tokens at 513 and two-rune tokens at 448]
Runes per token under the stated boundary rules. This chart contains no English reference distribution. Download the counts and conventions.

Joining pages matters. Parsing every page separately with the same within-page rules produces 2,928 pieces: some words are split by the sheet boundary. That is a different object, not an alternative spelling of the same count. The complete token ledger records the original start and end page and character offsets, including tokens that span pages.

LP2-21: three consecutive lengths of 11, 11 and 10

On LP2-21, three consecutive rune tokens have lengths 11–11–10. They are tokens 1,167–1,169 in the joined LP2-00–55 ledger, not word numbers printed on the page. The exact pattern occurs once among the ledger’s 2,894 overlapping three-token windows. This is a descriptive count under the conventions above, not an English-language probability.

	Ledger token	Rune sequence	Length

	1,167	ᚦᛖᚩᛄᚷᛋᛝᚣᛗᛟᚻ	11

	1,168	ᛗᚠᚦᛉᚦᚫᛋᛈᚣᚩᚠ	11: ten before the line wrap, one after

	1,169	ᛈᛟᛋᛖᚫᛇᛗᛚᛈᚾ	10


The middle token crosses a line wrap. Treating that wrap as a separator would split it into lengths 10 and 1 and erase the reported chain. Under the archived conventions, slash and line breaks are transparent while the surrounding hyphens delimit tokens. None of these three tokens crosses a page boundary or contains an apostrophe. The summary report now includes the matching tokens and their source offsets; the independent scanner checks the middle token’s 10+1 split.

A one-rune-for-one-rune cipher that preserves boundaries must preserve this length sequence. It does not follow that the three plaintext words have 11, 11 and 10 Latin letters: TH, NG and other multi-letter labels can represent single runes. Nor does this observation by itself reject English or establish a boundary-changing cipher. A comparison needs a frozen rune-conversion rule, a stated corpus and a rule for selecting unusual patterns. Choosing this chain after inspecting the page and then treating it as a preselected test would overstate its significance. No solved-text baseline or statistical significance result is claimed for this chain here.

Why an earlier summary has 2,902 tokens

The pinned historical summary is consistent with six additional length-one tokens. The archive contains exactly six isolated single decimal digits:

	Page	Digit or labels	Added tokens

	LP2-10	7	1

	LP2-36	1	1

	LP2-37	2, 3, 4	3

	LP2-38	5	1


Including these as length-one tokens reproduces all fourteen length proportions and the summary’s mean, median, minimum, maximum, quartiles, sample standard deviation and variance to numerical precision. The count becomes 2,902 tokens and 12,962 counted units; the extra six units are decimal digits, not missing runes.

	Convention	Length-one tokens	Total tokens	Total counted units

	Runes only	83	2,896	12,956 runes

	Runes plus six single digits	89	2,902	12,956 runes + 6 digits


This is a reconstruction consistent with the published summary, not proof of the original tokenization code’s intent. Its original per-token ledger was not available in the inspected repository. The difference also does not remove the reported contrast between two- and three-rune counts: those counts remain 448 and 720; only their denominator changes. The complete pinned-corpus comparison now reproduces that separate descriptive calculation with independent source and rank checks.


Which symbols occur across the complete reference corpus?

The complete symbol audit uses the same pinned source revision and first-2,902-token rule as the historical prefix comparison. It reads every source path, retains shorter files separately, and compares each selected character with our stored 29-rune alphabet. It does not remove headings, normalize characters or infer the missing conversion rules.

ᛂ (U+16C2, Unicode name RUNIC LETTER E) is the only character outside the stored alphabet in these selected prefixes. It occurs in 25,554 of the 25,565 eligible file-path prefixes. Eleven eligible prefixes contain only characters from the stored alphabet. The independent audit checks every source path and reconciles the byte hashes, eligibility flags and eligible-prefix length histograms with the earlier census.

	Population	Entries	Entries containing ᛂ	Occurrences of ᛂ

	Eligible prefixes, every path	25,565	25,554	538,869

	Eligible prefixes, distinct bytes	25,563	25,552	538,842

	Short files, every path	341	280	4,035

	Short files, distinct bytes	281	280	4,035


[Image: Outside-alphabet symbol coverage across four populations, with exact counts: 25554 of 25565 eligible paths, 25552 of 25563 distinct eligible blobs, 280 of 341 short paths, and 280 of 281 distinct short blobs]
All bars use the same proportion scale. The short-file denominator includes empty files; their absence of characters is not a conversion result.

What the two counts mean

Entries containing a symbol counts each selected prefix once, even if the symbol occurs many times. Occurrences counts each appearance. Path weighting counts every filename; distinct-blob weighting counts byte-identical files once. Neither makes different editions of the same work statistically independent.

Eligible prefixes contain exactly 2,902 selected tokens. Short files contribute only their available tokens to a separate population. Empty files belong to that short-file population and contain no characters; their absence of an outside-alphabet symbol is not evidence about a conversion convention.

What this changes about the comparison

A one-for-one relabeling of an extra symbol leaves every token length unchanged. Deleting it changes lengths and can create empty token slots. Dropping those slots changes the denominator; refilling the prefix changes which text is selected. These are separate choices, not interchangeable ways to clean the data. The twelve-file sensitivity example shows the distinction with explicit counts.

This audit identifies a reproducible difference between symbol inventories. It does not establish an intended converter, recover edition provenance, identify the manuscript language or supply a decryption rule. It inspects selected prefixes, not every character in every full text.

Reproduce and inspect

Extract the reference-data ZIP with folders intact. Use Python 3, Git, the Liberpedia reference files and a local source repository containing the pinned Git objects. The pipeline runs offline and executes no code from the source repository. Use a new output directory:

python scripts/run_corpus_symbol_audit.py SOURCE_REPOSITORY --output symbol-audit

The measurement stage saves source identities and per-blob checkpoints. The independent checker uses a different tokenization implementation, rebuilds every symbol count, checks duplicate rows, and reconciles byte hashes, eligibility and eligible-prefix length histograms with the earlier census. Only after those checks pass does the export stage create the tables and figure. Retain the report and receipt together.

Every file and its symbol counts (CSV) · Symbol totals (CSV) · Population counts (CSV) · Complete report (JSON) · Independent verification receipt. The pipeline script and its dependencies are included in the reference-data ZIP. The external corpus Git objects must be obtained separately; see the pinned-corpus reproduction instructions.



The earlier twelve-file check

The pinned Project Runeberg repository contains 25,906 files under files. We checked the first twelve filenames in Unicode lexicographic order, taking each file’s first 2,902 nonempty space-separated tokens. This is a deterministic convenience sample, not a random sample or a check of all books. Every selected file has enough tokens.

All twelve prefixes contain ᛂ (U+16C2), which is absent from our stored 29-rune alphabet. The historical script measures each token with Python’s len, so that symbol contributes to its length. This does not establish that the conversion is wrong: it establishes that its symbol inventory differs from the manuscript alphabet used in our audit. Dropping or substituting the symbol would change the experiment and needs a documented conversion rule.

	Corpus file	U+16C2 occurrences in first 2,902 tokens

	10002-8.txt	15

	10003-8.txt	17

	10004-8.txt	17

	10005-8.txt	19

	10006-8.txt	10

	10007-8.txt	16

	10008-8.txt	14

	10011-8.txt	15

	10012-8.txt	12

	10013-8.txt	18

	10014-8.txt	51

	10016-8.txt	34


Within these prefixes, U+16C2 is the only character outside the stored alphabet; each occurrence is in a different token. A symbol-inventory difference alone does not invalidate a word-length comparison. If the converter intends this character to stand for one rune, a one-for-one relabeling leaves every token length unchanged. Determining the intended convention still requires the converter’s provenance.

Relabeling and deleting are different operations

We replayed two explicit variants on the same twelve prefixes. Replacing each out-of-alphabet character by one stored rune preserves every length, as expected. Deleting it shortens 10–51 tokens per prefix. This second variant illustrates the effect of filtering to the stored alphabet; it is not a proposed correction to the corpus.

For example, 10014-8.txt has 51 affected tokens in its first 2,902 token slots. The deletion variant removes 51 counted units and leaves six slots empty:

	Counting convention	Length 2	Length 3	Empty slots

	Original characters	668	498	0

	One-for-one relabeling	668	498	0

	Delete U+16C2; retain slots	669	516	6


The table retains the original 2,902 slots so that the comparison isolates character deletion. Dropping the six empty slots would change the denominator to 2,896; refilling the sample with later tokens would change its membership as well. Neither additional operation is included here. Across the twelve prefixes, deletion changes the length-two count by −1 to +5 and the length-three count by −5 to +18. A mean reduction or a histogram change is not itself a statistical significance result. The report retains both complete histograms for every file.

To reproduce, obtain a local clone of the pinned corpus repository, then run the command below from a Liberpedia checkout. The script reads committed Git bytes, avoiding checkout newline conversion. It does not execute the corpus’s code. A partial clone may need network access to fetch missing source blobs.

python scripts/audit_runeberg_prefixes.py /path/to/project-runeberg

Download the audit script · Download the file hashes, counts and exact alphabet. The full prefix census and descriptive comparison are now independently checked. This does not reproduce an unavailable conversion pipeline or validate historical probability claims.

File entries are not independent texts

A separate audit of the complete pinned Git tree finds 25,906 corpus paths but 25,844 distinct file-content objects. This inventory covers every path; it does not decode or compute statistics for every text. We read the three repeated objects and independently compared the bytes at all 65 paths in those groups.

	Repeated content	File entries	Tokens per file	Eligible for a 2,902-token prefix?

	Empty file	61	0	No

	11052-8.txt and 11502-8.txt	2	144,714	Yes

	13689-8.txt and 20041010-13689-8.txt	2	109,251	Yes


The historical minimum-length rule would exclude the 61 empty files. It would retain both members of each nonempty pair, counting the same prefix twice. These two extra eligible entries are a known weighting issue, not a measured explanation of the reported manuscript differences. The later complete prefix census checks all 25,906 paths and finds 25,565 eligible paths representing 25,563 distinct eligible blobs. The other 341 paths are too short under that token rule; the empty files are only part of that excluded group.

Byte identity is narrower than literary identity: different editions or conversions of the same work can have different bytes. Conversely, a filename alone does not establish an edition, language, author or source. The pinned tree contains only its short README and the corpus files; it does not contain conversion code or an edition manifest. This records what is present at that revision, not what may exist elsewhere.

A faithful historical replay should preserve its file-by-file weighting and report these duplicates. A deduplicated comparison should be a separate variant with an explicit rule. Neither version supplies independent random samples merely because many files are present.

Reproduce the inventory

python scripts/audit_runeberg_inventory.py /path/to/project-runeberg

The script reads committed Git metadata and one blob for each duplicate group; it does not run third-party code. A partial clone may fetch those blobs. The inventory report includes every duplicate path, object identifiers, SHA-256 hashes, byte sizes and the exact token rule. The raw NUL-delimited Git tree listing preserves the full path inventory. The audit script is included in the reference-data bundle. These checks do not reproduce the full corpus statistics or their reported probabilities.

What is needed for an English comparison?

The checked-in corpus script takes the first 2,902 space-separated tokens of each eligible text. It does not draw a random passage. Its call to process_word_counts omits the required word_count argument, so this revision needs repair before execution. The statistics script uses an inclusive left-tail comparison, distribution <= value. These details matter to an exact reproduction.

Liberpedia has reproduced the manuscript-summary match above and the complete pinned prefix comparison: 25,565 eligible file paths, 25,563 distinct eligible blobs, and all 23 measures under both weights. The independent checks cover source bytes and exact ranks; they do not validate reported language probabilities or an unavailable conversion pipeline. Further variants must freeze their corpus revision, conversion rules, exclusions and sampling method. Check whether introductory material remains, whether editions duplicate one another, and whether a first-passage sample represents the question you intend to ask. Changing to random passages would be a new variant.

A left-tail fraction asks how often a reference value is no greater than the observed value. A claim of excess needs an upper-tail comparison, with ties handled explicitly. Testing many lengths and statistics and reporting only the most striking difference introduces selection. Set the question, direction and selection correction before a new comparison; see null models and search space and bounds.

Two code repairs to declare before a replay

Our pinned-source code audit checks two specific defects. It uses small synthetic inputs and does not run the corpus or reproduce historical probability claims.

Supply the requested prefix length. In create_results(word_count), the call supplies only filepath and instance_name, although process_word_counts requires word_count too. Python argument binding rejects that call. The repair is process_word_counts(filepath, instance_name, word_count).

Use the dataframe passed to the helper. check_empirical_p(pr_df, lp_df, statistic) reads pg_df from global scope when calculating the corpus mean and tail fraction. Its supplied pr_df is unused. Without that global it raises NameError; with a different global it silently uses the wrong distribution. Replace those two pg_df references inside the helper with pr_df.

The default plotting entry point sets a global pg_df before calling the helper, so the second defect need not change that execution. It matters when the helper is reused or called with another distribution. This is a reproducibility hazard, not proof that the published numerical results are incorrect.

	Synthetic check	Inclusive left-tail fraction at 2	Mean used

	Supply [1, 2, 3], but global is [9, 9, 9]; original helper	0/3 = 0	9

	Same inputs; parameter repair	2/3	2


These are arbitrary test values, not observed word-length proportions. The inclusive comparison counts the tie at 2. The audit verifies the original source bytes against their Git blob identifiers, checks the missing argument, and extracts only the two arithmetic functions for the synthetic check. It does not import pandas, execute plots, or alter the archived source.

python scripts/audit_corpus_pipeline.py /path/to/lp_experiments/code

Use the pinned source directory. The audit script and saved report are included in the reference-data bundle. A changed source file is rejected rather than silently treated as the audited revision. A full replay still needs pinned package versions and explicit aggregation, quantile, missing-value and sampling conventions.

What does a length difference imply?

If a transformation emits exactly one rune for every input rune and leaves the boundaries fixed, it preserves token lengths. A substitution can change which runes occur without changing this histogram. But a mismatch with one prose corpus does not uniquely identify a length-changing cipher. Conversion choices, style, headings, number labels and boundary conventions may also affect the comparison. See cipher invariants.

The 464-word column-balance experiment concerns a different population and statistic: four solved LP1 sections arranged in sixteen columns. It does not establish an English baseline for the unsolved pages. Its within-section shuffle variant preserves each section’s length distribution; the section-order variant also searches every arrangement in both the observed data and the controls. They address different choices in the same LP1 comparison, rather than supplying three independent confirmations.

Reproduce the count and inspect every token

Extract the reference-data ZIP with its folders intact. Python 3 is sufficient; no corpus download, network access or third-party package is required for this audit.

python scripts/rune_word_lengths.py --check
python scripts/test_rune_word_lengths.py

The first command reconstructs the reports and chart. The second uses an independent character scanner and checks every token against its original source span. Both checks passed. The measurement script, summary and source hashes, token ledger, and pinned historical CSV can also be downloaded individually.

To rebuild the local generated files after a deliberate change, run python scripts/rune_word_lengths.py --write. A changed input or counting convention defines a changed measurement; retain its provenance and compare it separately.

LP2-18: how two tokens become a 17-rune candidate

A proposed Fibonacci connection used a 17-rune sequence with prime-value sum 987. The sum reproduces, but the archived transcription places a clause separator inside that sequence. Under this guide’s token rules it is two tokens, not one long word.

	Archived token	Runes	Prime-value sum
	ᛠᛞᛇᛉᚳᛠᚩᛟᛖ	9	565
	ᛗᛈᛒᚦᛝᛋᚢᛡ	8	422
	Artificial concatenation	17	987

The relevant archived span is below. The first token crosses a / line-boundary marker, which is removed when reconstructing a word across manuscript rows. The dot before the second token is a clause separator and must remain a token boundary:

ᛠᛞᛇᛉᚳ/
ᛠᚩᛟᛖ.ᛗᛈᛒᚦᛝᛋᚢᛡ

In the archived UTF-8 text decoded to Unicode, the first token starts at character offset 84, the dot is at 95, and the second token starts at 96. These offsets are zero-based; they refer to the exact archived text, before removing line markers. Inspect the transcription and the original page. This is a check of the archived notation, not a new manual verification of every mark in the image.

Reproduce the boundary and sums

Run this Python from the extracted reference-data bundle or repository. It checks the separator as well as the arithmetic, so a matching total cannot hide a changed input:

import json
from pathlib import Path

raw = Path('text/lp2-18.txt').read_bytes().decode('utf-8')
alphabet = json.loads(Path('data/index.json').read_text(encoding='utf-8'))['alphabet']
prime = {entry['rune']: entry['prime'] for entry in alphabet}
left = 'ᛠᛞᛇᛉᚳᛠᚩᛟᛖ'
right = 'ᛗᛈᛒᚦᛝᛋᚢᛡ'
joined_rows = raw.replace('/', '').replace('\n', '')
assert left + '.' + right in joined_rows
assert raw[95] == '.' and raw[96:104] == right
for token in (left, right, left + right):
    print(len(token), sum(prime[rune] for rune in token))
# 9 565
# 8 422
# 17 987

987 is a Fibonacci number, but here it is the sum of a deliberately joined pair. That fact does not make the pair a single word, prove its ordinal in a section, or establish a cipher key. A study of adjacent-token sums could include it legitimately if that population and boundary rule were declared in advance. It would need to include all eligible pairs, not only the pair with an appealing total.

The transcription-checking guide explains how formatting-only differences can change a word-based experiment while leaving the whole-page rune stream unchanged. For a different question, the Fibonacci opening experiment tests a specified sequence as shifts against fixed opening texts. Neither result settles every Fibonacci-based proposal.

Sources and status

Manuscript inputs are the archived LP2-00–55 transcription files, each hashed in the report. The historical summary and code are pinned to mae3301/lp_experiments, revision cb5cdb9. The referenced corpus is Project Runeberg, revision a39e87e; the prefix audit processes only the twelve specified prefixes, while the separate tree inventory covers every path and decodes only the three repeated content objects. Counts and the summary reconciliation were checked on 20 October 2026.


A short-header example: BEING and THUS

The LP2-39 header-crib experiment tests twenty proposed words against three red runes. BEING needs four or five runes under the exact stored GP labels: EI is not one of those labels. THUS can use three or four. After this length check, seventeen segmentations remain for a complete affine-key search. WHY fits one key, but the three-symbol fit does not establish the reading. The experiment retains every rejected candidate and explains what a test beyond the header would need to show.


Word-local ciphers and repetition

The word-reset repetition experiment uses a deliberately different selection: separate pages, omit each page’s first and last token, and compare the remaining ciphertext tokens of at least four runes. It finds no exact repeats under either apostrophe policy and only four anagram pairs, all length four. Its explanation distinguishes a shared deterministic word function from a shared symbol substitution followed by word-local shuffling. Neither result proves that the unknown plaintext must repeat.


Could the plaintext be another language?
The eight-language parallel-corpus experiment compares the same FLORES passages in English, Welsh, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and Finnish. English is closest by word lengths; the order of other close candidates changes with the symbol representation. The report separates this conditional ranking from IoC and repeated-letter comparisons, and includes source files, a chart and offline reproduction scripts. These scores do not identify the plaintext language.


For the limits of this language comparison on actual manuscript prose, see the known-LP reading control. Its pool and individual sections can rank differently. The equal-token control compares samples of exactly 2,896 tokens: English remains the manuscript’s nearest tested profile, but the manuscript is farther from each language profile than that language’s observed reference samples. The language-comparison overview explains how all four related records fit together.


Does the 464-word balance depend on mixing sections?

The section-preserving variant keeps the same observed arrangement but shuffles lengths only within each section’s original slots. It still finds low column-mean variance under that model: 88 of 49,999 trials are at least as flat, giving a plus-one lower-tail estimate of 0.00178. The shared-scale histograms and slot map show what changes from the unrestricted baseline.

This is sensitivity to a null-model assumption, not independent confirmation. Both comparisons use the same previously selected arrangement and neither preserves coherent sentences or accounts for the original search over arrangements.


The unchanged-rune audit separates ordinary fixed points from recorded interruptions across the four LP1 sections. An equal input and output index does not by itself show that the key counter paused.

The six-width comparison tests a separate choice in the solved 464-word arrangement. It selects the smallest normalized imbalance across widths 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 and repeats that selection in every shuffled control. Its 0.12072 tail applies to that rule; it is not an adjustment of the smallest fixed-width p-value.

How do the four sections combine?

A balanced total can conceal differences that cancel. For each column, take the rune count supplied by one section and subtract the number of its words in that column multiplied by the overall mean, 1,796/464 runes per word. This gives that section’s excess rune count. Positive bars contribute more runes than this reference predicts; negative bars contribute fewer. Adding the four bars for a column gives the combined column’s excess.

[Image: Four section panels and their combined total show positive and negative excess rune counts in sixteen columns, using the same vertical scale]
Each section stays in its original slots. The reference is the whole object’s mean, not a separately fitted mean for each section. Column counts can differ within a section; the audit retains those differences.

To quantify the addition, square each column’s excess and sum over the sixteen columns. The four section totals add to approximately 1,620.38 runes², while squaring after the sections have been combined gives exactly 501 runes². The difference comes from pairwise cross terms: opposite contributions cancel, while contributions with the same sign reinforce one another. This identity describes the observed arrangement; it is not a probability or a measure of deliberate design.

If a column receives +3 excess runes from one section and −2 from another, their separate squares sum to 13. Their combined excess is +1, whose square is 1. The missing −12 is the cross term 2 × 3 × (−2). The downloadable report applies this same identity to every column and all six section pairs, with exact fractions.

The combined value also checks against the original balance statistic: its saved integer score is 128,256, and 128,256/16² = 501. The earlier shuffle experiments assess particular chance models; this breakdown explains the arithmetic of the observed score without adding a new test.

Extract the reference-data ZIP, retain its folders, and run python scripts/audit_section_contributions.py --output my-section-contributions.json with Python 3. The script rebuilds the original word inventory, checks the column totals by direct ordinal assignment, and verifies every pair contribution through a direct word-pair expansion. It performs no random trials. Exact counts and contributions (JSON) · Audit script · Figure script.

The proposed 928-word carrier

The carrier and word-matching guide contains the complete LP2-23–39 inventory, group-boundary diagram, halfway split and downloadable audit. The total is 928 rune-words; five decimal labels are counted separately. A matching total does not specify a grille operation.

Can a word identify a unique position?

In the solved 464-word arrangement, 216 ciphertext positions have a word form that occurs elsewhere in the same object. The word-lookup audit explains the difference between distinct forms and ambiguous positions, with the full occurrence lists and a comparison to decoded rune text.


For the broader approach and its other variants, see the language and corpus identification guide.

title: Doublets and the 4–2–1 count pattern
summary: Locate all 86 equal adjacent rune pairs, compare boundary rules, and distinguish the observed count pattern from cipher and probability claims.
text:
A doublet is a pair of equal adjacent symbols, such as F–F. In a rune stream, adjacency depends on what you remove: two runes separated by a word boundary become neighbors if that boundary is discarded. A count should therefore state its alphabet, pages and boundary rules before drawing conclusions.

What the archived pages contain

Keeping only the 29 alphabet runes in LP2-00–55, including headings, gives 12,956 runes and 86 doublets. Windows overlap: F–F–F contributes two F–F pairs. LP2-50 contains no alphabet runes under this rule, leaving 55 nonempty page streams.

	Boundary rule	Adjacent pairs	Doublets	Rate
	Keep page boundaries	12,901	86	0.667%
	Join all filtered pages	12,955	86	0.664%

Joining the 55 nonempty streams adds 54 pairs; none is a doublet. This does not make the conventions interchangeable: they have different denominators and different shuffle models. Both remove non-runes within a page, so they can count pairs across words, lines, headings and paragraph breaks. Neither is a word-internal count.

The separator audit identifies exactly which of the 86 cross stored marks: 60 are contiguous rune characters, three cross only a row wrap, 22 cross a hyphen and one crosses other punctuation. Under the published rune-token convention, 63 of 10,028 within-token pairs match. Seven separately stored LP2 reviewed-text layers leave the 86 pair identities and these category counts unchanged; they are not a second complete transcription or a manual check of all source images.

The placement audit measures where those 86 events occur. Thirteen nonempty pages have none, close to the 12.25 expected when 86 events are placed among the actual pages' edge slots. The shortest gap between successive event starts is six runes; its conditional reference is near the upper edge, while page-count variation and first/last-page-edge counts are within their stated ranges. These placement controls do not model plaintext or a cipher.

[Image: Doublet counts in the 29-rune alphabet order; O R C, J EO P and OE D A each have counts 4, 2, 1. The total is 86.]
The observed diagonal of the bigram count table: each bar counts one rune followed by itself. Blue marks the three 4–2–1 groups. Download all counts and source locations.

The three 4–2–1 groups

The count vector, in the stored Gematria Primus alphabet order, is:

F U TH
4 2  4

O R C
4 2 1

G W H N I
5 6 2 4 2

J EO P
4  2 1

X S T B E M L NG
6 3 2 0 4 2 3  2

OE D A
 4 2 1

AE Y IA EA
 7 2  2  3

The three contiguous 4–2–1 windows begin at zero-based alphabet indices 3, 11 and 22. The groups have 3, 5 and 8 other alphabet entries before them when you count the initial segment and then the gaps between the groups. Their start-to-start distances are 8 and 11, not 3, 5 and 8. State which quantity you mean when discussing a Fibonacci pattern.

These counts reproduce the observation. They do not establish that 421 was deliberately encoded, that O–R–C is plaintext, or that a Fibonacci rule decrypts a page. Sorting by count or changing the alphabet order changes the pattern being inspected. A chance calculation must specify whether 421, this order, these gap lengths and this page set were fixed beforehand or selected after looking at the data.

The report identifies every occurrence by page, zero-based rune ordinal, original character offset, line and column. A location in a joined chapter or an alternative page order will have a different ordinal. Use the source coordinates before comparing an unexplained list of indices.

Low compared with which model?

For a stream of N runes with frequencies f₁, f₂, …, the probability that a particular neighboring pair matches under a uniform random permutation of those runes is Σ fᵢ(fᵢ−1) / [N(N−1)]. There are N−1 neighboring positions, so the expected total is Σ fᵢ(fᵢ−1) / N. Overlapping pairs need not be independent for this expectation: we add their individual expectations.

Shuffling within each page separately gives an expected total of 439.166, compared with the observed 86. Shuffling the entire joined stream gives 446.668. These are two different reference models. The script retains exact fractions as well as decimal approximations.

An expectation is not a p-value. This audit has not computed a tail probability, searched candidate ciphers or adjusted for selecting an interesting pattern. Randomly permuting runes also does not model English grammar, word boundaries or every possible cipher. See null models and selection before using the size of this difference as evidence for a particular explanation.

The short-lag profile asks whether the deficit extends beyond adjacent runes. Under fixed-count shuffles within pages, lag one has 86 matches against 439.17 expected, while lags two through five have 435, 434, 451 and 463 matches, each within its seeded shuffle reference band. That distinction is useful for evaluating a proposed mechanism: a model that suppresses all nearby repeats makes a different prediction from one that acts only on immediate neighbors.

Why ciphertext autokey comes up

For the specific additive rule Cᵢ = Pᵢ + Cᵢ₋₁ (mod 29), subtract the previous ciphertext value: Pᵢ = Cᵢ − Cᵢ₋₁. At every ordinary feedback step, Cᵢ = Cᵢ₋₁ exactly when Pᵢ = 0. Thus the number of internal ciphertext doublets equals the number of zero-valued recovered symbols at those steps.

This identity holds for any input stream decoded by that rule. Observing few zeros after this subtraction does not independently confirm autokey; it restates the original doublet count. The initial symbol depends on a stated initial value, and resets or interruptions change which positions obey the rule. In the wiki’s zero-based alphabet, F has value zero, but a different alphabet assignment would change that label.

The rule Cᵢ = Cᵢ₋₁ − Pᵢ has the same zero condition. The different rule Cᵢ = Pᵢ − Cᵢ₋₁ instead gives Pᵢ = 2Cᵢ₋₁ at a doublet. Names such as “subtractive autokey” are insufficient: write the equation. Multiplication introduces another condition: Cᵢ = PᵢCᵢ₋₁ makes a doublet imply Pᵢ=1 only when Cᵢ₋₁ is nonzero modulo 29. A zero state breaks that inference and cannot be inverted by division.

The existing F-reset and F-skip experiments test specified feedback and periodic-IoC rules on LP2-54–55. They do not test all mechanisms that could reduce doublets across LP2-00–55. Deletion, inserted separators, reordering and adaptive keys are different hypotheses requiring their own invertibility rules and bounds.

What independent uniform keys would predict

The uniform-additive-key experiment tests one precise model: each key is independently uniform on all 29 residues and independent of the plaintext. With the recorded page boundaries, it predicts about 444.86 adjacent matches; the observed count is 86. The exact inclusive lower tail is about 1.0708 × 10^(−98). The record supplies the binomial argument, an independent recurrence check, a distribution chart and a runnable bundle.

This is a different null model from shuffling fixed rune counts. It was examined after the low count was already known, and its tail is not corrected for historical feature selection. It is not a rejection of every random-key construction. The following running-sum equation illustrates why the actual cipher equation matters.

When a doublet would mean EA

Consider the specific running-sum rule Cᵢ = Cᵢ₋₁ + Kᵢ(Pᵢ − 28) mod 29, where plaintext EA has index 28 and each key value is in 1–28. This is a proposed equation, not an established Liber Primus cipher. It has an exact property: the ciphertext repeats its previous rune if and only if the current plaintext rune is EA.

A repeat makes the difference Cᵢ − Cᵢ₋₁ zero. Every nonzero value has an inverse modulo the prime 29, so Kᵢ(Pᵢ − 28) = 0 forces Pᵢ = 28. Conversely, Pᵢ=28 makes the product zero for every allowed key. This reasoning needs no assumption about whether keys are constant, periodic or random.

	Previous ciphertext	Key	Plaintext	Next ciphertext	Repeat?

	7	5	EA = 28	7 + 5(28 − 28) = 7	Yes

	7	5	E = 18	7 + 5(18 − 28) ≡ 15	No

	7	0, outside the model	F = 0	7 + 0(0 − 28) = 7	Yes, without EA


Applied to the archived within-page count, this model requires 86 EA events at the 12,901 measured transitions. Page-initial plaintext runes are not constrained by that count because the preceding state lies outside the measured page edges. This is a necessary condition, not a recovered plaintext and not a rejection of the model. In particular, uniformly selecting nonzero keys does not imply a repeat probability of 1/29: for this equation, repeating is determined by whether the plaintext is EA.

The assumptions matter. Allowing a zero key permits a repeat with any plaintext. Changing to a composite modulus also requires care: modulo 28, a nonzero key can lack an inverse. For the analogous offset-27 rule, key 2 and plaintext 13 give 2(13 − 27) ≡ 0 mod 28, despite 13 not being 27. An extra position-dependent output mapping, skipped positions or internal resets needs a separate analysis.

The downloadable doublet report checks all 23,548 combinations of previous state, plaintext and nonzero key modulo 29. The independent checker uses modular inverses and verifies both counterexamples. This is an elementary algebraic argument with a complete finite check, not a claim that the external formal-proof archive was rerun.

The EA frequency control now uses actual decoded GP indices from solved pages rather than guessing rune boundaries from ordinary English letters. Solved LP1 has 20 EA runes at 2,782 within-page transition positions (0.719%); the unsolved doublet rate is 86/12,901 (0.667%). These close rates meet a necessary frequency plausibility check, but do not validate this equation or a key schedule. That record also shows how erasing word boundaries creates eleven false EA labels and examines the difference IoC under a separate conditional model.

The nonzero-difference check tests the stronger assumption that every nonzero key is independent and uniform. Its residue histogram restates the earlier difference IoC at fixed zero count; its adjacent-difference count adds an order-sensitive comparison. Neither recovers a key or establishes which plaintext rune occurs at a doublet.

The doublet-context control examines the ciphertext symbols at all 86 events and the differences immediately beside them. The repeated ciphertext rune can be any GP symbol under the EA-stalling equation; it is not a plaintext EA label. The observed symbol collisions and before/after difference imbalance sit within a control that fixes the zero mask and each page's nonzero difference inventory. This is a check of local ordering, not another independent test of the marginal difference histogram.

Reproduce the counts

Download the reference-data bundle or use the repository. Python 3.12 and its standard library are sufficient. Run from the extracted root:

python scripts/rune_doublets.py --check
python scripts/test_rune_doublets.py

Counting and chart script · Independent checks · Counts and complete position ledger. Use --write to regenerate the report and chart. The report hashes all 56 text files and the alphabet index. Unknown Runic Unicode characters cause an error rather than disappearing silently.

The checker recounts pairs through overlapping regular-expression matches, verifies every recorded source coordinate, and compares the shuffle expectation against exhaustive permutations of small synthetic examples. These checks reproduce the archived transcription; they do not independently resolve ambiguous handwriting.

Distances between successive doublet symbols

A different analysis extracts one symbol from each doublet occurrence and asks how far apart successive extracted symbols are in the 29-rune alphabet. For example, aabcdeefgghijkll gives the event sequence a e g l. These distances concern alphabet positions, not the number of intervening runes on the page.

Using the archived LP2-00–55 inputs above, retain overlapping equal-rune pairs within each page, including headings and ignoring non-runes. Concatenate the resulting events in page order, then compare successive events. A triple occurrence such as AAA contributes two overlapping doublets and therefore two A events; it is not collapsed into one run.

	Quantity	Reconstructed value
	Doublet events	86
	Successive event pairs	85
	Pairs crossing a page boundary	41
	Sum of circular distances	734
	Mean circular distance	734 / 85 ≈ 8.635294
	Expected mean after uniformly shuffling these events	≈ 7.288098

For indices a and b, use d = min((b − a) mod 29, (a − b) mod 29). Its possible values are 0 through 14. A directed difference uses (b − a) mod 29 instead and can distinguish, for example, +5 from −5. Those are different statistics and should not be substituted for each other.

The reconstruction does not reproduce the proposed mean of 8.81. Its shuffled-order expectation does agree with the approximate 7.29 baseline. The proposal does not provide enough input and implementation detail here to identify the source of the mean difference. Consequently its quoted p-value is not adopted as a verified result.

What is being shuffled?

The expectation above holds the multiset of 86 extracted event symbols fixed and randomizes their order. It does not shuffle all manuscript runes and extract a fresh set of doublets. Those operations preserve different information and answer different questions.

If symbol a appears c(a) times among N events, the probability that two consecutive shuffled positions contain a then b is c(a) × (c(b) − [a = b]) / (N(N − 1)). Multiply each such probability by the circular distance and sum over all a,b. Every adjacent position pair has this expectation, so it is also the expected mean. The script checks the result independently by enumerating all ordered pairs of distinct event positions.

An observed mean above this expectation is a descriptive comparison, not a significance test. A permutation p-value needs the full distribution and a stated tail. If several lags, distance groups or boundary rules were tried before selecting the reported pattern, a confirmatory test must account for those choices. In particular, resetting event comparisons at page boundaries would remove 41 of the 85 comparisons and define a different measurement.

Inspect every comparison

python scripts/doublet_distances.py --check

Use the reference-data bundle with its folders intact. The script recomputes doublets from the archived text through rune_doublets.py. The complete JSON ledger preserves all 85 pairs, source positions, page-boundary flags, directed differences, circular distances, the histogram and input hashes. Run without options to print the report, or with --write to regenerate the stored JSON.

The event-lag experiment now recounts lags 1–3: lag three contains 10 forward +4 matches among 83 comparisons (12.05%), with 75 comparisons crossing page boundaries. The fixed-event shuffle expectation for +4 is 8/215 (3.72%). The experiment publishes all directed bins and distance-group counts, but does not verify the proposed significance levels. See null models and selection and search bounds.

[Image: All 29 lag-three directed differences, split by page boundary. Ten +4 matches comprise three within-page and seven cross-page comparisons; brown marks show shuffle expectations.]
Inspect the full lag-three distribution. Only eight comparisons stay within a page; 75 cross pages. Brown marks are expected counts, not significance thresholds. Complete results and plotting script.

Continue from the observation

Read n-grams for other repeated windows, lag matches for equal runes farther apart, and word lengths for the effect of token boundaries. A fixed reversible substitution renames symbols but preserves equality at each position; it cannot change the total number of doublets.

This is a descriptive audit with explicit comparison expectations, reproduced on 20 October 2026. No new cipher-search result or adjusted probability is claimed.


For one mechanism that can reduce visible repeats without removing plaintext symbols, see the homophonic-substitution example. Its invented alphabet illustrates a possibility; it does not identify the cause of these measured counts.

title: Night Thoughts: Young, Blake and a proposed book lookup
summary: Distinguish author, publisher, illustrations and editions; reproduce the 729-rune scope without treating a proposed book key as established.
text:
Night Thoughts is a proposed book source for further investigation, not an identified source of a Liber Primus passage or a demonstrated key. Its connection with William Blake makes it a reasonable work to inspect, but Blake’s involvement does not establish that the puzzle used this book.

Young, Edwards and Blake are different people

	Person	Role in the illustrated book
	Edward Young	Author of the poem
	Richard Edwards	Bookseller and publisher who commissioned the illustrations
	William Blake	Artist and engraver
	R. Noble	Printer of the 1797 edition

The Metropolitan Museum’s 1797 volume records these roles. Its catalogue describes a poem in nine sections, 537 watercolor designs, and 43 engravings published in the first installment. The planned continuation was not issued. A watercolor design, an engraved page and a later text edition are therefore different objects; “Blake’s version” is not an adequate identifier for a cipher input.

Inspect the illustrated volume and its images at the Met. For the terminology, see plates, impressions and copies. The separate Liber Primus cover guide identifies the Blake compositions proposed for that collage; those identifications do not identify Night Thoughts as its source.

What kind of text is it?

The 1853 edition transcribed by Project Gutenberg presents Young’s poem with a life, critical dissertation and explanatory notes by George Gilfillan. Its title page names James Nichol in Edinburgh, James Nisbet and Co. in London, and W. Robertson in Dublin. This is a later edited text, not the 1797 illustrated volume.

The passage around Night IV, line 729 considers reason and Christian faith in an argument about death and immortality. The line includes “Hold her sacred still,” referring to reason. The surrounding lines matter: selecting the phrase alone removes the argument it belongs to. A resemblance to Liber Primus themes such as knowledge or inner discovery is a comparison to examine, not a verified quotation. See testing knowledge and authority for the manuscript’s own statements.

The 729-rune proposal: what can be checked

One proposed lookup takes the rune count of LP2-00–02 and uses it as a line number in Night Thoughts. The manuscript-side count reproduces from the archived transcriptions when headings are included and every non-rune is removed:

	Page	Alphabet runes
	LP2-00	262
	LP2-01	266
	LP2-02	201
	Total	729

[Image: LP2-00, first page in the proposed 729-rune scope]
LP2-00 · 262 runes
[Image: LP2-01, second page in the proposed scope]
LP2-01 · 266 runes
[Image: LP2-02, third page in the proposed scope]
LP2-02 · 201 runes

To reproduce those counts using the repository or reference-data bundle, run:

python scripts/rune_ioc.py lp2-00
python scripts/rune_ioc.py lp2-01
python scripts/rune_ioc.py lp2-02

The reports include input hashes and counting conventions; the IoC guide explains their other fields. The sum 729 is both 27² and 9³, equivalently 3⁶. Those are properties of the same integer, not independent confirmations of a proposed source.

The Google Books volume supplied with the proposal remains an unresolved edition reference in this audit: its title page and pagination have not been verified here. Do not silently substitute the Gutenberg edition and claim to have reproduced its page numbers. A chapter or “Night” number, a printed page, a verse-line number and a scan-image number are different coordinates.

What a reproducible test still needs

Fix the source. Record the edition, exact copy or scan, and file hash. If using a modern transcription, identify it separately from the historical book.
Define the lookup. Specify which Nights are eligible, whether numbering restarts, and how headings, dedications, footnotes and wrapped lines are handled. “Line 729” can point to several passages when numbering restarts.
Freeze the extracted text. Preserve the full line and its neighbors, spelling and punctuation, before choosing a normalization or rune conversion. Distinguish extracting every eligible line from choosing the ones that sound relevant.
Name the cipher operation. A selected passage is not yet a key. Specify the algorithm, alphabet, direction, key phase, interruptions, target pages and success criterion.
Report all candidates. Include all tested Nights, editions and transformations, not only the most suggestive phrase. Separate a literal textual match from a statistical or cryptographic result.

A reported search of many books without the source files, extraction rules, candidate list and outputs cannot establish that this particular lookup has been tried. No such cipher-search result is reproduced on this page. Related starting points are search space and bounds, documenting an attempt, and the Emerson book-cipher control, where a specific source and explicit coordinates can be checked.

Sources and status

Met object 2021.164.2: the illustrated 1797 volume supports the production history. Project Gutenberg ebook 33156 supplies the later edition’s title page and poem text. These establish bibliographic facts and readable context; neither establishes use by the puzzle authors. The three manuscript counts were recomputed from Liberpedia’s archived text on 20 October 2026.

title: Hashes, addresses and retrieving the target
summary: Separate exact-byte checks, protocol encodings and network retrieval; understand what Tor chronology and GNUnet identifiers do and do not establish.
text:
The LP2-56 target gives a value to compare with a page’s hash. It does not directly supply a location or specify the page’s exact byte representation. Keep three questions separate: what is the content, how is it identified, and where can it be obtained?

Choose the question before choosing the test

	Question	What a test needs	What a negative result covers
	Does this saved file match?	Exact bytes, declared hash algorithm and target	Those bytes under that algorithm
	Does a specified protocol encoding match?	Exact file, encoder version, parameters and output field	That file and encoding
	Can this network identifier retrieve content?	A complete identifier, compatible client, bounded attempt and logs	That retrieval attempt under its recorded conditions

For example, encoding 75 manuscript images and 11 archived responses would be an 86-file candidate test if all inputs and operations were documented. Even a fully reproduced mismatch for all 86 would not establish that an unknown target cannot be hosted on the same network. Conversely, a retrieval timeout would not show that a correctly constructed candidate has the wrong digest.

Moving content does not necessarily change its hash

If two local files contain exactly the same bytes, the same deterministic hash algorithm produces the same digest for both. Their filenames and hosting addresses do not enter the calculation unless they are deliberately included in the input.

This gives a useful distinction for old puzzle material: a page’s original address might stop working while a byte-identical copy remains verifiable elsewhere. That is a possibility, not evidence that a copy exists. Visually similar pages are not necessarily byte-identical: a rewritten link, an inserted banner or a changed newline can alter the input. See checksums and the local candidate checker.

Onion versions and chronology
